title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
authors: Chubin Zhang,Bo An
abstract:
Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened.
Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step.
Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working.
We show that it does not.
On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist.
Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early.
We call this failure phantom progress.
It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other.
When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself.
We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress.
Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow.
Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory.
Across RoboMME’s released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed.
Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining.
A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.
introduction:
Many manipulation tasks cannot be solved from the current observation alone.
A robot asked to pick up a cube three times and then press a button sees much the same scene before its second pick as before its third, so it has to remember how many picks it has made.
Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies address this by conditioning each action on a memory of the episode so far [41, 44, 48, 11].
A simple and widely used way to fill such a memory is by time: the policy samples past frames uniformly over the episode and stamps each frame with its time step.
This design covers the whole episode at a fixed cost, and on RoboMME [11], a benchmark built to test memory, the strongest released policy uses exactly this design.

However, time passes even when nothing happens.
Real robots often wait for a slow planner, for an operator who has paused them, or for a safety monitor to clear.
They also hesitate, or reach for an object and come back empty-handed.
We call such an interval a null event.
It takes time, and the robot may even move, yet nothing the task depends on changes.
A memory that records what happened should therefore pass over a null event as if it had not occurred.
A memory filled by time cannot do so, because the interval receives its share of sampled frames and time stamps like any other stretch of the episode.
This raises a simple question:

We find that it cannot (Fig. 1).
On the two counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the released policy pause twice for 5 seconds, or roll its wrist back and forth for as long.
Success falls from 47 to 16 of 50 on PickXtimes and from 44 to 10 on SwingXtimes.
Almost every failure is an early stop, in which the policy presses the button before it has made the required number of repetitions.
The robot thus perceives progress that never happened.
We call this failure phantom progress.
One might suspect that the interruption itself disturbs the robot, for instance by leaving its arm in an unusual pose.
We therefore repeat each event with its frames withheld from memory.
The robot pauses or fidgets exactly as before, but its memory never sees the interval, and success returns to within three episodes of the baseline.
The failure therefore lies in what the policy remembers.

Why would a policy mistake waiting for working?
We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut.
Demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, so elapsed time alone predicts how many repetitions are done 89% and 80% of the time on the two tasks, and over 92% on regular demonstrations from two real teleoperation datasets.
Since demonstrations contain almost no idle stretches, imitation learning never penalises a policy for reading progress from time.
If the policy indeed reads progress from time, rescaling the time stamps alone should shift its failures in a predictable direction.
It does: with no null event and the frames unchanged, a faster clock makes the policy stop early, and a slower one makes it repeat (Sec. 5.2).
The obvious remedy is then to remove the time encoding.
Surprisingly, a policy trained from scratch without it still fails under pauses (21 and 14 of 50), because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of a memory sampled by time (Sec. 5.3).
The shortcut thus lies in how memory is indexed, and the time stamps are only one of its carriers.
Consistently, among RoboMME’s released designs, every memory indexed by time collapses under null events, a memory that selects tokens by pixel change is hurt less by pauses than by fidgets, and memories indexed by sub-goals withstand both null events on PickXtimes (Sec. 5.4).

The diagnosis also suggests where to fix the failure.
Training with injected pauses changes the data but keeps the index, so at best it can teach the policy to discount the null events that we know how to synthesise.
It does not even achieve this: pause augmentation does not remove the failure, and it impairs counting when no null event occurs.
Changing the index should work instead.
Indexing memory by events collapses every stretch in which the world returns to a state it was already in.
Applied at test time without retraining, it recovers half or more of the lost success under pauses, fidgets and air-grasps alike (Sec. 6).

We summarize our contributions as follows:

Phantom progress. Brief null events make memory VLAs that fill memory by time stop early, and the damage passes through memory alone. Comparing visible with hidden null events, together with rescaling the time stamps, gives a protocol for testing whether any memory policy tracks events or elapsed time (Sec. 4).

A shortcut in the index. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut that lives in how memory is indexed, so that removing the time stamps does not remove it, and we show that vulnerability follows the index across RoboMME’s released designs (Sec. 5).

Fixes suggested by the diagnosis. Pause augmentation does not remove the failure, whereas indexing memory by events recovers much of the loss without retraining (Sec. 6).

1. Phantom progress. Brief null events make memory VLAs that fill memory by time stop early, and the damage passes through memory alone. Comparing visible with hidden null events, together with rescaling the time stamps, gives a protocol for testing whether any memory policy tracks events or elapsed time (Sec. 4).

2. A shortcut in the index. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut that lives in how memory is indexed, so that removing the time stamps does not remove it, and we show that vulnerability follows the index across RoboMME’s released designs (Sec. 5).

3. Fixes suggested by the diagnosis. Pause augmentation does not remove the failure, whereas indexing memory by events recovers much of the loss without retraining (Sec. 6).

title: TanCRAFT: Context-Reasoned Anticipatory Feedback for Assembly Tasks
authors: Sassan Mokhtar,Lars Doorenbos,Marius Bock,Sina Mokhtar,Katharina Beckh,Dominik Bach,Juergen Gall
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
abstract:
Preventing human error in physical assembly tasks requires assistance systems that can intervene before mistakes are made. This is especially challenging in settings where users are free to choose the construction order and correctness depends on the evolving assembly rather than a fixed next step.
We present TanCRAFT, a four-stage real-time predictive assistance system that tracks the scene state, reasons about the current partial assembly, forecasts the near-future motion of manipulated pieces, and intervenes when the predicted placement is incompatible with the target.
We instantiate our framework and confirm its effectiveness in a controlled tangram assembly task through offline benchmarks and a within-subject user study.
Our findings show that the predictive feedback significantly reduces mistakes relative to unguided and reactive sessions, while yielding the lowest mean perceived workload and shortest mean completion time.
Overall, these results demonstrate the value of predictive feedback for error prevention and provide a step toward cost-aware assistance for automation and human-robot workcells.
introduction:
Human error remains a significant contributor to failures and quality defects in manual assembly, industrial production, and human-robot workcells [1, 2, 3]. While some mistakes are easily reversed, others are costly once completed. The cost therefore depends not only on whether errors are detected, but also on when. For example, a misplaced component or unsafe action may be easy to correct before commitment, but costly, time-consuming, or even unsafe after completion. This motivates the need for assistance systems that go beyond post-hoc error detection and are capable of real-time error forecasting and prevention.

Anticipating errors is challenging because systems must infer human actions, intentions, and potential mistakes from external observations. Moreover, anticipation alone is insufficient for assistance, as it does not address how a system should act to prevent the mistake.
In this context, previous predictive-assistance methods anticipate supportive robot behaviors or human assembly actions [4, 5]. TRAFA [6] extends prediction to proactive error feedback but operates in a sequential task with a fixed next correct action.
Still, many real scenarios, such as kit or furniture assembly, are far less constrained, letting users choose their own strategy, revise placements, and manipulate pieces without committing them. This freedom makes interaction more natural, but error anticipation substantially harder. To address this challenge, we propose TanCRAFT, a real-time predictive assistance framework for non-sequential assembly comprising four stages: Track, Reason, Forecast, and Intervene.

We instantiate the framework in a controlled tangram assembly task, which recently gained popularity in robotics assembly and manipulation tasks because it combines objective correctness with an open construction order, interchangeable pieces, and exploratory manipulation [7, 8], i.e., the same properties that make unconstrained assembly a difficult task.
Unlike prior works, where robots assemble the pieces, we use tangram to study predictive assistance to humans, as it provides a natural way to induce human error without the costs associated with a full industrial setup.
We validate our system through offline benchmarks, and evaluate the full system in a within-subject user study comparing two variants of TanCRAFT to unguided and reactive (post-hoc) feedback conditions.
The user study shows that predictive feedback significantly outperforms both no-feedback and reactive feedback baselines in mistake reduction, while also achieving the lowest mean perceived workload [9], the highest success rate, and the shortest mean completion time.

In short, the main contributions of this work are:

We introduce TanCRAFT, a real-time framework for predictive assistance in non-sequential assembly tasks.

We show through a user study that predictive feedback significantly reduces mistakes, while achieving the lowest mean workload and shortest mean completion time.

We will release the code, trained model weights, and multi-view tangram assembly dataset
upon acceptance.

1. We introduce TanCRAFT, a real-time framework for predictive assistance in non-sequential assembly tasks.

2. We show through a user study that predictive feedback significantly reduces mistakes, while achieving the lowest mean workload and shortest mean completion time.

3. We will release the code, trained model weights, and multi-view tangram assembly dataset
upon acceptance.

title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
authors: Ilia Larchenko,Gleb Zarin,Atindra Nair,Keerti Manney,Vitaly Kleban,Mirko Kiefer,Anjana Yodaiken
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: Code:this https URL; checkpoint:this https URL; project page:this https URL
abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution [1], which is based on π0.5\pi_{0.5} [10]. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392.
introduction:
The BEHAVIOR Challenge [4, 3] evaluates robot policies on long-horizon household activities in the OmniGibson simulator, built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The 2026 edition doubles the 2025 task set: 100 activities, from turning on a radio to cooking a meal, each with 200 teleoperated demonstrations (20,000 episodes, 211M frames or about 1,950 hours, in the LeRobot [6] format). The robot is the same Galaxea R1Pro: a holonomic base, a 4-joint torso and two 7-DOF arms with parallel grippers, observed through a head camera and two wrist cameras plus proprioception. An episode is a full success if all goal predicates are satisfied, which scores 1. Otherwise its q-score (we also call it Q) is the fraction of satisfied predicates. Scores are averaged over instances and then over tasks. The time limit of an episode is 1.5×\times the mean duration of the human demonstrations of the task (2×\times in 2025). The 50 tasks of 2025 are included with the same demonstrations; the other 50 are new.

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune a pretrained vision-language model to output robot actions [8]. The π0\pi_{0} family [9, 10] pairs a PaliGemma VLM [15] with a smaller “action expert” trained by flow matching [18] to generate chunks of continuous actions, optionally co-trained with discrete FAST action tokens [12]. Many alternatives have appeared since, such as GR00T [13] and, increasingly prominent, MolmoAct2 [14]. Yet more than a year after its release (paper in April 2025, code and weights in September 2025 [11]), π0.5\pi_{0.5} is still widely used as a base for fine-tuning: both top 2025 BEHAVIOR solutions were built on it [1, 7]. We built our 2026 solution on top of our 2025 one, so we kept its π0.5\pi_{0.5}-based architecture. For this reason, in parts of this report we call our learned policy simply π0.5\pi_{0.5}.

A second line of work uses large language models to control robots directly: by choosing among learned skills [27], writing control code [28], or orchestrating a low-level policy. With frontier models that can use tools for hours, this has become a practical option in simulation. GPT-6 Astra [29], released in September 2026, was strong enough to solve some BEHAVIOR tasks that our learned policy could not, so our final submission routes 14 tasks to an Astra-based agent (Section 9).

Our 2025 solution [1] won the first BEHAVIOR Challenge. It took π0.5\pi_{0.5} and changed the following: trainable task embeddings instead of text prompts, correlated noise for flow matching, a learnable mixture of all VLM layers’ keys and values for the action expert, a stage-prediction head with voting (“System 2”), a FAST auxiliary loss, several flow samples per VLM forward pass, and correlation-aware inpainting at inference. The 2025 checkpoints were clearly undertrained: the loss was still falling when the deadline came, and four checkpoints split the 50 tasks between them. The LeHome Challenge solution [2] of one of our team members was built on top of the 2025 BEHAVIOR solution and introduced several engineering fixes and improvements that we inherit here as well. The 2025 runner-up [7] also starts from π0.5\pi_{0.5} and studies the effect of image resolution, of the training data and of rejection-sampling fine-tuning.

A recipe for growing a task-conditioned VLA from 50 to 100 tasks without retraining from scratch: semantic stages from skill annotations, similarity-based initialization of new task and stage embeddings, and a 21-dimensional action space matching teleoperation controls (Section 3).

A recipe for growing a task-conditioned VLA from 50 to 100 tasks without retraining from scratch: semantic stages from skill annotations, similarity-based initialization of new task and stage embeddings, and a 21-dimensional action space matching teleoperation controls (Section 3).

Registers, scratch tokens and attention sinks at several levels of a VLA; moving the pretrained SigLIP attention-sink outliers into the registers by parameter surgery on a running training made the attention maps readable (Section 4).

Variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching and a way to choose the number of flow samples from one gradient-noise measurement (Section 5).

An evaluation infrastructure that makes cross-cloud rollouts inspectable and reusable through provenance, diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators per GPU faster than real time in aggregate (Section 7).

An LLM agent route with GPT-6 Astra for 14 tasks where the learned policy is weak and the agent performed better (Section 9).

Code and models. Code: https://github.com/Robot-Learning-Collective/behavior-1k-solution-2026. Checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/IliaLarchenko/BEHAVIOR2026VLA. The 2025 checkpoint we start from: https://huggingface.co/IliaLarchenko/behavior_submission. Project page, including evaluation videos and visual examples: https://robot-learning-collective.github.io/behavior-1k-2026/.

1. A recipe for growing a task-conditioned VLA from 50 to 100 tasks without retraining from scratch: semantic stages from skill annotations, similarity-based initialization of new task and stage embeddings, and a 21-dimensional action space matching teleoperation controls (Section 3).

2. Registers, scratch tokens and attention sinks at several levels of a VLA; moving the pretrained SigLIP attention-sink outliers into the registers by parameter surgery on a running training made the attention maps readable (Section 4).

3. Variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching and a way to choose the number of flow samples from one gradient-noise measurement (Section 5).

4. An evaluation infrastructure that makes cross-cloud rollouts inspectable and reusable through provenance, diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators per GPU faster than real time in aggregate (Section 7).

5. An LLM agent route with GPT-6 Astra for 14 tasks where the learned policy is weak and the agent performed better (Section 9).

title: SIGMO: Sigmoid Gated Interaction-Aware Motion Planning
authors: Avinash Singh,Manish Saroya,Fatemeh Cheraghi Pouria,Faizan Tariq,Jovin D'sa,David Isele,Yosuke Sakamoto,Sangjae Bae
abstract:
Despite the widespread adoption of autonomous vehicle technologies, reliable navigation within cluttered environments remains arduous due to the necessity of interaction-aware strategies; example scenarios include: narrow passages with multiple agents, lane changing in dense traffic, and crossing unsignalized intersections. These scenarios often require highly proactive strategies, simultaneously demanding interpretability and quick adaptability, which challenge end-to-end and data-driven methods. An effective strategy requires: scalability to multiple agents, adaptability to changes in other agents’ behavior, and harmony with surrounding traffic without freezing or becoming overly conservative. To meet these requirements, we present SIGMO, a sigmoid-gated interaction-aware motion planner, with two main contributions. First, we formulate polynomial sigmoid functions that analytically estimate yield scores of surrounding agents using physics-grounded interaction features that capture driving intuitions. Second, we integrate the polynomial sigmoid functions into a receding-horizon planner, which facilitates interaction-aware planning with arbitrary trajectory predictions. We validate SIGMO in interaction-intensive  simulations and hardware experiments. The results show that SIGMO balances proactive and defensive behavior while remaining computationally lightweight, serving as a strong baseline in a mobility stack. The simulation and hardware experiment videos are available here:
 https://sites.google.com/view/sigmoid-polygate.
introduction:
Autonomous vehicles have progressed from research prototypes to commercial deployments, yet reliable navigation in cluttered, interaction-intensive environments remains challenging. Representative scenarios include traversing narrow passages shared with multiple agents, merging into dense traffic, and crossing unsignalized intersections. In such settings, classical robust planning is often insufficient because there may be no independently “safe” gap into which the ego vehicle can progress without interacting with other agents. Instead, the ego vehicle must negotiate: proactively encouraging other agents to yield while remaining defensive when they do not. Overly conservative behavior can result in the well-known “freezing robot” problem [1], whereas overly aggressive behavior can compromise safety. An effective planner must therefore (i) scale to multiple agents, (ii) adapt rapidly to changes in other agents’ behavior, and (iii) remain compatible with surrounding traffic while providing interpretable decisions.

A substantial body of work has investigated interaction-aware planning. Game-theoretic approaches [2, 3, 4] explicitly model the mutual influence among agents, but their computational complexity can grow rapidly with the number of participants, limiting scalability. Learning-based methods, including end-to-end policies [5, 6, 7] and reinforcement learning (RL) [8, 9, 10], are attractive for capturing complex interactive behaviors. However, limited interpretability, reliability, and robustness to distribution shift remain significant barriers to deployment in safety-critical settings [11, 12]. Optimization-based planners augmented with neural interaction predictors, such as NNMPC [13, 14] and IANN-MPPI [15], provide another approach by explicitly evaluating how other agents may respond to candidate ego actions within a receding-horizon framework. Nevertheless, these methods require repeated inference of a prediction model, often a recurrent neural network, conditioned on individual candidate rollouts. Consequently, their computational cost grows with both the number of samples and the number of agents. Moreover, their learned interaction models may generalize poorly beyond the behaviors and agent types represented in the training data. Thus, a lightweight and interpretable mechanism for estimating an agent’s willingness to yield, without repeated action-conditioned inference and without assuming a particular prediction model, is still needed.

To address this gap, we present SIGMO, a sigmoid-gated interaction-aware motion planner, with two main contributions. First, we introduce polynomial sigmoid functions (“Polygate”) that analytically map physics-grounded features (time-to-collision, recent acceleration, relative velocity, path priority, and body proximity) to the probability that a surrounding agent yields. The formulation captures intuitive driving behaviors through interpretable features, and its parameters, namely the inflection point and sharpness, have a direct physical interpretation and require minimal tuning.
Second, we integrate Polygate into a sampling-based receding-horizon control framework, Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [16], where the estimated yield probability modulates an interaction-aware risk term. Polygate is evaluated from geometric features of each candidate rollout rather than from a prediction model conditioned on it, so it avoids the repeated inference required by prior approaches [13, 15] and remains compatible with any choice of prediction model. This enables efficient interaction-aware planning while retaining an interpretable decision mechanism.

We evaluate SIGMO in interaction-intensive simulated scenarios, including narrow-passage negotiation with pedestrian crossing and merging into dense traffic. We then conduct the generalizability analysis with MetaDrive [17] initialized by Waymo Open Dataset [18]. We demonstrate SIGMO with a 1/10 scaled F1Tenth racecar in a merging scenario. The results demonstrate that SIGMO balances proactive negotiation and defensive behavior in various scenes while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Gaussian Process-Augmented Model Predictive Contouring Control for 6-DoF Trajectory Tracking with a Holonomic AUV
authors: David Dörner,Giancarlo Troni,Ignacio Torroba,Ivan Stenius
abstract:
Small, holonomic Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) enable close-range inspection of underwater structures from arbitrary viewpoints, requiring accurate position and attitude tracking under state and input constraints. Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) naturally handles these requirements, but relies on an accurate dynamics model, which is difficult to obtain underwater.
In this paper, we present a nonlinear MPCC in all six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) for a holonomic AUV and alleviate the inaccuracies in the dynamics by augmenting the nominal model employed with residual dynamics learned via Gaussian Process (GP) regression.
The learned residual is embedded in the optimal control problem through a zero-order robust optimization scheme, which keeps the controller real-time capable at 25 Hz.
A simulation ablation shows that residual selection is essential when designing the controller, and simulation and in-water experiments with the Multimodality, Observing, Low-cost, Agile (MOLA) AUV validate the resulting controllers against a nominal MPCC and a field-proven Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller.
introduction:
Close-range inspection of underwater structures such as wrecks, pipelines or mines requires precise maneuvering and the ability to observe a target from multiple viewpoints.
Torpedo-shaped Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), such as the Kongsberg Hugin and the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) LRAUV, are well suited to surveying large areas, but their limited maneuverability makes these inspection tasks challenging for them.
Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) are commonly used for such tasks, but they require a support vessel and crew for operation.
Small, holonomic AUVs, such as the Multimodality, Observing, Low-cost, Agile (MOLA) AUV of MBARI, offer an autonomous alternative: they can control position and attitude independently, allowing them to maintain a desired viewing direction while moving around a target.
Exploiting this capability, however, requires a controller capable of following complex position and attitude references while respecting state and input constraints for safe operation near underwater structures.

Model Predictive Control (MPC) [24] naturally incorporates these requirements by solving a constrained optimal control problem over a receding horizon.
However, its performance relies on an accurate model of the system dynamics, which is a challenge in itself for AUVs: the hydrodynamic parameters are hard to identify and change with environmental and mission-specific conditions, such as different payloads.
Recent works therefore apply learning-based methods to improve the model used in the MPC [1, 2], but they either restrict the dynamics to four Degrees of Freedom (DoF) or remain validated in simulation only.

In this paper, we close this gap with the following contributions:

We present a nonlinear Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) in all six DoF that exploits the holonomic actuation of the AUV to track position and attitude references independently. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-time deployment of such a scheme on a holonomic AUV.

We augment the nominal model with Gaussian Process (GP) residual dynamics, embed them into the MPCC via a zero-order robust optimization scheme, and show in a simulation ablation that the choice of which residuals to learn is decisive for the resulting performance.

We validate the controllers in-water on the MOLA AUV against a well-tuned Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller and demonstrate improved attitude tracking on a lawnmower survey as well as a spiraling inspection maneuver.

1. We present a nonlinear Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) in all six DoF that exploits the holonomic actuation of the AUV to track position and attitude references independently. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-time deployment of such a scheme on a holonomic AUV.

2. We augment the nominal model with Gaussian Process (GP) residual dynamics, embed them into the MPCC via a zero-order robust optimization scheme, and show in a simulation ablation that the choice of which residuals to learn is decisive for the resulting performance.

3. We validate the controllers in-water on the MOLA AUV against a well-tuned Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller and demonstrate improved attitude tracking on a lawnmower survey as well as a spiraling inspection maneuver.

title: ForeseeDrive: Future-Token Conditioning for Anticipatory Generative Driving
authors: Shaokai Wu,Xunchu Zhou,Pinzhi Wang,Bo Dong,Yuting Hu,Yanbiao Ji,Qiuchang Li,Xiao Cui,Qi Kong,Hongtao Lu,Yue Ding
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Generative driving planners can represent diverse ego futures, but a downstream scorer can choose only among sampled candidates; it cannot recover an absent maneuver. We present ForeseeDrive, which turns future scene evolution into a deployable interface for shaping candidate generation. Rather than reconstructing dense future states or scoring a fixed menu, ForeseeDrive derives query-indexed tokens from logged actor motion, occupancy evolution, route interactions, and TTC margins, and predicts the same token space from present context at deployment. The tokens condition trajectory geometry before candidates materialize. A zero-token-gated residual path and candidate-preservation loss limit unnecessary drift, while a TTC-margin guard targets brittle safe-to-unsafe boundary crossings. Under their respective benchmark protocols, ForeseeDrive reaches 89.2 PDMS on NAVSIM navtest, 0.41 m average L2 and 0.05% collision rate on nuScenes validation, and a 76.50 driving score on Bench2Drive. Controlled DiffusionDrive/NAVSIM diagnostics show an exact zero-token no-op, a small aligned-over-shuffled selected-PDM advantage under preservation, mixed oracle-best quality, and localized TTC-boundary failures. Together, the benchmark results and bounded mechanism tests support future-conditioned generation as a practical interface for anticipation. Code is included in the supplementary materials.
introduction:
Autonomous driving planning maps recent observations, map context, and route goals into safe, progressive ego motion [1, 43, 4, 48, 2, 8]. Recent end-to-end and generative planners reduce brittleness by representing multiple ego futures rather than committing to one trajectory [6, 15, 21, 29]. Yet a generative planner can still fail even when the appropriate behavior is clear in hindsight. The challenge is not only uncertain interaction: the planner must instantiate ego modes before those interactions fully unfold. Once a candidate set is materialized, a downstream scorer can only reorder sampled trajectories; it cannot recover a yielding, braking, nudging, or passing maneuver absent from that set. As Figure 1 illustrates, anticipation can therefore fail as a support-allocation problem before it becomes a ranking problem.

This view exposes a mismatch between future prediction and trajectory generation. Existing future-centric methods demonstrate the value of actor forecasting, occupancy/BEV prediction, and future-aware planning [10, 22, 13, 31, 53, 55, 52]. A dense rollout, however, describes the scene broadly, whereas a generator needs compact future evidence that changes which ego modes receive probability mass. Conversely, future-aware scoring introduces anticipation only after the candidate menu is fixed and remains bounded by sampled support. What is missing is a deployable, planner-facing future representation that acts before candidate materialization.

We propose ForeseeDrive to provide this interface. Its central idea is to distill future scene evolution into compact tokens that answer action-relevant planning queries and enter the generator before sampling. During training, logged actor motion, occupancy changes, route interactions, and time-to-collision (TTC) margins supervise the token space; at deployment, a predictor estimates the same variables using only present observation history, map, and route. The predicted tokens can reshape trajectory geometry and mode allocation rather than only the final scores of a fixed set.

The resulting representation is queryable and action-facing: tokens answer local planning questions rather than reconstruct every actor state or BEV cell. They capture whether an actor is becoming route-relevant, whether a reachable corridor will be contested or cleared, and whether an interaction lies near a TTC-sensitive boundary. This makes the representation lower-dimensional than a dense rollout, richer than a scalar risk score, and better aligned with generative planning decisions.

Generation-time future conditioning creates a second tension: the signal must be expressive enough to move candidate modes, yet restrained enough not to corrupt strong candidates from a pretrained planner. ForeseeDrive resolves this tension with an architectural zero-token no-op, candidate preservation, and a margin-aware TTC guard. The preservation loss limits nonzero-token drift when future evidence is weak or irrelevant. The guard targets narrow safe-to-unsafe boundary crossings rather than imposing a broad clearance preference, which would also penalize controlled interactions [37, 7, 8].

Experiments evaluate both benchmark performance and the proposed mechanism. On NAVSIM navtest, ForeseeDrive reaches 89.2 PDMS and 83.5 EP; on nuScenes validation, it attains 0.41 m average L2 and 0.05% collision rate; and on Bench2Drive, it reaches a 76.50 driving score and 53.06 success rate. Same-backbone diagnostics then separate generation from selection: zero tokens exactly preserve the base candidates, aligned tokens modestly outperform shuffled tokens on selected PDM under preservation, and TTC replay localizes boundary-crossing failures. Oracle-best quality remains mixed, so we interpret these diagnostics as evidence for controllable support allocation, not universal support expansion.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate anticipation in generative driving as a support-allocation problem and expose the structural limit of fixed-candidate future-aware scoring. Second, we introduce a deployable future-token interface that distills logged future evolution into queryable, action-facing variables and injects them before candidate materialization. Third, we develop a restrained integration strategy with exact zero-token preservation, base-candidate regularization, and a TTC-margin guard; we evaluate it across three benchmarks and use controlled diagnostics to separate fixed-menu scoring, mode selection, and generation-time conditioning.

title: From Prediction to Action: Learning Physical Context for Deformable Linear Object Manipulation
authors: Chengxiao Dong,Alessio Caporali,Hongyu Lan,Gianluca Palli
abstract:
A representation that accurately predicts a deformable object’s response is not necessarily the one most useful for choosing manipulation actions. We study this distinction between predictive utility and decision utility in planar single-grasp shape control of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs). As a common decision backbone, we introduce Geometry–Pointer–Flow (GPF), a geometry-grounded policy that separates grasp-location selection from grasp-conditioned motion generation.
Its geometry-only variant reduces one-step executed shape error by 32.8% relative to a DLO-specific diffusion policy, while using 18.7×\times fewer parameters and achieving approximately 193×\times faster inference.
On this backbone, we compare physical context represented by ground-truth parameters, estimated parameters, and learned interaction-history representations, for both forward prediction and executed control.
For prediction, ground-truth physical parameters reduce next-shape error by 15.8% over geometry alone, and estimated parameters are slightly more predictive than interaction history. This ordering does not carry
over to control: estimated parameters provide no detectable one-step control gain, whereas history-conditioned GPF reduces executed error by 9.9% relative to geometry-only GPF across 470 paired simulation trials. In closed loop, interaction history improves strict-threshold attainment in simulation and yields the strongest zero-shot performance on hardware.
All policies are trained exclusively in simulation and transferred to the physical robot without real-world training or fine-tuning.
These results show that physical context should be evaluated by the decisions it supports rather than by predictive accuracy alone. Code will be released upon acceptance.
introduction:
Deformable linear objects (DLOs), such as cables, ropes, hoses, and wires, are challenging to manipulate because similar geometries can respond differently to the same action due to variations in stiffness, friction, and interaction history [1]. Effective manipulation therefore requires reasoning about both geometry and physical response.

This has motivated two complementary directions: learning DLO dynamics models to predict action outcomes
[2, 3, 4], and
conditioning manipulation policies on explicit physical parameters or
learned latent representations [5, 6].
More broadly, online system identification and rapid adaptation exploit similar information to adapt control under changing physical conditions [7, 8, 9].
Throughout this work, we use the term physical context to denote information that characterizes how the object responds to interaction, whether through explicit parameters or learned latent representations.

This raises a fundamental question about the role of physical context: is the information that best predicts an object’s response also the information most useful for choosing how to manipulate it? The two objectives may not align: a representation may be highly informative for next-state prediction yet less useful for action selection if it does not preserve control-relevant information. This distinction is closely related to control-oriented system identification, where improved predictive accuracy does not necessarily yield improved control performance [10].
For learned policies, an additional challenge is how physical context is represented and integrated into the policy.

In this work, we distinguish between the predictive utility of
physical context, namely its ability to improve prediction of an action’s outcome, and its decision utility, namely its ability to improve action selection.
We study this distinction in planar single-grasp DLO shape manipulation by comparing three physical-context representations (Oracle, Estimated, and Hist) against a geometry-only baseline.
Unlike the explicit parameterizations, interaction-history context is not constrained to recover predefined physical quantities and can retain information from recent action–response history. Predictive utility is evaluated with a separate forward-response model, while decision utility is evaluated through a learned manipulation policy. Fig. 1 summarizes the study: controlled simulation (a) generates alternative physical contexts (b), whose predictive and decision utility (c) are compared (d) before real-world zero-shot evaluation (e).

We study this question primarily in simulation using AGX Dynamics
[11, 12], which provides controlled physics-based interactions and known material and contact parameters for comparing physical context in prediction and control. To assess decision utility without imposing a predefined physical model, we condition a common learned policy on each context and evaluate executed control. The resulting framework compares explicit parameters and interaction representations by how well they support action selection. We instantiate it with Geometry–Pointer–Flow (GPF), a geometry-grounded policy that separates where to grasp the DLO from how to move the selected grasp-point.

Our evaluation first establishes GPF as a strong manipulation backbone, then compares the predictive and decision utility of physical context. Context that improves prediction does not necessarily benefit action selection: Estimated parameters substantially improve forward prediction but provide no detectable executed-control gain, whereas interaction-derived history context gives the strongest observed control performance among deployable representations.
We finally evaluate zero-shot transfer from simulation to real-world DLO manipulation, without real-world policy training or fine-tuning.

To summarize, the main contributions of this work are:

Predictive versus decision utility of physical context.
We compare explicit physical parameters, estimated parameters, and interaction-history context across prediction and control, showing that improved response prediction does not necessarily translate into improved action selection.

Predictive versus decision utility of physical context.
We compare explicit physical parameters, estimated parameters, and interaction-history context across prediction and control, showing that improved response prediction does not necessarily translate into improved action selection.

A geometry-grounded policy for DLO manipulation.
We introduce GPF, which separates grasp-location selection from
motion generation and provides a common backbone for
evaluating the decision utility of alternative physical contexts.

Interaction-history adaptation and zero-shot validation.
We show that history-derived context improves strict-threshold attainment in simulation and transfers zero-shot to the physical robot, where it yields the strongest closed-loop performance among the deployed controllers.

We compare explicit physical parameters, estimated parameters, and interaction-history context across prediction and control, showing that improved response prediction does not necessarily translate into improved action selection.

2. A geometry-grounded policy for DLO manipulation.

title: Elastic-WAM: Adaptive Spatiotemporal Imagination for Efficient Robot Control
authors: Haitian Li,Tianfu Li,Xuxi Zhao,Zizheng Liu,Yangcheng Yu,Yiwen Hou,Zeyu Xiao,Mutian Xu,Ziqian Yang,Haonan Chen,Lin Shao
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
World-Action Models improve robot control by predicting future visual dynamics, but iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference overhead.
Recent approaches reduce this cost through partial future denoising, yet typically rely on fixed refinement budgets.
Our empirical observations reveal that preferred refinement depths vary across tasks and states, while different future regions exhibit varying relevance to action generation.
Motivated by these findings, we propose Elastic-WAM, which adaptively allocates world refinement computation across temporal denoising time and spatial future space.
A unified spatiotemporal refinement demand field governs when to stop world refinement, how far to advance each denoising step, and which regions to refresh.
We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes, and learn it through a three-stage action-grounded supervised procedure.
At inference, the learned field guides recurrent sparse world refinement to improve task success while reducing inference overhead.
Evaluations across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world long-horizon manipulation demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance with reduced inference latency.
Project page: https://lihaitian.com/Elastic-WAM
introduction:
World-Action Models (WAMs) have shown that predicting future visual dynamics can improve robot control [37, 3, 1, 31, 9].
However, iterative denoising of future videos incurs substantial inference overhead [2, 20].
Recent studies show that intermediate video representations can already support action prediction without complete denoising [25, 24, 19].
Explicit video generation can even be removed at inference while retaining future prediction as a training objective [40].
Nevertheless, these approaches typically adopt a fixed future refinement budget, regardless of the current task or execution state [13, 10].
Consequently, a fixed budget may waste computation in some states while limiting action quality in others [30].

To investigate this limitation, we examine how future video refinement affects downstream action quality across different tasks and states on 10 selected tasks from LIBERO-Plus benchmark [12].
As demonstrated in Fig.  (a.1), the number of denoising steps yielding the highest success rate varies from one to four.
Even within the same task, different states favor different refinement depths, as shown in Fig.  (a.2).
Beyond refinement depth, action-to-video attention maps reveal uneven attention across future video regions (shown in Fig.  (a.3)), motivating selective refinement of regions most relevant to action generation [38].
Together, these observations motivate adaptive allocation of world refinement computation across both temporal denoising time and spatial future video regions.

To this end, we propose Elastic-WAM, which models the demand for world refinement through a unified spatiotemporal field, as illustrated in Fig.  (b).
Its total mass governs when to stop world refinement, its temporal profile determines how far to advance each denoising step, and its spatial variation identifies which future video regions to refresh.
We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes that separate global refinement demand from relative regional priorities.
We learn this field through three stages of action-grounded supervision, progressively optimizing the temporal profile, relative spatial priorities, and overall refinement demand.
At inference, we start with a dense joint denoising step, use the learned field to guide subsequent sparse world refinement, and continue action denoising after world refinement stops.

We evaluate Elastic-WAM across in-distribution [21], out-of-distribution [12, 49], and more complex manipulation simulation benchmarks [4], as well as a real-world long-horizon tea preparation task.
Our results demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance among methods without large-scale embodied pretraining, while reducing inference latency by 32.2% compared with Joint-WAM on RoboCasa-GR1, as shown in Fig. (c).

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate adaptive world refinement through a unified spatiotemporal demand field, jointly governing when to stop, how far to advance, and where to refresh future video representations.

We develop an action-grounded supervised learning framework and recurrent sparse inference strategy, enabling adaptive refinement with a frozen WAM backbone.

We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, while substantially reducing inference latency.

1. We formulate adaptive world refinement through a unified spatiotemporal demand field, jointly governing when to stop, how far to advance, and where to refresh future video representations.

2. We develop an action-grounded supervised learning framework and recurrent sparse inference strategy, enabling adaptive refinement with a frozen WAM backbone.

3. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, while substantially reducing inference latency.

title: Koopman Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
authors: Wenjian Hao,Paulo C. Heredia,Shaoshuai Mou
abstract: We propose a Koopman model-based reinforcement learning (K-MBRL) algorithm for controlling nonlinear robotic systems with unknown dynamics. The K-MBRL learns a control policy by minimizing an approximate policy objective that combines the analytical immediate cost with an estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step predicted state. To this end, we develop a stochastic Koopman operator-based learning method to approximate the unknown nonlinear dynamics in a linear representation, while a critic function estimates the remaining future cost. This formulation offers two key advantages. First, the linear Koopman dynamics simplify the model-dependent policy gradient computation to a constant matrix product, enabling computationally efficient policy improvement. Second, one-step model propagation mitigates the accumulation of prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts while retaining long-term cost information through the critic. The learned policy enables real-time control through feedforward evaluation without online optimization. We establish policy learning convergence guarantees under standard stochastic approximation assumptions. Simulations on HalfCheetah and quadruped four-legged locomotion tasks demonstrate strong sample efficiency and improved performance compared with classical model-free and model-based reinforcement learning baselines. A pendulum swing-up task is used to assess policy gradient approximation accuracy and conduct ablation studies on the learning mechanism and key hyperparameters. The proposed K-MBRL is further validated on a physical quadruped robot performing a challenging sequence of maneuvers: rising to an upright posture supported by two rounded rear feet, maintaining balance during bipedal walking, and safely returning to the ground, as shown in Fig. 1.
introduction:
Learning-based control has become a promising approach for controlling complex robotic systems whose system dynamics are unknown or difficult to model accurately. In particular, reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of robotic tasks (Kober et al., 2013), including legged locomotion (Hutter et al., 2016) and manipulation (Li et al., 2024). Many of these advances rely on model-free RL (MFRL) (Sutton and Barto, 2018), which avoids explicit dynamics modeling but typically requires substantial interaction data for policy learning (M. Moerland et al., 2023). Such policies are often obtained in simulation before deployment on physical robots. In contrast, classical model-based optimal control methods, such as the linear quadratic regulator and model predictive control (MPC) (Anderson and Moore, 2007), can achieve effective closed-loop control without training data when accurate system dynamics are available. However, obtaining accurate dynamics models for robotic systems remains challenging due to nonlinearities, underactuation, intermittent contact, unmodeled actuator dynamics, and variations in payload and terrain (Spong et al., 2006).

Model-based RL (MBRL) enjoys both benefits of MFRL and model-based optimal control by learning the dynamics from interaction data and using the learned model for policy improvement (Doya, 2000). Its improved sample efficiency over MFRL
makes it a promising approach for robotic control applications where collecting physical interaction data is costly. Many existing MBRL methods rely on multi-step model propagation for policy gradient estimation and optimization (Sutton, 1990; Deisenroth et al., 2011; Janner et al., 2019) or online planning (Nagabandi et al., 2018; Chua et al., 2018; Hansen et al., 2022; Askari et al., 2025). Along these methods, prediction errors can accumulate over the rollout horizon, leading to inaccurate cost estimates and potentially biased policy gradients (Tanaka, 1996). Moreover, the nonlinear deep neural networks (DNNs) commonly used for dynamics learning (Hernandaz and Arkun, 1990; Draeger et al., 1995) can make repeated model propagation and differentiation computationally expensive, particularly for online policy improvement on physical robots (Nan et al., 2026).

Observation of these two limitations motivates us to develop a new framework for MBRL based on the following two key ideas. First, we approximate the policy gradient by combining the immediate cost with a critic-function-based estimate of the remaining future cost evaluated at the one-step predicted state, which aims to mitigate the accumulation of model prediction errors while retaining long-term cost information, as also explored in model-based value gradient methods (Heess et al., 2015). Second, we introduce a deep Koopman model (DKM) to approximate the unknown dynamics based on the Koopman operator and deep neural networks (DNN). This is motivated by that Koopman operator theory (Koopman, 1931) offers a promising approach to represent nonlinear dynamics well through a linear representation in a lifted space, and also by recent advances in using DNNs to search suitable lifting functions (Morton et al., 2018).
These considerations motivate the integration of policy learning with one-step predictions from linear Koopman dynamics for efficient policy optimization.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

A Koopman model-based reinforcement learning (K-MBRL) algorithm is developed for iterative policy optimization of nonlinear systems. The optimal policy is approached iteratively along with approximating the system dynamics and estimating the policy objective. The algorithm approximates the policy objective by combining the analytical immediate cost with a state-action critic estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step state predicted by the learned deep Koopman model (DKM). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to integrate stochastic DKM learning with state-action critic-based policy optimization. The linear DKM facilitates policy gradient computation, while one-step propagation mitigates the accumulation of model prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts.

The proposed K-MBRL algorithm is validated through simulations on complex nonlinear robotic systems and challenging indoor and outdoor bipedal locomotion experiments on a physical quadruped robot, demonstrating improved control performance, faster convergence, and lower computational cost compared with baseline methods.

Policy convergence guarantees of K-MBRL are provided in the presence of coupled dynamics and critic updates under a fixed-dataset setting. The analysis further characterizes how dynamics and critic approximation errors affect policy convergence, providing theoretical insights into policy learning under both perfect and imperfect approximations.

Notation. We use ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| to denote the Euclidean norm. For a matrix A∈ℝn×mA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, ∥A∥F\parallel A\parallel_{F} denotes its Frobenius norm, and A′A^{\prime} represents its transpose.

The algorithm approximates the policy objective by combining the analytical immediate cost with a state-action critic estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step state predicted by the learned deep Koopman model (DKM). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to integrate stochastic DKM learning with state-action critic-based policy optimization. The linear DKM facilitates policy gradient computation, while one-step propagation mitigates the accumulation of model prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts.

title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics
authors: Qinfeng Zhu,Weiguang Zhao,Ke Sun,Xihao Guo,Yunxi Jiang,Rui Zhang,Lei Fan,Kaizhu Huang
abstract: Foundation models such as GPT and Claude have shown strong capabilities in spatial understanding and embodied intelligence. These advances make agentic robotics a promising path toward artificial general intelligence in robotics. However, we find that using foundation models to control robots poses serious safety risks, and comprehensive safety evaluation is still lacking. We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. Its 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs. In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop. We evaluate six state-of-the-art foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7. These models generally show high harm rates. We also evaluate two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API and PokeBot’s RoboAPI. We further propose the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH), which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics and can be integrated into nearly any agentic architecture. LEASH leverages a decision model (Jev or OpenAI’s Decisions API) to implement task, action, and commit gates, which review the task, each action, and each irreversible operation in their visual context. The planner and all three gates share a common safety policy. Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces harm across all six foundation models. It largely preserves their task completion performance and adds little time and token overhead.
introduction:
“Every agentic robot is a good puppy,
until you walk it without a leash.”

Achieving artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a central goal of research in embodied intelligence. Several research directions have emerged in recent years, including vision-language-action (VLA) models [77, 29, 6, 24] and world action models (WAMs), which jointly predict future observations and actions [28, 67, 31, 54]. However, generalization remains a major challenge for these approaches. Multimodal foundation models benefit from scaling both data and model size [19] and exhibit strong generalization. This makes them well suited to serve as a robot’s “brain” for task planning [2, 22, 32, 21]. The release of GPT-6 Astra [42] has sparked growing interest in agentic robotics. Researchers have found that it can control robotic arms in a zero-shot setting [72, 74] and achieve high-quality results on complex tasks such as drawing. Despite slow execution, high token costs, and limited dexterous manipulation [39, 65], researchers see agentic robotics as a promising path toward AGI in robotics.

Although agentic robots have become far more capable, their safety has received much less attention. Despite the strong reasoning of foundation models, are the agentic robots built on them actually safe? We see three reasons for concern. First, classical robot safety enforces explicit constraints during planning and execution [30, 17, 52, 7]. Such methods may produce a collision-free trajectory for a robotic arm while still allowing it to place an electronic device in water. Agentic robots plan and act in open scenes, so they face many more of these semantic hazards. Second, robot control with foundation models is becoming easy to deploy, so unsafe behavior can quickly reach real users. Leading models, including GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok, support plug-and-play robot control, and researchers have developed harnesses that make such control more effective [13, 73, 9]. Third, existing safeguards fall short. Foundation models and their harnesses include safeguards, such as automated review in the Codex harness [40], but these safeguards are not designed for the three-dimensional physical world. Studies of the safety boundaries of robot control with foundation models [23, 49, 48, 55] consider limited scenarios and focus mainly on task-level safety. As the epigraph suggests, an agentic robot is a clever and lovely puppy. Yet even the cleverest puppy can run wild, so we should always walk it on a leash.

To evaluate these risks, we introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for safety in agentic robotics. RoboRisk includes 92 tasks in simulation and 13 tasks on physical robots. The tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs (Supp. Table S3). In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop, in simulation and on a physical robot.

Figure 1(a) shows Claude Opus 5.5 dropping a phone into a bowl of water, and Fig. 1(b) shows GPT-6 Astra carrying a cup of milk over a power strip. We conduct an extensive evaluation of six leading foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT-6 Astra [42], GPT-6.1 Sol [44], GPT-6 Luna [43], Claude Opus 5.5 [4], Gemini 4 Argon [14], and Grok 4.7 [61]. The results in Fig. 1(c) reveal substantial safety risks across all six models, with Harm Rates (HRs) ranging from 9.06% to 76.92%. Our evaluation also includes two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API [12] and PokeBot’s RoboAPI [46]. In addition, we observe an unexpected sim-to-real gap [58], which we term the Human-Presence Gap. Some foundation models become overly cautious when people are present in physical robot settings. They struggle to balance task execution with human-robot collaboration, whereas they proceed smoothly in similar scenes in simulation.

To address these risks, we put the puppy on a leash: the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH). LEASH is a model-agnostic safety layer that can be integrated into nearly any agentic robotics architecture. It leverages the Jev decision model or OpenAI’s Decisions API [41] to implement three safety gates: a task gate, an action gate, and a commit gate. Unlike existing safeguards that mainly check text, these gates ground every review in the current camera images and supervise the whole agentic loop, from the task to each action and each irreversible operation. The planner and all three gates share the same safety policy. LEASH treats the planner as a black box and requires no retraining, so it can protect new commercial models as soon as they are released. Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces HR. Like a good leash, it does so without spoiling the walk: task completion is largely preserved, and the extra time and token costs are minimal.

Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. It covers five risk categories with 92 tasks in simulation and 13 tasks on a physical robot.

We propose LEASH, which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics. It combines two simple, broadly applicable, and effective components: safety gates and a shared safety policy.

We evaluate six leading foundation models and, for the first time, two robot-specific APIs on RoboRisk. LEASH reduces HR for every planner while preserving task success, and we identify a Human-Presence Gap between simulation and the physical robot.

1. We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. It covers five risk categories with 92 tasks in simulation and 13 tasks on a physical robot.

2. We propose LEASH, which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics. It combines two simple, broadly applicable, and effective components: safety gates and a shared safety policy.

3. We evaluate six leading foundation models and, for the first time, two robot-specific APIs on RoboRisk. LEASH reduces HR for every planner while preserving task success, and we identify a Human-Presence Gap between simulation and the physical robot.

title: Model-Free Runtime Measurement of Task-Relevant Information
authors: Dimitris Panagopoulos,Adolfo Perrusquía,Yang Xing,Weisi Guo
comment: extended data tables, appendix included. Code available
abstract: Autonomous systems increasingly monitor physical kinematics, environmental states and task completion outcomes. While existing work provides methods to plan information seeking actions and interpret acquired observations, current approaches do not monitor whether the live process of information gathering is functioning properly. Consequently, such systems can remain operationally active without resolving outstanding mission requirements. To address this limitation, we introduce Acquisition-State Telemetry (AST), a model free architecture that evaluates ongoing information acquisition from observable evidence relative to declared task requirements. Specifically, a domain interface maps raw observations into task resolution coordinates and normalized comparative representations, which are processed by a fixed causal monitor. This monitor emits two continuous real time signals that quantify (i) prospective progress across unresolved requirements and (ii) informational friction generated when recurrent evidence yields negligible informational gain. We evaluated a single, unadjusted monitor configuration across eight diverse domains including search and rescue dialogue, spatial grid exploration, hierarchical capability acquisition, continuous robotic manipulation, and probabilistic intent estimation. We show that across these domains the friction channel distinguished unproductive stagnation from purposeful exploration prior to task completion, while remaining muted during post completion activity. Furthermore, in closed loop reinforcement learning experiments under early termination constraints, we demonstrate that penalizing informational friction allowed agents to sustain high mission success, whereas unpenalized policies and baselines with matched operational costs failed to complete required tasks.
introduction:
Autonomous cyberphysical systems mostly monitor physical kinematics, environmental surroundings, and binary task completion outcomes [1]. In particular, sensors track physical trajectories and actuators measure mechanical loads, whereas downstream success metrics record whether an objective was achieved. However, the ongoing process of acquiring the information required to achieve those objectives remains unmonitored at runtime. When operating in dynamic or incompletely modeled environments, an autonomous agent can sustain continuous operational activity while making no material progress toward its mission requirements [1]. For example, a search and rescue conversational assistant may repeatedly question witnesses without clarifying the coordinates of a missing person [2, 3, 4]. Similarly, a mobile robot may explore a partitioned environment while traversing repetitive loops [5, 6] and a probabilistic estimator may ingest continuous observations without resolving ambiguity among competing hypotheses [7, 8, 9]. Because conventional monitors track operational activity rather than information acquisition, systems displaying identical levels of activity can follow fundamentally different epistemic trajectories (Fig. 1).

Current decision-making and diagnostic paradigms do not solve this problem because each addresses a different operational level. Within the observe–orient–decide–act (OODA) framework [10], information acquisition contributes to orientation, where observations acquire meaning relative to operational goals. Methods in active sensing, Bayesian experimental design, and information seeking optimize action selection by predicting future information gain [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. However, these policies assume their forward observation models are dependable and lack mechanisms to verify whether the actual runtime gathering process is yielding progress. Conversely, conversational breakdown detectors and interaction quality estimators assess surface level coherence and retrospective outcomes [19, 20, 21, 22, 8, 23, 24, 25], but they rely on domain specific heuristics that cannot generalize across heterogeneous physical or algorithmic systems. Similarly, intrinsic motivation and curiosity driven exploration incorporate novelty bonuses into reinforcement learning [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 2, 31, 32]. Although they reward environmental novelty, they do not verify whether that novelty resolves declared mission objectives. This leaves a critical gap that directly motivates this study. Specifically, we lack a real-time, independent monitor that can continuously track whether incoming evidence is actually satisfying task requirements, completely separate from the policy gathering it.
Developing such an independent observer presents a fundamental conceptual challenge. In classical control engineering, separating state estimation from feedback control is achieved through observers such as Kalman and Luenberger filters, which rely on known physical dynamics to infer internal states from sensor measurements [33, 34]. However, modern autonomous systems span vastly different domains and share no common physical laws.

To bridge this divide, we introduce Acquisition-State Telemetry (AST), a model-free monitoring framework that adopts declared task requirements, rather than physical dynamics, as the invariant reference frame. By decoupling domain semantics from monitoring logic, AST models interaction as a trajectory through a task-referenced coordinate space. A domain-specific interface projects incoming evidence into cumulative resolution scores across declared requirements alongside normalized representations for temporal comparison. A fixed causal monitor then processes this sequence to emit two continuous runtime channels: (i) prospective progress across unresolved requirements and (ii) informational friction, which detects recurrent evidence when ongoing activity fails to advance open objectives.

We evaluated a single, unretuned monitor configuration across eight diverse experimental substrates spanning human dialogue, spatial grid exploration, capability unlocking, continuous robotic manipulation, and internal Bayesian intent estimation [35, 36, 37, 5, 38, 39, 9]. The experiments establish three primary empirical findings. First, informational friction reliably distinguishes unproductive stagnation from purposeful information-seeking across both linguistic and physical domains, while remaining muted during post-goal actiity. Second, the measurement remains robust when substituting expert human scoring with automated language model ensembles. Third, in closed loop reinforcement learning under early termination constraints, penalizing informational friction enables agents to complete mission requirements, whereas unpenalized policies and operational cost baselines fail due to persistent looping. Together, these results demonstrate that task-referenced acquisition telemetry provides a domain-agnostic foundation for runtime epistemic supervision in autonomous systems.

title: DexSeed: Expanding Human Hand-Object Interactions into Robot Demonstrations for Dexterous Policy Learning
authors: Huaijin Pi,Zehong Shen,Yong Wang,Kechun Xu,Changpeng Wang,Dingkun Wei,Xueyang Wang,Wenjia Wang,Xing Zhu,Yujun Shen,Taku Komura
abstract:
We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning.
Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples.
Meanwhile, human hand–object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions.
Turning these interactions into VLA training data further requires coverage of different objects and manipulation locations, together with executable arm and finger actions, and visual observations.
To achieve this, we present DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot data from human hand–object interactions.
Our key idea is to expand human sequences while preserving their grasps and realizing the resulting motions under arm-tracking dynamics in physics simulation.
Specifically, we organize source sequences by grasp mode with shared language descriptions.
InteractionMesh-based retargeting and arm trajectory augmentation adapt these sequences to the robot hand, different object geometries, and pick-and-place locations while preserving local hand–object relationships.
An RL finger-control policy produces executable rollouts, while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories.
Rendered observations and recorded actions from successful rollouts are paired with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA.
Experiments show improved contact fidelity in retargeting and more reliable whole-arm execution than the evaluated baselines.
Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment further demonstrate that a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated demonstrations can execute language-specified grasps.
Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DexSeed/.
introduction:
Dexterous hands enable robots to manipulate objects through coordinated finger motion and rich hand–object contacts.
Vision-language-action (VLA) models learn to map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, providing a framework for learning manipulation skills from demonstrations [1].
Applying these models to dexterous manipulation requires diverse robot data that capture coordinated arm and finger actions together with visual observations and language instructions.
In this work, we study how to generate physically executable robot demonstrations at scale to support dexterous VLA learning.

Existing demonstration-generation methods expand robot datasets across object poses, scene layouts, and motion trajectories, but typically rely on teleoperated demonstrations as their starting point [2, 3, 4].
Collecting these source demonstrations is costly for dexterous hands, as teleoperation requires coordinating many joints while maintaining stable hand–object contact [5, 6, 7].
Reusing existing human hand–object datasets offers an alternative source of diverse manipulation behaviors without collecting new teleoperated demonstrations [8, 9].
Retargeting and physics-based imitation methods transfer these interactions to robots by addressing differences in hand morphology and contact dynamics [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16].
Expanding these transferred interactions into VLA training datasets requires varying object geometries and manipulation locations while retaining the demonstrated grasps.
Such variations can alter hand–object contacts, and arm-tracking errors during execution can further disrupt the intended interaction.
The resulting demonstrations must therefore preserve the grasp across these variations and provide physically executable arm and finger actions paired with visual observations.

To address this need, we propose DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot demonstrations from human interactions.
Our key idea is to organize human interactions by grasp, expand them while preserving hand–object relationships, and obtain executable demonstrations through reinforcement learning with the robot arm included in simulation.
Specifically, we group human sequences by grasp similarity and select representative modes, each paired with a shared description of how to grasp.
InteractionMesh-based retargeting [17] first adapts the sequence to the robot hand and compatible object geometries while preserving local hand–object relationships.
We combine the resulting hand references with whole-arm pick-and-place trajectories for different object starting positions and placement targets.
To realize these references under arm-tracking dynamics, we train an RL finger-control policy in IsaacLab [18] while the robot arm tracks precomputed joint trajectories, allowing the policy to learn finger corrections under the resulting wrist-tracking errors.
We render observations from the policy’s successful rollouts and pair them with the recorded robot actions and corresponding grasp descriptions to form training demonstrations.
The resulting data are used to fine-tune a VLA that jointly controls the arm and fingers to execute language-specified grasps.

We select 8 representative grasp modes from the GRAB dataset [8] and use 19 source sequences from these modes to generate a robot-centric dataset of 25270 demonstrations.

We further show that a dexterous VLA fine-tuned exclusively on our simulation-generated demonstrations with rendered observations can be deployed on a real robot without collecting real-robot action demonstrations.

We develop an InteractionMesh-based data generation method that preserves hand–object interactions during retargeting and transfer across different object geometries. For each source sequence, a physics-based imitation policy is jointly trained on its augmented references to obtain executable robot rollouts.

We construct a robot-centric dataset of 25270 demonstrations from 19 human sequences spanning 8 representative grasp modes, and demonstrate its utility through simulation evaluation and real-world deployment of a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated data, without real-robot action demonstrations at deployment.
