title: A human-in-the-loop Control Paradigm for Construction Robotics: From VR-Guided Teleoperation to Semi-Autonomous Dual-Arm Operation
authors: Jinhua Chen,Xiaoji Xu,Zhongyuan Liao,Huang Zhenmin,Zhang Ye,Changying Xiang
abstract: Construction tasks in hazardous and unstructured environments require both human adaptability and robotic precision, yet existing approaches often treat teleoperation and autonomy as separate control modes. This paper presents a human-in-the-loop control paradigm that enables structured transitions among VR-guided teleoperation, semi-autonomous shared control, and rule-based autonomous execution for contact-rich dual-arm construction tasks. The proposed system combines immersive VR guidance, a manually defined library of reusable skill primitives, and a shared-autonomy framework with explicit human–robot role allocation and command-priority rules. This integration allows operators to retain supervisory and corrective authority while delegating repetitive and precision-critical actions to the robot. The paradigm is validated on a dual-arm platform through representative façade-installation tasks. Results show that autonomous execution provides the best performance under well-calibrated nominal conditions, whereas semi-autonomous control improves resilience when environmental disturbances exceed the predefined autonomous pipeline’s correction capability. Semi-autonomous control also substantially reduces subjective operator workload compared with full teleoperation. These findings demonstrate that effective construction-robot control should adapt human involvement to task and environmental uncertainty, using autonomy for repeatable operations and shared control for disturbance recovery.
introduction:
The construction industry is undergoing a profound transformation driven by automation and robotic technologies. Rising labor costs, stringent safety regulations, and accelerated urbanization have intensified the demand for solutions that enhance productivity while reducing occupational risks. In this context, robotic systems are increasingly viewed not only as tools for task execution, but as enablers of new human–robot collaboration paradigms capable of operating safely and effectively in complex construction environments [19].

Many construction operations, including structural assembly, surface maintenance, component installation, and on-site inspection, require dexterous dual-arm manipulation [2] comparable to human bimanual coordination. These tasks are typically performed in unstructured and hazardous settings such as high façades, outdoor scaffolds, and mechanically or thermally unstable sites. The present study is motivated by such high-altitude façade work, but all physical validation is conducted in a controlled laboratory mock-up rather than at height. Prolonged manual operation under such conditions increases physical fatigue and accident risk, highlighting the need for robotic systems that can combine precise manipulation with adaptability and operational reliability [24].

While industrial robots have achieved a high level of autonomy in structured factory environments [22], directly transferring these capabilities to construction sites remains challenging. Fully autonomous control is often impractical due to uncertain geometries, variable material properties, and accumulated perception and localization errors. At the opposite extreme, pure teleoperation imposes a high cognitive burden on operators and scales poorly to multi-stage or bimanual tasks. These limitations motivate human-in-the-loop approaches that explicitly integrate human spatial reasoning and decision-making with robotic precision and repeatability [11].

Despite recent progress in shared autonomy, two critical challenges remain. First, it is difficult to design autonomous control strategies that are sufficiently robust and generalizable to handle diverse contact-rich construction tasks such as drilling, screw fastening, and bracket assembly in dynamic environments. Second, effective construction robotics requires a control paradigm that supports transparent, safe, and flexible transitions between human guidance and autonomous execution, rather than treating teleoperation and autonomy as disjoint modes.

To address these challenges, this paper proposes a human-in-the-loop control paradigm for construction robotics that enables a structured transition from VR-guided teleoperation to semi-autonomous dual-arm operation. Within this paradigm, immersive VR interfaces provide intuitive human guidance and situational awareness during complex or uncertain task phases, while recurrent task patterns are encapsulated into autonomous skill primitives. A shared-autonomy framework allows smooth blending and switching between human input and autonomous execution, enabling reliable handling of critical contact phases in high-risk construction operations.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A task-level human/autonomy allocation framework for multi-stage, contact-rich dual-arm construction operations, enabling structured transitions between VR-guided teleoperation, semi-autonomous shared control, and rule-based autonomous execution under predefined conditions.

A dual-arm robotic system integrating immersive VR guidance with a manually defined rule-based skill library for drilling, bracket placement, and screw fastening.

A shared-autonomy formulation with skill-level control weights, explicit command-priority rules, and Subtask Allocation Ratio (SAR) analysis for quantifying human–robot role allocation.

A physical evaluation of drilling, bracket pick-and-place, and
dual-arm screw fastening, including N=10N{=}10 novice operators in TeleOp and
Semi-Auto, unmanned rule-based Auto repetitions, environmental-robustness
testing for drilling, and a drilling-task Raw NASA-TLX assessment of subjective workload.

2. A dual-arm robotic system integrating immersive VR guidance with a manually defined rule-based skill library for drilling, bracket placement, and screw fastening.

3. A shared-autonomy formulation with skill-level control weights, explicit command-priority rules, and Subtask Allocation Ratio (SAR) analysis for quantifying human–robot role allocation.

title: RedirectMimic: Local Motion Content Redaction for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
authors: Zepeng Wang,Xiaochuan Shi
abstract:
Humanoid motion interfaces should accommodate application-specific movement constraints while retaining useful reference behavior. Local content redaction requires a controller to replace selected movements even when it continues to receive the original reference. Removing the tracking incentive for those movements leaves their replacement unspecified. We introduce RedirectMimic, which separates the reference observed by the actor from the target used to train its execution. A rule-generated edited reference guides tracking rewards during proximal policy optimization, while the deployed observation and action interfaces remain unchanged. We evaluate pose- and speed-defined arm editing in Unitree G1 simulation using a tracker pretrained on 7,509 motion clips. On the overhead-arm task, RedirectMimic reduces core-window content occurrence to 2.7%, compared with 58.9% for reward zeroing and 32.8% for anti-tracking. It achieves 94.2% core-window joint success, combining content suppression, fall-free execution, and local retention. On the speed-defined task, fast outward arm movements occurred at similarly low rates under all three local editing methods. Across both tasks, RedirectMimic achieved the lowest replacement error among these methods and tracked unedited motions with accuracy comparable to that of the pretrained controller.
Project page: https://xiaopeng-whu.github.io/RedirectMimic/.
introduction:
Motion tracking provides a practical interface between human demonstrations and humanoid control, including whole-body teleoperation and data collection [1, 2]. Physics-based imitation methods learn diverse motor skills from reference trajectories [3, 4, 5], and large motion collections broaden the behaviors available to a controller [6]. Faithful reproduction, however, is not always the desired deployment behavior. A reference may contain an arm movement that a particular application excludes, embedded within otherwise acceptable locomotion or gestures. This calls for selective editing that replaces the specified movement while retaining the rest of the motion.

Figure  illustrates this local objective. The controller must execute a suitable replacement while maintaining balance and the surrounding movement. Arm motion and balance are dynamically coupled: a local joint edit can affect torso and leg execution even when their reference coordinates remain unchanged. Useful redaction therefore combines content suppression, replacement fidelity, and physical retention.

Recent work studies selective behavior modification in humanoid policies [7] and motion generators [8, 9], as well as learned policy redirection [10]. Local humanoid editing couples this objective to the preservation of surrounding physical behavior. The resulting control question is how a tracker can learn a chosen replacement while its input continues to request the original movement.

We address this question with RedirectMimic. An offline rule constructs a paired reference (m,m~)(m,\widetilde{m}), preserving the root trajectory and all unedited joint coordinates. During fine-tuning, the actor continues to observe mm and the robot state, while tracking rewards use m~\widetilde{m}. Ordinary proximal policy optimization (PPO) [11] updates the existing actor and critic. An edit-window start distribution increases exposure to the sparse replacement objective. At deployment, the actor retains the original observation and action interfaces.

The central distinction is between suppressing a movement and specifying its replacement. Reward zeroing removes the incentive to track the selected arm, whereas anti-tracking rewards deviation from it. Neither objective specifies where the arm should go. In G1 simulations of pose- and speed-defined edits, the arm followed the prescribed replacement more closely when that trajectory guided training.

Our contributions are threefold:

Local redaction under original-reference inputs. We formulate selective motion replacement as policy editing, requiring the controller to retain surrounding motion while its input continues to specify the original behavior.

Paired-reference policy fine-tuning. We introduce RedirectMimic, combining rule-generated tracking targets and edit-window sampling to train local replacements under the original-reference observation interface.

Evidence for explicit replacement targets. Matched comparisons in G1 simulation show the highest overhead-arm joint success and lowest replacement error across both tasks among local methods. Trajectory analysis distinguishes faithful replacement from threshold suppression.

1. Local redaction under original-reference inputs. We formulate selective motion replacement as policy editing, requiring the controller to retain surrounding motion while its input continues to specify the original behavior.

2. Paired-reference policy fine-tuning. We introduce RedirectMimic, combining rule-generated tracking targets and edit-window sampling to train local replacements under the original-reference observation interface.

3. Evidence for explicit replacement targets. Matched comparisons in G1 simulation show the highest overhead-arm joint success and lowest replacement error across both tasks among local methods. Trajectory analysis distinguishes faithful replacement from threshold suppression.

title: LaST0.5: A Generalist World Action Model with Interaction-Centric Latent Reasoning
authors: Xuheng Zhang,Yiming Zhang,Jialin Gao,Hao Chen,Jiaming Liu,Ji Li,Runzhong Huang,Yinxi Wang,Chenyang Gu,Zihan Yang,Yaowei Liu,Zhonghao Yan,Ziyu Guo,Renrui Zhang,Peng Jia,Pheng-Ann Heng,Shanghang Zhang
abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation, endowing policies with strong capabilities for modeling temporal and physical dynamics. Existing WAMs, encompassing both video-first action prediction and joint video–action modeling, directly transfer global physical representations from world models to action generation. However, global scene representations may underemphasize local robot–object interactions, creating a mismatch between representations optimized for world evolution and those required for manipulation.
To bridge this gap, we propose LaST0.5, a novel WAM that introduces an interaction-centric physical representation between world modeling and action generation. Specifically, LaST0.5 learns a compact interaction-centric latent space under the supervision of visual interaction cues between the robot and the environment. This reasoning space is instantiated as a latent expert that bridges the world expert and the action expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture. Furthermore, LaST0.5 performs adaptive world-to-action transfer by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, using progress consistency to adjust action execution and trigger future resampling.
Finally, we pretrain LaST0.5 on a large-scale robotic data corpus comprising over 14k hours of data, establishing interaction-centric physical reasoning as a scalable and effective paradigm. LaST0.5 achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, surpasses the previous state of the art on ten evaluated RLBench tasks, and demonstrates robust long-horizon execution and precise dexterous manipulation in real-world experiments.

title: Optimization-Based Path Planning for Industrial Manipulators: Experimental Validation in Additive Manufacturing
authors: Shiva Ganesh Murali,Valentin Bhend,Deepak Ingole,Gabriele Fadini,Alisa Rupenyan
comment: Submitted for the review in ECC 2027
abstract: Robotic additive manufacturing requires joint paths that reconcile robot feasibility with process-specific geometry. We develop an offline optimization-based path planner that combines joint-path regularity and self-collision penalties with process costs and constraints, so that a new process enters through its own reference, residuals, and tolerances. Full-path and boundary-coupled chunked optimization handle references of different lengths. Iterative Weight Tuning (IWT) determines the cost weights from the gaps between Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and their targets. In carbon-fiber winding and robotic 3D printing, the planned paths meet the geometric tolerances and all KPI targets, and both paths are executed on a UR10e, without extrusion for printing, with joint-level tracking recorded during execution.
introduction:
In robotic manufacturing, the process determines how the robot must move the tool or workpiece [1]. In additive manufacturing, robot configurations must accommodate the process geometry and tolerances along an ordered reference while respecting joint limits, self-collision clearance, and path continuity [2]. The planner must therefore translate the ordered process reference into a joint-space path that respects these requirements.

We address the offline path-planning problem highlighted in Fig. 1. The planner selects joint configurations along the ordered process reference using robot and process costs and constraints. Time parameterization then provides a reference for online tracking with joint-state feedback.

Sampling-based methods search admissible configurations and connections on constraint manifolds [3, 4]. IKLink links inverse-kinematic solutions along prescribed end-effector references [5]. Winding additionally requires core-relative fiber directions and fiber–robot clearance models. Printing requires nozzle-pose tolerances along the reference.

Optimization-based planners express costs and constraints. Covariant Hamiltonian Optimization for Motion Planning (CHOMP) uses covariant gradients, Stochastic Trajectory Optimization for Motion Planning (STOMP) uses stochastic perturbations, and TrajOpt uses sequential convex optimization [6, 7, 8]. cuRobo combines parallel inverse kinematics, geometric planning, and trajectory optimization [9]. Their kinematic and collision-handling tools require application-specific reference construction and process residuals for winding and printing. Local optimization remains sensitive to initialization.

Once a path is fixed, execution introduces timing and feedback requirements. Optimal control and Model Predictive Control (MPC) address these requirements with custom trajectory-optimization and MPC formulations [10] and with robust tube MPC which handles model uncertainty through corridor-based planning [11]. Receding-horizon optimization supports reactive motion within its horizon, while coordinating configurations over the complete manufacturing reference would require the same process geometry together with execution models and timing assumptions.

Learned models offer another way to generate candidate paths or initialize numerical optimization. Motion Policy Networks learn reactive motion from depth observations [12], while DiffusionSeeder and Planning with Environment Representation, Sampling, and Trajectory Optimization (PRESTO) generate candidate paths for numerical refinement [13, 14]. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has also been combined with conventional planning and neural inverse kinematics for redundant manipulators [15], and with inverse-Jacobian control for simulated deburring [16]. At the execution stage, data-driven trajectory generation and compensation have targeted residual vibration and tracking error in pick-and-place tasks [17]. For winding and printing, a learned planner would need training tasks and inputs or rewards that represent the process geometry. Its paths would also need to be checked against the relevant tolerances.

Manufacturing planners incorporate process tolerances [2], optimize orientation and timing [18], and enforce coupled-system constraints [19]. Graph-based methods address winding sequences [20]. The question here is how core-relative fiber references and prescribed nozzle poses can each be converted into joint paths while coupling process agreement, path regularity, and clearance over the ordered samples.
Pointwise inverse kinematics does not couple these path-wide requirements, so we integrate their residuals and constraints in a common robot-stage optimization. This coupling introduces one weight per cost term. The weights trade process agreement against regularity and clearance, while acceptance is decided by process tolerances, so manual tuning must be repeated for each process. Constrained Bayesian optimization has tuned the parameters of a contouring planner jointly with low-level controller gains against motion performance metrics [21], and NMPC weights have been tuned with Bayesian optimization [22] and adapted across repeated winding tasks [23]. We therefore pair the formulation with Iterative Weight Tuning (IWT), which determines the weights from the gaps between the evaluated metrics and their tolerances. The contributions of this work are as follows:

A process-aware joint-path formulation that couples winding fiber alignment or printing nozzle poses with joint regularity, self-clearance, and joint bounds. Both applications use forward kinematics to evaluate their process residuals within a common robot-stage optimization.

An adaptation of our Iterative Weight Tuning (IWT) method [23] to select robot and process cost weights for both winding and printing. Empirical sensitivities relate weight changes to robot and process Key Performance Indicator (KPI) errors, enabling regularized norm-optimal updates without differentiating through the path optimizer. The tuning uses clearance and fiber-alignment KPIs for winding and position- and orientation-tracking KPIs for printing.

A two-stage winding planner that converts groove transitions into a sequence of contact points and fiber directions in the core frame. The robot stage uses that fixed sequence to plan the motion of the core while accounting for fiber–robot clearance and enforcing an angular tolerance at groove endpoints.

A printing implementation that limits the number of active configurations per optimization. Fixed neighboring configurations and joint-difference penalties couple adjacent chunks, and alternating forward and reverse sweeps propagate the boundary updates.

Section II presents the path-planning formulation and weight-tuning procedure.

title: ReACT: Reflection-Consistent Modulation and Cross-Load Consistency for Humanoid Velocity Tracking Under Asymmetric Loads
authors: Xianghui Wang,Aoran Fu,Liyou Luo,Shanze Wang,Xiaoyu Shen,Dan Zhang,Wei Zhang
abstract: In recent years, humanoid loco-manipulation has progressed to whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport. A basic requirement underlying these tasks is carrying the object to its destination, which depends on the locomotion controller accurately executing velocity commands from the navigation policy. However, carrying an object in one hand introduces a persistent asymmetric upper-body load that can degrade velocity tracking. Persistent tracking biases can accumulate into position and heading deviations, increasing the risk of collisions and navigation failure. To address this problem, we present ReACT, a framework for accurate velocity tracking under asymmetric upper-body loads. Reflection-consistent disturbance modulation uses the estimated wrench to modulate actor features for load compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations. Cross-load tracking consistency training compares loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands to promote consistent velocity tracking across loading conditions. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved velocity tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads. Real-world experiments demonstrate collision-free goal reaching in all 40 tested navigation trials under unilateral hand loads with a fixed mapless navigation policy.
introduction:
In recent years, humanoid loco-manipulation has enabled increasingly complex object interactions [1, 2], including whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport [3, 4]. A basic requirement underlying these tasks is carrying the object to its destination while navigating among obstacles [5, 6], which requires the locomotion controller to accurately track velocity commands throughout the transport phase. Unlike wheeled mobile manipulators on statically stable bases [7], a walking humanoid robot must maintain balance while carrying the payload, as support contacts switch during each stride. In practice, objects are commonly carried in one hand, introducing a persistent asymmetric upper-body load that can degrade velocity tracking even when walking remains stable [8]. Such degraded tracking can manifest as persistent lateral or yaw-rate biases, which accumulate into position and heading deviations and increase the risk of collision or goal-reaching failure during navigation.

Existing methods improve locomotion under external loads from several directions. Dynamics randomization [9] and adversarial disturbance training expose policies to variations in dynamics and external forces to improve robustness [10, 11]. FALCON jointly trains upper-body and lower-body policies with a force curriculum, learning force-adaptive loco-manipulation from proprioceptive history [3]. ADAPT incorporates analytical disturbance feedback into the locomotion policy, improving velocity tracking and reducing directional drift under asymmetric hand payloads [8]. Its reported trajectories, however, still show residual lateral drift under larger unilateral loads [8]. For the same velocity command, different load conditions require different compensatory joint responses. The challenge is to adapt these responses to the estimated disturbance while maintaining accurate velocity tracking with minimal variation across loading conditions.

To address this challenge, we present ReACT, a framework for accurate velocity tracking under persistent asymmetric upper-body loads on humanoid robots. Reflection-consistent disturbance modulation uses the estimated wrench to scale and couple reflection-even and reflection-odd actor features, enabling load-dependent compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations. Cross-load tracking consistency training compares motion responses across loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands, promoting consistent velocity tracking across loading conditions. Quantitative simulation on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot shows that ReACT achieves accurate velocity tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads. Ablation studies support the effectiveness of both components. Real-robot mapless navigation under asymmetric loads demonstrates collision-free goal reaching in the tested scenarios with a fixed navigation policy.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We propose reflection-consistent disturbance modulation, which uses the estimated external wrench to modulate the policy response for load compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations.

We develop cross-load tracking consistency training, which compares motion responses across loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands to reduce velocity tracking variation across loading conditions.

We validate ReACT through quantitative simulation, ablation studies, and real-robot mapless navigation on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating accurate velocity tracking in simulation and collision-free goal reaching in the tested real-robot navigation scenarios.

title: Learn-To-Propagate: Distributionally Robust Motion Planning for Nonlinear Uncertain Systems
authors: Eduardo Figueiredo,Adrien Banse,Qi Heng Ho,Raphael Jungers,Morteza Lahijanian,Luca Laurenti
abstract:
Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees.
To address these limitations, we propose Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest), a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for nonlinear stochastic systems with unknown initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system’s state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete.
Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods
while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.
introduction:
Motion planning has become a central problem in robotics, enabling autonomous systems to operate safely in complex environments while avoiding obstacles. Applications span domains such as autonomous driving, aerial navigation, and robotic surgery. In this context, sampling-based algorithms have emerged as particularly successful approaches (Cortés and Siméon, 2020), where samples from the state and control spaces are used to efficiently construct search trees and compute collision-free trajectories. However, real-world robotic systems are often subject to uncertainty arising from process and measurement noise, external disturbances, and imperfect knowledge of the system dynamics. Unfortunately, existing approaches either rely on linear-Gaussian assumptions to obtain tractable safety guarantees or accommodate more general uncertainty at the expense of formal correctness guarantees (Blackmore et al., 2011; Luders et al., 2010; Luders et al., 2013; Ho et al., 2022; Prattis et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
This work aims to bridge this gap by developing a motion planning framework for uncertain systems that provides both correctness and completeness guarantees.

Among approaches that seek formal safety guarantees under uncertain disturbances, two broad directions have emerged. The first assumes that disturbances have bounded support, reducing safety checks to a worst-case reachability problem (Wu et al., 2022; Danielson et al., 2020). While effective in some settings, these methods often become overly conservative when the support of the uncertainty is large. A second direction relies on distributionally robust optimization (DRO) (Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn, 2018), constructing sets of plausible probability distributions, referred to as ambiguity sets, and evaluating worst-case probabilities over these sets (Summers, 2018; Hakobyan and Yang, 2020; Renganathan et al., 2020; Lindemann et al., 2021; Gracia et al., 2026). Yet, most existing DRO-based approaches are limited to linear or locally linearized systems, can be overly conservative, and either require a predefined ambiguity set or face challenges in learning sufficiently tight ambiguity sets from data. To address these limitations, we show how recent advances in Wasserstein-based distribution learning (Figueiredo et al., 2026; Fournier and Guillin, 2015) and nonlinear uncertainty propagation (Figueiredo et al., 2025) can be combined to enable safe motion planning for nonlinear stochastic systems with unknown disturbance distributions.

In this paper, we propose Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest), a novel and computationally efficient motion-planning algorithm that combines DRO, sampling-based planning, and nonlinear uncertainty propagation to handle stochastic systems with unknown initial state and disturbance distributions. Leveraging recent results in optimal transport, our approach estimates a compact ambiguity set centered around a discrete distribution that is guaranteed, with high probability, to contain the true underlying system distributions.
Critically, Wasserstein ambiguity sets admit a highly tractable propagation rule through Lipschitz continuous dynamics, with their radii expanding at most linearly with the Lipschitz constant of the dynamics. Consequently, these sets can be efficiently propagated while preserving computable bounds on distributional uncertainty, avoiding the need for relearning at every propagation step. This property enables rapid exploration of the planning tree and substantially reduces the computational burden associated with exhaustive sampling. Combined with existing DRO results (Gao and Kleywegt, 2023), this allows us to synthesize motion plans that carry formal collision-avoidance guarantees despite underlying distributional uncertainty.

L2P-DR-Forest grows a forest of trees in stages. Each new tree is rooted at a node of an existing tree, and the ambiguity set at this root is re-learned from samples rolled out through the controller leading to that node. Thus, the planner propagates ambiguity sets cheaply within each tree and re-learns tight ones only at the selected restart nodes.
We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., any controller it returns solves the planning problem with the prescribed confidence, and probabilistically complete, i.e., if a control sequence is robustly feasible with some margin and the noise is sub-Gaussian, then, run for an unbounded number of stages with growing sample sizes, it returns a controller with probability one.
We evaluate L2P-DR-Forest on a range of nonlinear robotics benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves high task-success rates while enforcing safe controllers. In contrast, comparable methods that do not provide formal safety guarantees exhibit substantially lower reliability.

In summary, our main contributions are:

A novel distributionally robust sampling-based motion planning algorithm, L2P-DR-Forest, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first motion planner that provides formal, high-confidence safety guarantees for nonlinear systems with unknown distributions.

An extension of data-driven distributionally robust algorithms to learn distributions with unbounded support from data, which is critical to formally reduce the uncertainty in our motion planner over forest expansion.

A formal proof that L2P-DR-Forest is correct and probabilistically complete.

An empirical evaluation including a neural model of a tractor trailer showing that our approach substantially outperforms comparable methods both in terms of success rate and planning time.

Motion planning under uncertainty is commonly posed as a chance-constrained problem (Blackmore et al., 2011; Luders et al., 2010; Luders et al., 2013; Kothari and Postlethwaite, 2013; Dai et al., 2019), where the probability of unsafety (e.g., collision) must satisfy a given upper bound at every time step.
There are two inherent challenges in such problems: (i) uncertainty propagation through the dynamics, and (ii) bounding the probability of unsafety.
Most of the existing approaches assume linear or linearized dynamics and Gaussian uncertainty to obtain tractable probability bounds or approximations. Extensions to non-Gaussian uncertainty use moment-based bounds (Wang et al., 2020; Jasour and Williams, 2019), which provide formal guarantees under restrictive assumptions, such as access to the relevant moments and their dynamics. Even when these assumptions hold, such methods can be overly conservative or computationally expensive.

For nonlinear systems, a common alternative is to assess safety statistically from sampled rollouts. This accommodates general dynamics and noise distributions, but naive Monte Carlo estimation can require many samples to resolve small collision probabilities, motivating variance-reduction techniques (Janson et al., 2017). Sampling also underpins model predictive control methods such as MPPI (Williams et al., 2017), whose original formulation does not provide finite-sample probabilistic safety certificates. Among sampling-based planners, ϵ\epsilon-RandUP-RRT (Wu et al., 2022; Lew et al., 2022), which we use as a baseline in Section 5, checks collision avoidance using ϵ\epsilon-padded convex hulls of propagated particles. The finite-sample guarantees of its underlying reachable-set estimator depend on bounds on quantities such as Lipschitz constants, packing numbers, and sampling coverage, which can be difficult to obtain tightly in practice.

To mitigate these issues, scenario-based planning (De Groot et al., 2025) has been introduced. It provides distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees from i.i.d. samples drawn from the true uncertainty distribution. These methods have been applied to nonlinear model predictive control and motion planning among uncertain obstacles, but they assume the robot dynamics are deterministic. These guarantees extend to nonconvex decision problems, although certification requires suitable feasibility conditions and bounds on the number of supporting scenarios. In contrast, in this work, we focus on offline, sampling-based planning for nonlinear systems with unknown disturbance distributions, with probabilistic safety guarantees derived from finite data.

Distributionally robust optimization addresses uncertainty about the underlying probability law by optimizing against the worst-case distribution within a set of plausible distributions, called an ambiguity set. In motion planning, ambiguity sets have been defined through means and covariances for linear systems with additive process noise (Summers, 2018), and as Wasserstein balls centered on empirical distributions constructed from samples of obstacle motion within model predictive control (Hakobyan and Yang, 2020). Closely related work (Gracia et al., 2026) learns Wasserstein ambiguity tubes from trajectory data under unknown disturbance distributions and incorporates them into a probabilistically complete sampling-based planner. Its construction exploits linear or feedback-linearizable dynamics to decouple uncertainty propagation from nominal planning, allowing the ambiguity tube to be learned offline and reused during search. In contrast, we propagate learned ambiguity sets through nonlinear Lipschitz continuous dynamics and re-learn them during search, using a forest of trees to mitigate growth in their radii.

1. A novel distributionally robust sampling-based motion planning algorithm, L2P-DR-Forest, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first motion planner that provides formal, high-confidence safety guarantees for nonlinear systems with unknown distributions.

2. An extension of data-driven distributionally robust algorithms to learn distributions with unbounded support from data, which is critical to formally reduce the uncertainty in our motion planner over forest expansion.

3. A formal proof that L2P-DR-Forest is correct and probabilistically complete.

4. An empirical evaluation including a neural model of a tractor trailer showing that our approach substantially outperforms comparable methods both in terms of success rate and planning time.

title: Game-Enhanced Embodied Learning with Event and Foresight Pretraining
authors: Lianlei Shan,Han Jin,Yaunchao Ma,Xinpeng Chen,Linhao Zhou,Xin Bin
abstract: Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model. Coverage-preserving anchor selection constructs one-second targets, and an attention mask prevents teacher-forced future actions from entering foresight queries. The selected corpus contains 394 recordings across 20 games, with 223.36 hours of recorded timestamp span and 2,072,084 training anchors. After 12,400 game-pretraining updates, we compare the resulting initialization with the public base under the same suite-specific robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success increases from 1,718/2,000 (85.90%) to 1,811/2,000 (90.55%), a gain of 4.65 percentage points. Suite gains are 9.2, 6.8, 0.2, and 2.4 points on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. The 40-task breakdown shows 24 improvements, 10 declines, and six ties. These results support the practical value of the complete game-pretraining stage in this evaluated setting, while revealing heterogeneous task outcomes. The comparison includes additional optimization and does not isolate the effects of game data, the two objectives, or training variability.
introduction:
Embodied policies learn from observations paired with actions and subsequent environmental changes. Human gameplay provides the same broad interaction structure: a player observes a scene, issues keyboard or mouse commands, and observes their consequences. These recordings are a potential source of auxiliary supervision for robot-capable models. Our question is how to train on that non-robot action space while retaining the policy’s native robot interface, and what downstream changes accompany the additional training stage.

D2E demonstrates that desktop interaction can support embodied pretraining (Choi et al., 2026), while InternVLA-A1.5 provides a robot-capable architecture with learnable foresight queries supervised by a frozen video model (Ma et al., 2026). Adapting game interaction to this architecture is not direct: game actions are expressed as keyboard and mouse events rather than robot controls, action and video targets must be aligned over physical time, and teacher-forced future events must not leak into features available at inference. The central challenge is therefore to extract auxiliary supervision from game interaction while maintaining causal, history-only conditioning and preserving the model’s native robot-control pathway.

To address these constraints, our procedure builds one-second action and video targets from recorded human gameplay. Coverage-preserving sampling combines a sparse-anchor pass that reduces repeated starting points with a recovery pass that restores valid anchors for otherwise uncovered actions. Next-event prediction learns from recorded human commands, while the foresight pathway receives future visual supervision conditioned only on available history. Target-action tokens cannot enter the foresight queries. The trained components subsequently initialize native robot fine-tuning.

To assess transfer, we compare the game-pretrained initialization with the public base across all four LIBERO suites, holding suite-specific robot training and rollout protocols fixed. The game-pretrained initialization produces 93 additional successes in 2,000 episodes, increasing aggregate success from 85.90% to 90.55%. Spatial and Object account for 80 of these 93 net additional successes. Full task-level results show both improvements and regressions, so the aggregate benefit is not interpreted as a uniform task-level effect.

Taken together, our contribution is a concrete training route for using non-robot interaction as auxiliary supervision without converting game commands into robot actions. The route combines coverage-preserving game sampling, causal event-and-foresight training, transfer to InternVLA-A1.5’s native robot pathway, and a complete four-suite evaluation. Table 1 identifies which components are inherited from D2E and InternVLA-A1.5 and which adaptations are evaluated in this study.

title: WAM is capable in BEHAVIOR-1K: the 2nd-place solution to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
authors: Yelin He,Jiaquan Ye,Xinming Wei,Wenjie Xiao,Gengming Zhang,Guoting Wei,Xianbiao Qi,Rong Xiao
comment: . Technical report for Team IF1001's 2nd-place solution to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge at CoRL 2026. Challenge website:this https URL
abstract:
This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3.
We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.

title: Camera equalisation of an 11.5x drop in environmental illuminance: four imitation-learning policies on an SO-101 arm
authors: Simon Cowling
abstract: Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated. Four imitation-learning policies (ACT, SmolVLA, Diffusion Policy and π0.5\pi_{0.5}) were trained on the same 50 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. Each was run for ten rollouts at about 520 lux and again at about 45 lux, an 11.5×\times reduction. Success was 20/40 in normal light and 19/40 in low light: a change of −2.5-2.5 percentage points (95% CI −23-23 to +19+19), with no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity (interaction p=0.86p=0.86). The recorded video shows why: mean image brightness was only 3% lower in low light on the front camera and 19% lower on the wrist camera. Both cameras were set to automatic exposure and white balance, which most likely absorbed the difference; exposure was not locked in this experiment. An accidental repeat of one 10-rollout block reproduced its success count (7/10) but matched the first block at only 6 of 10 placements, consistent with chance. We conclude that lux alone does not describe what a policy sees. Camera settings, and image statistics compared with the training recordings, are the quantities to report and control. Data and code are public.
introduction:
This note asks how much the success of four learned manipulation policies changes when the room light drops about tenfold, and why.

Visuomotor policies map camera images to robot actions. Lighting changes those images everywhere at once, and a simulated perturbation benchmark ranks lighting among the changes that hurt manipulation policies most [8]. A natural safeguard in real-robot evaluation is to fix the light and log illuminance in lux, assuming that equal lux means equal inputs.

We tested that assumption on a common low-cost setup: an SO-101 arm [6] driven through LeRobot [5], with two off-the-shelf USB cameras. Four widely used policies were trained on identical demonstrations: ACT [1], SmolVLA [3], Diffusion Policy (DP) [2] and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [4]. We then benched them at the recording light level and at about one eleventh of it. The contributions are:

A paired real-robot comparison of four policies under an 11.5×\times illuminance drop: 80 rollouts, with effect estimates and intervals.

Measurements of what the cameras actually recorded. The images were barely darker, so the finding concerns the camera pipeline more than the policies.

A same-day repeat of one block, which shows how much a single 10-rollout block varies on its own.

Practical recommendations for reporting and controlling lighting in small real-robot benchmarks.

title: RiSE-Drive: Risk-Sensitive Long-Horizon Candidate Evaluation for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
authors: Yu Zhao,Hongyi Duan,Ming Yin,Hongyuan Zhang,Fan Yang,Hongzhi Wang,Xiubo Liang
comment: including supplementary material. Published in ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26)
abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving aims to map raw multi-view observations directly to a safe, rule-compliant, and route-progressive future ego trajectory in a unified learned planner (Jiang et al., 2023; Chitta et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Weng et al., 2024). Modern systems increasingly adopt a generate-and-select paradigm, where a proposal module enumerates multiple feasible futures and a selector chooses one for execution (Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a; Kirby et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025). Under behavior-grounded evaluation such as NAVSIM and NAVSIM-v2 (Dauner et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2025), the central challenge is therefore not only to generate plausible candidates, but to evaluate which candidate remains best under long-horizon interactions and future uncertainty.

Among recent ResNet-34-based planners, MindDrive (Sun et al., 2025) is a strong representative of richer future reasoning. Yet, at the surface level, even strong planners can remain brittle in safety-critical long-tail scenes and perturbed rollouts: several candidates may receive similar nominal scores, while the selected one fails after downstream interactions. The deeper reason is that candidate quality is not a deterministic scalar, but a distribution of long-horizon consequences induced by uncertain future conditions. Existing methods still largely compress this uncertainty into point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome estimates, without explicit candidate-conditioned counterfactual rollout and lower-tail risk modeling. As a result, hidden tail failures remain invisible to the selector, and ranking becomes unstable exactly when robustness matters most.

We address this limitation with RiSE-Drive, a risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluator for end-to-end driving. RiSE-Drive leaves the upstream perception and proposal-generation pipeline unchanged and modifies only the evaluation stage. For each candidate, it predicts a compact set of future-condition branches, performs candidate-conditioned latent consequence propagation, decodes one long-horizon outcome sample for each branch, estimates an outcome distribution through ordered quantiles, and ranks candidates using a criterion that combines the mean, lower-tail Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) (Rockafellar and Uryasev, 2002), and cross-condition instability. This design directly targets the root cause above: branchwise rollout captures delayed interaction effects, distributional estimation exposes hidden tail failures, and CVaR-based ranking favors trajectories that remain reliable not only in expectation but also in the lower tail under plausible future deviations. Instantiated on top of DrivoR (Kirby et al., 2026), RiSE-Drive is orthogonal to backbone scaling and isolates the value of better candidate evaluation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify a central evaluation mismatch in candidate-based end-to-end driving: candidate quality should be modeled as a distribution over future-condition-dependent long-horizon outcomes, rather than reduced to a single deterministic score.

We propose RiSE-Drive, a unified evaluator that combines future-condition modeling, candidate-conditioned latent consequence propagation, distributional outcome estimation, and CVaR-based risk-sensitive ranking to make trajectory selection explicitly tail-risk aware.

RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM-v1 (Dauner et al., 2024), NAVSIM-v2 (Cao et al., 2025), and HUGSIM (Zhou et al., 2025a). Under a matched DrivoR setup (Kirby et al., 2026), it improves PDMS from 93.1 to 94.2, EPDMS from 48.3 to 51.3, and average HD-Score from 35.7 to 39.5, while consistently improving safety-critical and closed-loop robustness on hard and perturbation-heavy settings.

title: Softness is something you also need! Why compliance helps control: information metrics of a passive walker with compliant ankle
authors: Fabio Bonsignorio,Elisabetta Barletta,Sorin Dragomir,Francesco Esposito,Enrica Zereik
abstract: This document provides additional detailed information, in particular mathematical definitions and proofs, related to the paper. They are referenced in the paper text where they were considered suitable.
introduction:
This work builds on [1], utilizing the findings from [2].
In [1] it is argued that there are good reasons to believe that ’intelligence’ (and ’meaning’) are ’emerging’ traits arising from the evolution of loosely coupled networks of intelligent ’embodied’ and ’situated’ agents.
The author, in line with the approach proposed by Rolf Pfeifer in “How the body shapes the way we think” [3], elaborates a preliminary quantitative comprehensive theory that aims to enable us to predict the interaction between the agents’ ‘morphology’, or mechanical structure and dynamics, and the emergence of ‘intelligence’ and ‘meaning’ in physical systems.

Specifically, a number of relations are derived with a objective to clarify:

The relationship between an embodied agent’s information/computing capability and its dynamics (morphological computation)

The behavior of computing and information capacities in a multi-body agent system

How networks of embodied agents give rise to ’intelligence’ and ’meaning’

This work has a narrower scope.
Our objective is to elucidate the significance of softness, or compliance, in robotics and natural embodied agents and provide quantitative guidance for hybrid hard and soft bodied robots.

title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
authors: Santosh Mohan Rajkumar,Debdipta Goswami,Stephanie Stockar
abstract: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.
introduction:
Quadratic programming (QP) problems arise in a wide range of applications, including statistics, machine learning, finance, and model predictive control (MPC) for robotic and control systems [1, 2, 3]. They also appear as subproblems in nonlinear optimization algorithms, such as sequential quadratic programming (SQP). Many of these applications lead to convex QP problems. Among these applications, MPC requires solving an optimization problem within each control sampling period, making computational efficiency critical for real-time operation [4]. With linear prediction models, convex quadratic costs, and linear constraints, each MPC update requires solving a convex QP problem, yielding a formulation commonly referred to as linear MPC (LMPC).

Common solution approaches for QP problems include interior-point (IP), active-set (AS), operator-splitting (OS), and proximal methods.
Representative IP methods include HPIPM [5], qpSWIFT [6], PIQP [7], and Clarabel [8] (with QP as a special case). Although IP methods often converge in relatively few iterations, each iteration requires solving a potentially expensive linear system. They are also generally more difficult to warm start, limiting their ability to exploit similarities between successive QP problems in MPC [9].

AS methods, such as qpOASES [10] and DAQP [11], readily support warm starting and can be highly efficient when initialized with the correct active set. However, their combinatorial worst-case complexity in the number of constraints can limit their scalability to large-scale QPs [9]. OS methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), such as OSQP [2], and related proximal methods, such as ProxQP [12], are increasingly used in robotic MPC owing to their ease of warm starting and suitability for applications requiring moderate solution accuracy [13, 14]. Moreover, their computational structure offers opportunities for parallelization. Nevertheless, their convergence rates can be slower than those of other methods, particularly when high-accuracy solutions are required [7].

Although most established QP solvers are CPU-based, GPUs offer opportunities to accelerate large-scale QP solving through massive parallelism and higher memory bandwidth, enabling concurrent execution of independent computations and faster data movement [13]. Growing interest in MPC for robotics and control using world models [15, 16], locally linear latent dynamics [17], and Koopman-based linear, bilinear, or semi-linear representations [18, 19, 20] further motivates GPU acceleration to meet the real-time computational demands of large-scale MPCs. Moreover, modern robotics increasingly relies on GPUs for parallel simulation, inference, and learning [21, 22, 23]. Integrating CPU-native QP solvers into such pipelines can introduce additional latency through frequent CPU–GPU data transfers [24]. Together, these considerations motivate GPU-native QP solvers that keep optimization data and computations on the device.

This work presents FAME​-​QP\mathrm{FAME}\text{-}\mathrm{QP}, Fused ADMM with Multimode Execution for QP solution, a GPU solver for the dense QPs of linear MPC. Its contributions are: (i) constraint-dependent operator representations that reduce operator storage by up to 4×4\times and iteration time by up to 3×3\times, relative to treating all constraint rows as dense; (ii) fused single- and two-kernel iterations with CUDA graph replay and automatic selection using device calibration and problem-specific timing; (iii) initial penalty selection through cached-operator probing and lazy operator updates for changing QP matrices; (iv) numerical and simulated robotic MPC evaluations demonstrating lower latency than the competing GPU methods evaluated in each benchmark, with matched solution accuracy on random QPs and comparable closed-loop control performance; and (v) an open-source implementation.

GPU QP solvers.
cuOSQP [13] parallelizes OSQP through indirect linear solves, while qpax [25] and CuPIQP [26] implement IP methods on GPUs, with CuPIQP exploiting kernel fusion and CUDA graph replay.
The closest approach is ReLU-QP [9], which reformulates ADMM as a weight-tied neural network and caches pre-inverted operators for penalty adaptation.
Its dense operator and repeated dispatch introduce computational and execution overhead, while its offline precomputation limits online matrix updates.
FAME​-​QP\mathrm{FAME}\text{-}\mathrm{QP} retains the pre-inversion and penalty-bank approach but uses smaller, constraint-dependent operators, fused graph-replayed iterations, and lazy operator updates.

GPU MPC solvers.
MPCGPU [27] and TurboMPC [28] accelerate nonlinear MPC through GPU implementations of SQP and structured linear algebra.
π\piMPC [29] exploits parallelism across the prediction horizon through consensus ADMM, while CUDA MPC [30] reduces execution overhead using a persistent cooperative kernel and CUDA graphs.
These methods exploit structure at the optimal-control level, whereas FAME​-​QP\mathrm{FAME}\text{-}\mathrm{QP} accepts dense convex QPs directly, including general constraint matrices and online matrix changes.

Positioning.
Our contribution lies in combining constraint-dependent operator representations with automatic selection between fused single- and two-kernel iterations, initial penalty probing, and lazy matrix updates.
The execution configuration is selected through device calibration and problem-specific timing, targeting the latency of individual MPC solves.

title: CIALLO: Learning Shared Intent Representations for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
authors: Choo Sin Wai,Dake Zhong,Jingye Zhang,Zhifang Liu,Siyao Xiao,Zirong Ding,Yuhong Zhang,Kangjie Chen,Dongbin Zhang,Guorui Song,Guocun Wang,Peng Jiao,Haoqian Wang
abstract: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0% for fully finetuned π0\pi_{0}. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3% success on LIBERO and 52.7% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.
introduction:
A grasp demonstrated by one robot can teach another what to reach for and how an object should move, even when their joint coordinates and control rates differ. Cross-embodiment learning seeks to reuse experience from existing robots to provide control knowledge for a new body [32, 14, 27]. Pretrained vision-language models supply broad semantic knowledge [22, 2], but grounding that knowledge in an unfamiliar action interface still requires substantial amounts of robot demonstration data. A reusable action codec could make these demonstrations more useful for task learning by reducing the need to adapt the underlying control representation.

Recorded actions entangle behavior with the coordinates and control conventions used to execute it. Similar motions can be expressed as end effector displacements or joint angles, with different dimensions, numbers of arms, and temporal resolutions. Shared action layouts and embodiment-specific modules allow policies to consume heterogeneous data [14, 27, 46]. Yet action reconstruction alone, even with embodiment-conditioned encoding and decoding, does not require similar behaviors across robots to have similar representations. Visual changes and grounded language connect different control sequences that produce similar visual effects or serve compatible task goals. We therefore align action representations through these shared cues to learn a codec that transfers across embodiments with only brief calibration.

We introduce CIALLO (Cross-embodiment Intent All In One Space), an action codec for transferring control knowledge across robots. CIALLO separates a shared representation of short-horizon behavior, intent, from the body and control schema used to realize it. Building on latent action learning and action–vision alignment [49, 5, 52, 6], CIALLO aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in one space. The visual and text branches anchor actions to their effects and task context, encouraging nearby representations for compatible behaviors across embodiments. A shared decoder reconstructs actions from all three representations, preserving the control information needed to execute them (Figure 1A). An essential vector EE, arm and axis embeddings, and execution times supply the embodiment-specific context. The same codec weights therefore support different action dimensions, control rates, and single- or dual-arm configurations.

The aligned action codec then provides the interface for policy learning. From one recording of at most 10 seconds, we fit only the new robot’s essential vector and arm and axis embeddings, keeping the shared network fixed. We freeze the calibrated codec and train a policy to predict intent from observations and instructions. The action encoder and decoder supervise this prediction (Figure 1B–C). Calibration establishes how the codec realizes behavior on the new body, while task demonstrations teach the policy which intent to produce. We pair the codec with Qwen3.5-4B [38] through StarVLA [43], forming Qwen-CIALLO without large-scale robot-action pretraining of the Qwen backbone.

We pretrain CIALLO on eight embodiments and evaluate reuse on real SO-101 and single-arm Piper configurations absent from pretraining (Piper pretraining uses a simulated dual-arm configuration). Calibration takes approximately 30 minutes per robot, after which the codec remains frozen. In simulation, where the action decoder is also finetuned, Qwen-CIALLO reaches 97.3% on LIBERO after 10k policy steps and 80.8% on LIBERO-Plus without further training. One policy trained jointly on RoboTwin 2.0 achieves 52.7% after 40k steps. These evaluations test both adaptation to new robots and policy learning across tasks with the shared action codec.

title: Joint-State Inference for Autonomous Excavators Using Cab-View Vision-Control Fusion
authors: Junwei Li,Jian Pan,Mengchi Cai,Shuai Zhao,Xizhuo Jiang,Zheng Wang,Qing Xu,Keqiang Li,Jianqiang Wang
abstract: Reliable state feedback of excavator front-end mechanisms is essential for autonomous excavation, yet retrofitting existing machines with dedicated joint sensors, external cameras, or visual markers can increase deployment and maintenance burdens. This paper proposes a closed-loop autonomous excavation framework for continuous inference of excavator joint states using onboard visual observations and control-related temporal information. The framework encodes structural cues from the current cab-view image, models short-term motion trends from historical joystick commands, and introduces a rolling state buffer for the bucket joint to preserve temporal continuity under severe occlusion. Mechanical joint-range constraints are incorporated into the learning objective to suppress infeasible estimates. The current cab-view image and inferred states are supplied to an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)-based control policy for online action generation. Experiments in an AGX Dynamics for Unity simulation environment under diverse operating conditions evaluate joint-state inference and end-to-end task execution. Across 20 autonomous excavation trials, the framework achieved a 95% task-completion rate, with an average joint-state-inference-and-control latency of 10.11 ms per step. The bucket-joint inference achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.965∘0.965^{\circ}. These results demonstrate a sensor-light and computationally efficient joint-state-inference approach that can support closed-loop autonomous excavation with reduced dependence on additional sensing infrastructure.
introduction:
Excavation operations are commonly conducted in unstructured and highly disturbed environments. Although traditional manual operation can accomplish complex tasks by relying on the experience of skilled operators, long-term continuous excavation requires substantial human involvement and relies heavily on operator expertise. Autonomous excavation technology provides a promising approach for improving excavation safety, operational efficiency, and standardization (Zhang et al.  2021). However, achieving continuous and stable autonomous operation places stringent requirements on joint-state inference accuracy, decision-making efficiency, and execution reliability. Therefore, a reliable joint-state inference and autonomous control framework with reduced dependence on additional state-sensing devices is a fundamental prerequisite for high-quality autonomous excavation (Dadhich et al.  2016).

Existing autonomous excavation systems typically rely on additional state-sensing devices to measure excavator joint states, which provide critical feedback for motion planning, process adjustment, and task execution (Lee et al.  2022; Kim et al.  2020). Such devices, including hydraulic cylinder displacement sensors, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and inclination sensors, can directly measure excavator states. However, their deployment generally requires hardware installation and system modification, increasing deployment cost and structural-integration complexity, as well as requirements for calibration, maintenance, and fault diagnosis. Moreover, excavators often operate under dust, vibration, and mechanical impacts, which may compromise the measurement stability and long-term reliability of these devices. Therefore, continuous acquisition of excavator joint states without extensive hardware modification, followed by their use as state feedback for autonomous operation, is important for the intelligent upgrading of existing excavators (Ito et al.  2021).

Previous research on excavator state acquisition has mainly focused on marker-assisted measurement and vision-based perception for estimating the working-mechanism pose. Marker-assisted methods can provide high-precision pose measurements under controlled conditions. However, they depend strongly on specific equipment configurations and experimental setups, requiring marker installation and manual configuration on excavators. These constraints hinder rapid deployment across excavator platforms, while the marker systems increase configuration complexity and maintenance cost in practical applications (Soltani et al.  2017). Vision-based joint-state estimation methods typically use externally mounted fixed cameras to capture excavation images and infer working-mechanism states through object detection, keypoint extraction, or visual reconstruction. Although these approaches reduce mechanical modification, they are constrained by camera placement, viewing geometry, and field conditions, which limits their use in changing work areas and long-term autonomous operation (Guo et al.  2021; Roberts et al.  2020; Nakamura et al.  2020). Moreover, severe occlusion can require complex visual-processing pipelines or multi-stage optimization, increasing computational cost and hindering continuous state feedback for real-time closed-loop control. Existing approaches therefore still struggle to combine accurate state acquisition, convenient deployment, and real-time closed-loop operation.

Representative cab-view scenes from real and simulated excavation settings, including typical partial and severe working-mechanism occlusions, are shown in Fig. 1.

To address the limitations of existing autonomous excavation systems, including their dependence on additional state-sensing devices, high modification costs, and incomplete closed-loop operation, this paper proposes a low-cost, robust closed-loop autonomous excavation framework. The framework replaces the conventional device-dependent state-measurement paradigm with a lightweight state inference module that continuously estimates excavator joint states. It establishes a complete workflow from joint-state inference and real-time feedback to autonomous decision-making and action execution. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

A perception–execution-coupled closed-loop autonomous excavation framework is developed, integrating joint-state inference, real-time feedback, autonomous decision-making, and task execution into a unified pipeline. The framework enables continuous and stable excavation under the tested simulated excavation conditions, supporting the intelligent upgrading of excavators.

A state inference module that does not require additional state-sensing devices is designed. It uses intrinsically available excavator information to estimate excavator joint states, reducing dependence on additional sensing hardware and the costs of intelligent retrofitting and long-term maintenance.

Extensive simulation experiments validate the framework. The results demonstrate low joint-state inference and control-execution latency, a high task-completion rate, and a high demonstration-normalized excavation yield. The inferred joint states are also robust to visual appearance variations, including illumination and component-color changes.

title: Ego Guidance: Enhancing Robot Policy Learning with Action-Free Human Egocentric Videos
authors: Lin Long,Tianren Ma,Zhong Chu,Di Wu,Maosong Cao,Qixiang Ye,Junbo Zhao,Shanghang Zhang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision.
Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction.
We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales.
We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.
introduction:
Embodied AI models are still in their infancy, eagerly absorbing every valuable source of world knowledge. Among these sources, human egocentric videos are particularly promising. Their large-scale availability, ease of acquisition, and close connection to the open-world environment make them an important potential source of data for embodied intelligence [1, 2, 3, 4]. However, precise action annotation is expensive to acquire, making most of the resources available only in video form (which we call action-free). In this work, we investigate whether such action-free data can provide benefits to robot policy learning without action restoration.

Guided by first-principled considerations, rather than adopting a World Action Model (WAM) architecture [5, 6, 7] that performs diffusion in a generative latent space, we start from a simpler and well-optimized Vision Language Model (VLM) backbone, expand it into a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT), and jointly optimize the model with action and visual state prediction.
Building on this Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), we investigate how different encoders for representing the predicted state affect performance.

We further conduct preliminary studies on several important factors, including data cleaning, diversity trade-off, and the scalability potential of pretraining with action-free egocentric videos.
