title: NIF-VIO: Visual--Inertial Odometry Across Inertial and Non-Inertial Reference Frames
authors: Zichao Shu,Lijun Li,Zhuochen Li,Zetao Chen,Jianyu Wang
abstract: Conventional visual–inertial odometry (VIO) assumes that observations from cameras and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) are jointly consistent in an inertial reference frame. However, this assumption breaks down under non-inertial conditions. Inside accelerating or rotating carriers, visual observations of the interior reflect carrier-relative motion, while IMU measurements contain additional carrier-induced components, which can compromise conventional fusion. We therefore present NIF-VIO for localization relative to the local environment across inertial and non-inertial reference frames. It adapts visual–inertial fusion based on measurement consistency. As inertial conditions change, early constraint isolation is combined with local reoptimization to limit error propagation before inconsistency confirmation and repair the affected local geometry. Under non-inertial conditions, a compact model with temporally shared parameters is introduced to account for carrier motion while preserving inertial information that complements visual constraints. Experiments on public benchmarks and a self-collected dataset demonstrate that NIF-VIO achieves competitive performance under inertial conditions and improved localization accuracy and availability under non-inertial conditions. The code and dataset will be publicly available upon acceptance.
introduction:
Visual–inertial odometry (VIO) combines complementary visual and inertial measurements to estimate ego-motion [20, 3, 26, 19]. Conventional VIO assumes that the observed environment is stationary in an inertial reference frame, enabling consistent fusion of the two modalities [24]. However, real-world operation may extend to settings inside moving carriers such as cars, trains, and elevators [5, 14, 4]. For localization tasks defined relative to the local environment, the reference frame is fixed to the carrier and becomes non-inertial when the carrier accelerates or rotates. Visual observations of the interior provide information about device motion relative to the carrier, whereas measurements from an inertial measurement unit (IMU) also include carrier-induced effects. This mismatch leads to inconsistent constraints under the conventional VIO model and can cause severe estimation errors or even failure [15, 14].

Visual odometry (VO) can avoid this conflict by relying on vision alone [12]. However, IMU measurements can improve robustness under inertial conditions by complementing visual observations over short time scales [1]. With appropriate modeling, they can also contribute to relative state estimation under non-inertial conditions [18]. For carrier-relative localization, some existing methods use an additional carrier-mounted IMU to account for carrier motion and retain inertial constraints, but require carrier-side instrumentation and data access [15, 29]. Observation selection offers another way to handle visual–inertial conflicts [27]. A multi-motion extension supports carrier-relative tracking, but the corresponding pose optimization still relies on visual constraints alone [28]. These considerations motivate a visual–inertial framework that uses only device-side sensors to maintain continuous localization while retaining useful inertial constraints across changing inertial conditions.

To this end, we propose NIF-VIO. Fig. 1 illustrates its target scenarios and how it adapts fusion as inertial conditions change. Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose a unified VIO framework for continuous localization relative to the local environment across inertial and non-inertial conditions, without carrier-side sensing.

We develop a transition-handling strategy that combines early constraint isolation with local geometric repair to mitigate error propagation and geometric distortion caused by delayed inconsistency confirmation.

We formulate selective inertial constraints through a structured carrier-motion model with temporally shared parameters and soft motion priors, preserving useful inertial information for relative localization under non-inertial conditions.

We introduce a dataset spanning car, subway, and elevator scenarios, with carrier-relative reference trajectories for benchmarking localization under changing inertial conditions.

1. We propose a unified VIO framework for continuous localization relative to the local environment across inertial and non-inertial conditions, without carrier-side sensing.

2. We develop a transition-handling strategy that combines early constraint isolation with local geometric repair to mitigate error propagation and geometric distortion caused by delayed inconsistency confirmation.

3. We formulate selective inertial constraints through a structured carrier-motion model with temporally shared parameters and soft motion priors, preserving useful inertial information for relative localization under non-inertial conditions.

4. We introduce a dataset spanning car, subway, and elevator scenarios, with carrier-relative reference trajectories for benchmarking localization under changing inertial conditions.

title: An IoT Based Approach for Platform Independent Positioning Service
authors: Anh-Van Vu,Dongsoo Han
abstract: KAIST Indoor Localization System (KAILOS) was introduced in 2014 and became one of the world-first complete indoor positioning solutions. It is mainly based on the WiFi signal to estimate location and provide positioning service via mobile application that has many restrictions by the Operating System. This study proposes an extended architecture of KAILOS to make use of the IoT device for removing the barriers of the mobile-app-based approach and conveniently providing indoor positioning service. Design of the IoT device that contains hardware and software is also presented. Via this study, we prove that the IoT-based approach is promising and can be a crucial feature to widen applications of indoor localization services.
introduction:
In recent years, the explosive development of the fourth industrial revolution has created enormous demands for inventing new technologies and improving old technologies for industrial and real-world applications. Indoor positioning is one of such technologies. It will provide unprecedented services in many aspects as fueled by the success of outdoor positioning technologies. Indoor positioning technology is expected to be the next significant leap for completing the global positioning system. Therefore, many researchers around the world are focusing on this direction.

In 2014, KAIST introduced the KAIST Indoor Localization System (https://kailos.io/) [1]. KAILOS is a complete indoor positioning system consisting of techniques and tools developed for three main components: KAI-Map, KAI-Pos, and KAI-Navi. With KAILOS, it aims at two primary objectives. Firstly, the system can provide indoor localization services to any area where Wi-Fi fingerprinting is available. Secondly, KAILOS provides the service with the required accuracy while maintaining simplicity in building indoor maps and radio maps. With built-in tools, KAILOS allows anyone to contribute to data collection through a standard 6-step process, including Building Registration, Floor Registration, Path and POI Registration, Fingerprint Collection Planning, Fingerprint Collection, and Radio Map Construction. It is known that KAILOS is one of the most accurate WiFi-based indoor positioning systems. As a result, KAILOS has been used in many places since 2014, such as universities, museums, and office buildings.

Although KAILOS is a complete and stable system, its positioning services are provided to end-users through mobile applications running on Android and IOS, the two most popular operating systems for smartphones globally. On the platform, the user’s device must acquire wifi-fingerprinting, bluetooth fingerprinting, and other sensor data for location estimation. However, the access to the signals is limited partially or totally by the OS. For example, in the IOS operating system, the application is not allowed to scan WiFi signals from the surrounding environment, while the Android OS provides an API for this purpose with restrictions on scanning frequency and scanning time (both foreground and background scan) that may cause a serious problem with consistent localization. Further, the installation of the application causes inconvenience for occasional users and one-time users. These problems significantly limit the scalability of KAILOS in fields.AP

To eliminate the dependence on operating systems and enrich the applications of KAILOS, this paper presents a new approach based on Internet of Things (IoT). Accordingly, we propose an extended architecture of KAILOS system with the participation of specially designed wearable devices that assist smartphone users in accessing KAILOS services regardless of the operating system. The IoT device is equipped with multiple connectivities and sensors, including LTE, WiFi, BLE, GNSS, light sensor, pressure sensor, and inertial sensor. By being interfered deeply to the physical layer, the device allows continuous data collection at high sampling rates to feed the KAILOS engine for estimating the precise location. Users can easily access locating services via mobile web browsers by scanning a barcode printed on the IoT device without installing any smartphone application. The approach based on IoT enables a plug-and-play service.

In the remaining part of the paper, we will briefly describe the related works (Section II), then focus on explaining the overall structure of the extended architecture (Section III), and the design of the IoT device (Section IV). In Section V, we will present the experimental setup and results of the evaluation. The final part of the paper is Section VI, where we draw our conclusion with the limitation of the study and future works.

title: From Egocentric Human Video to Robot Manipulation in the Era of Embodied Intelligence
authors: Yi Wang,Jingqiu Wu,Lei Yao,Zhaoshuo Li,Haoyu Zhu,Yirui Zhou,Huaiyuan Xu,Ying Zheng,Chuang Yang,Lap-Pui Chau
abstract: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data’s contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.
introduction:
Embodied intelligence studies how agents perceive, learn, and act in the physical world, with robot manipulation focusing on interactions that change object states to achieve task goals. Robot manipulation policies demand robot-object interaction experience that covers different tasks, objects, and environments [149]. Collecting this experience directly on robots requires physical platforms, repeated task execution, teleoperation, and scene setup. However, these collection requirements restrict both the scalability and variety of robot demonstrations available for policy learning [111; 71]. This limitation motivates supplementing robot demonstrations with hand-object interaction (HOI) videos.

Egocentric human video (EHV), recorded by human-worn cameras during everyday activities, provides such HOI experience and a potential of scalability and variety. Large-scale EHV datasets record human activities across tasks and environments without requiring a robot to perform each interaction [34; 50]. In an egocentric view, the camera often records the demonstrator’s hands, manipulated objects, and their changing spatial relationships at close range [148]. Its temporal structure reveals how interactions unfold, including action ordering, object state changes, and task progression. These spatial and temporal cues offer interaction priors and task information for learning visual representations and manipulation policies.

Human video leaves the robot’s control problem underspecified. Specifically, human hands and robot end-effectors differ in morphology and motion capabilities. Human-worn and robot-mounted cameras also observe interactions from different viewpoints. Moreover, EHV does not record robot action commands, and visual observations alone cannot fully determine the forces and contact dynamics required for execution. Existing approaches attempted to exploit EHV through cross-domain alignment of human and robot demonstrations [71] and visual representation pretraining [118]. Recently, latent action pretraining derives action-like targets from visual transitions without recorded action labels [189]. We use the term Ego2Robot learning for learning manipulation-relevant knowledge from EHV and grounding it in the capabilities of the target robot.

Existing reviews address robot learning from robot demonstrations, general human videos, and embodied manipulation [31; 38; 101; 190; 212], where the comparisons with ours are shown in Table 1. Recently, Ma et al. [101] organize human-video-based learning into task-, observation-, and action-oriented transfer pathways. Feng et al. [43] distinguish latent actions, predictive world models, and explicit 2D/3D supervision for VLA learning. Our review examines how EHV observation conditions affect robot manipulation through Ego2Robot learning. We therefore compare what information is derived, how robots use it during training or deployment, and what additional data or grounding is required.

Figure 1 illustrates the four learning paradigms and the data resources that support them. We distinguish four paradigms according to how human video contributes to Ego2Robot learning: 1) explicit embodiment transfer explicitly converts EHV’s human manipulation behavior into robot-format training data; 2) explicit action and task supervision extracts interpretable signals from EHV that guide policy learning or execution; 3) egocentric video representation pretraining learns visual representations from EHV for downstream manipulation; and 4) latent action and dynamics modeling learns action abstractions and predictive models from EHV’s visual experience. Alongside them, we consider EHV as the primary source of human experience, robot demonstrations as a source of embodiment-specific grounding, and synthetic and simulated data as resources for augmentation and physically grounded learning.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we organize Ego2Robot learning into four paradigms and review their supporting data sources, as shown in Figure 1. Second, we compare the information used by these paradigms and examine how first-person observation constraints affect their additional supervision and grounding requirements. Third, we identify open challenges in physically feasible transfer, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control. We consider both training-time knowledge transfer and deployment-time use of demonstrations and feedback.

Scope and literature selection.
The core literature reviewed in this paper satisfies two criteria: it uses EHV as a source of training data, supervision, or task information, and it connects that information to robot manipulation through policy learning, planning, or execution. Studies using mixed data sources are included when their use of EHV is explicitly documented; their inclusion does not imply that reported gains can be attributed to EHV alone. We consider both peer-reviewed publications and publicly available preprints as literature in this paper. Foundational video-learning methods, perception models, robot demonstrations, and synthetic data resources are discussed as methodological context or complementary grounding rather than evidence of Ego2Robot learning in their own right.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 presents the problem formulation and four learning paradigms.
Section 3 reviews the supporting training data landscape.
Section 4 discusses open challenges and future directions, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

title: Few-Shot Residual Adaptation of Pretrained Latent World Models
authors: Jakub Suliga,Pankhuri Vanjani,Nisarga Nilavadi,Wolfram Burgard,Rudolf Lioutikov
abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.
introduction:
World models predict how observations evolve under
robot actions and have been used to support planning and control
[7, 4, 25]. Latent world models are particularly promising because they can learn task-relevant representations without predicting every pixel, enabling efficient model-based control from visual observations [1, 29, 5].
A central challenge is that a model trained under one set of physical conditions may be deployed under another. Changes in center of mass, friction, payload, actuator properties, or contact dynamics can alter the effect of the same action even when the task, visual appearance, and goal remain unchanged [14, 15, 2].
Existing approaches often address this mismatch by retraining the model [13], estimating
physical parameters [14, 2], adapting a policy [15, 11], or randomizing dynamics during training [18]. These strategies can be effective, but they may require substantial data, access to the training procedure, a suitable parameterization of the dynamics, or prior knowledge about the deployment shift.

In this work, we study how a pretrained latent world model can be efficiently adapted from a few interactions. We keep the pretrained model frozen and learn lightweight residual corrections from its prediction errors. These corrections are trained self-supervised from observed transitions, requiring neither rewards nor knowledge of the changed physical parameters. We inject them at two points in the latent dynamics pipeline: within the predictor and on its predicted latent state.
We evaluate this setting in simulation and on a real robot under shifted
center-of-mass and modified friction setting. These changes reduce the success of the
frozen world model to near zero, while adaptation from only three interaction
episodes recovers most of the lost performance. We find that adapting
both inside the predictor and at its output works better than adapting either
location alone. Our diagnostics further show that much of the correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while the large control gap between general- and
shifted-dynamics adapters suggests that some of the learned correction depends
on the dynamics seen during adaptation.

Our main contributions are:

Dynamics-shift failure: We show that physical dynamics shifts can break control while the task and controller remain fixed.

Few-shot residual adaptation: We restore control from a few self-supervised interactions while keeping the pretrained world model frozen.

Dual-site correction: We show that adapting both inside the predictor and on its output outperforms single-site alternatives.

title: GEMOR-GS: Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM
authors: Yuchen Yang,Ming Ding,Xinyu Wu,Hesheng Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR–inertial–visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation.
3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable because it supplies the explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model.
In this paper, we present a novel method, GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable.
The refined model can give the environment a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making, such as object detection, path planning, relocalization, and mapping.
In order to improve the quality of the 3DGS map, before modeling, the LiDAR–camera extrinsic is estimated offline first by a direct-method LiDAR–camera alignment over dedicated calibration segments.
It can be reused by all following online and offline processes.
Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian map parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR–projection objective.
Then, the method rebuilds the final global reconstruction from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted. For the robot SLAM lifecycle, this method can recover the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss by an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement.
Experiments on several different datasets (one self-collected and five public sequences) quantified each element.
Our offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3–19.9 dB.
Compared with another method (Gaussian-LIC2), our method can improve the 𝐏𝐒𝐍𝐑\mathrm{PSNR} by approximately 9 dB.
Held-out relocalization succeeds on 86–100% of queries on most estimated sequences, and its reliability is tied to extrinsic quality.
The experiment result shows that the proposed method can improve the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map.
It can be used as a dependable robot world model representation for robot SLAM and downstream tasks.
introduction:
In recent years, 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) has become the dominant explicit radiance-field representation for SLAM and dense reconstruction, and LiDAR–inertial–visual (LIV) tightly coupled SLAM systems augmented with it promise robots a photorealistic and metrically consistent world representation [8, 29, 5].
Beyond rendering benchmarks, 3DGS models are also increasingly deployed as world-model representations:
embodied agents build Gaussian world representations of goal states for visual rearrangement [21];
end-to-end driving stacks use splatting as the scene representation of a predictive world model [28];
and object-centric Gaussian world models learn action-conditioned rigid-body dynamics to support model predictive control [10].
This trend assigns the SLAM-produced 3DGS map a more demanding role than that of an offline asset scored by rendering metrics.
The map must serve as a queryable and dependable world representation that supports localization, mapping, and downstream decision-making over continuous operation.
Geometric accuracy (calibration and poses), appearance fidelity (reconstruction quality), and re-enterability (relocalization) are first-order prerequisites.

However, most current LIV fusion pipelines are still not queryable and dependable enough for robot SLAM and world-model deployment.
Geometric accuracy demands trustworthy spatiotemporal calibration.
LiDAR–camera extrinsic residuals and the nearest-pairing offset are written into every keyframe’s depth–color binding, and hence into the Gaussian supervision.
The ghosting observed in fused maps mixes three coupled sources: spatial extrinsic residuals, the temporal pairing offset, and pose suboptimality.
The online filter produces only locally optimal Markov estimates of pose and absorbs extrinsic residuals only up to the observability limit.
A trustworthy calibration should be applied to ensure the accuracy of the extrinsic.
The extrinsic must be estimated before refining the poses and map.
And the propagation of extrinsic quality into reconstruction and relocalization must be quantified, not just be assumed.
Appearance fidelity demands a global refinement stage.
The real-time budget admits only limited per-frame optimization over a field-of-view (FoV) sliding window, without densification and with low-order spherical harmonics.
Therefore, the online map remains a tracking aid rather than the final reconstruction.
The benefit of calibration and pose refinement must propagate into reconstruction quality, which requires a global reconstruction stage that inherits the refined calibration and poses.
Re-enterability demands a recovery mechanism in the robot SLAM lifecycle.
Tracking loss is inevitable in real deployments, arising from fast rotation, motion blur, lighting change, and dynamic occlusion.
If the 3DGS map does not provide the ability to recover the pose, a robot cannot re-enter the map, resume mapping, or support downstream tasks.
Most existing 3DGS SLAM work stops at offline rendering evaluation.
For using 3DGS mapping in robot SLAM, the lifecycle of tracking, loss, recovery, and resumption would be an indispensable consideration.

In this research, we present a novel method — GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM), which is a LiDAR–inertial–visual SLAM system that estimates poses under a real-time budget and archives keyframes.
It upgrades the SLAM-produced 3DGS map from an offline render asset to a dependable robot world model.
It is a representation whose geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability can be relied upon by localization, mapping, and downstream decision-making over continuous operation for a robot even when tracking loss occurs.
In this method, for the extrinsic calibration, a direct-method module is used to estimate the LiDAR–camera extrinsic offline over dedicated calibration segments and supplies it to other modules.
The offline track then refines keyframe poses and the Gaussian map alternately, purifying the depth–color supervision that drives Gaussian training.
For offline mapping, a global reconstruction stage re-initializes the Gaussian model from the refined keyframe schema and executes global densification, pruning, and spherical-harmonics order elevation, turning the online sliding-window map into the final high-fidelity reconstruction.
For relocalization, a bypass module matches XFeat descriptors against a lightweight relocalization database, obtains a coarse pose by RANSAC-PnP, and refines it by Gaussian RGB-D warp alignment, enabling the robot to recover its global pose after tracking loss.

This work makes the following three primary contributions:

A global-optimized reconstruction stage.
Our method promotes the online map—a FoV sliding-window tracking aid—to the final reconstruction, so that refinements in calibration and poses translate into gains in appearance fidelity.
The stage re-initializes the Gaussian model from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted, and executes global densification, pruning, and spherical-harmonics order elevation.
It can make the 3DGS map more photorealistic and metrically consistent.

A relocalization module for the robot SLAM lifecycle.
Our method recovers the global pose from the 3DGS map through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement.
Based on the globally optimized and reconstructed 3DGS map, the re-embedded pose can be estimated accurately enough to resume mapping and support downstream tasks.

A calibration-quality-controlled mapping framework.
Our method makes the geometry that supervises Gaussian training trustworthy by evaluating the quality of the extrinsic calibration offline.
The extrinsic is estimated by an adopted direct-method LiDAR–camera alignment [9] over dedicated calibration segments.
The residuals will be written into every keyframe’s depth–color binding and pose filtering will absorb them only up to the observability limit.
Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian map parameters will be refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR-projection objective.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 reviews related works, covering the background of 3D Gaussian splatting and the recent 3DGS SLAM systems.
Section 3 presents the method: the system overview and the three main modules: the calibration refinement module, the global reconstruction module and the relocalization module.
Section 4 reports the experiments, including the setup, the extrinsic calibration evaluation, the online and offline reconstruction evaluation, and the relocalization evaluation.
Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines some future directions.

title: Differentiable Filtering for Inertial Odometry
authors: Yaru Gu,Ting Zou
abstract:
Accurate inertial odometry is critical for autonomous systems but suffers from unbounded drift caused by the integration of sensor noise and biases. In approaches such as TLIO, neural pseudo-measurements are trained independently of their downstream filter. This paper introduces Differentiable Filtering for Inertial Odometry (DFIO), a learning framework that embeds the update stages of an error-state Kalman filter directly into a computational graph. Following standalone pre-training, DFIO jointly
optimizes the displacement and covariance output heads using
posterior-position supervision through differentiable measurement
updates. The proposed system is validated on public pedestrian motion datasets featuring both calibrated and uncalibrated inertial measurements. Experimental results on a pedestrian dataset demonstrate that DFIO reduces mean absolute and one-second relative translation errors by 13.2% and 39.6% relative to the TLIO baseline, and by 7.7% and 17.4% relative to its pre-trained counterpart. Furthermore, evaluations on uncalibrated smartphone inertial data indicate that the proposed method effectively mitigates translational drift and maintains trajectory alignment under highly noisy sensor conditions. Source code will be made publicly available.
introduction:
Reliable estimates of position and orientation are essential for a multitude of engineering applications, including robot navigation [1], autonomous-vehicle localization [2], the registration of virtual content in augmented reality [3], and pedestrian motion tracking [4, 5], to name a few. For mobile platforms, inertial measurement units (IMUs) offer a compact, low-cost source of high-rate motion information. Because they measure angular velocity and specific force without observing the surrounding scene, they remain useful when external positioning signals or visual features are unavailable [6, 7]. These advantages make inertial odometry (IO) an important component of autonomous navigation, but obtaining accurate trajectories from inertial measurements alone remains challenging.

Strapdown inertial navigation first integrates angular velocity to estimate orientation, then uses that orientation to transform specific force into a navigation frame and recover velocity and position [8]. Biases, measurement noise, and orientation errors therefore affect not only individual estimates but also the subsequent trajectory, causing drift to accumulate over time [6]. Calibration can reduce systematic errors, including nonlinear scale-factor effects [9], but residual errors and stochastic noise still propagate through the integration [10].

A common way to control this drift is to introduce complementary observations. Chen et al. [4] combined learned pedestrian motion increments with Bluetooth localization in a particle filter. In robotic navigation, Alkhawaja et al. [11] fused depth-based localization with inertial estimates using cascade-correlation networks, while Zhang et al. [12] combined learned optical-flow tracking with visual–inertial optimization under changing illumination. These approaches demonstrate how additional observations can complement inertial integration. When such observations are unavailable, however, an IMU-only estimator must instead draw on information about the motion itself.

Learning-based IO provides a way to extract this information from data [13]. Methods such as IONet [14] and RoNIN [15] learn motion increments or velocities from inertial sequences and compose them into trajectories. Their predictions capture regularities that are difficult to express through sensor calibration alone, but prediction errors can still accumulate during trajectory reconstruction. Hybrid methods therefore combine learned motion measurements with analytical IMU propagation: TLIO [7] supplies displacement measurements and their covariances to an extended Kalman filter (EKF), while DIVE [16] uses learned velocity measurements in an on-manifold EKF. The filter balances these learned motion priors against its propagated estimate according to their uncertainties.

When learned predictions are fused with an inertial prior, training can also account for their effect on the resulting state estimate. In TLIO and DIVE, the measurement networks are trained against reference displacement or velocity targets. Such supervision improves the local predictions, but does not directly optimize the state estimate obtained after the filter combines them with its prior. Differentiable filtering provides a means of bringing that downstream objective into training [17, 18]. This idea is already relevant to inertial navigation: AI-IMU Dead-Reckoning [19] and the pedestrian method of Wang et al. [20] train covariance adapters using errors in the filter’s estimated motion. These methods learn how strongly to trust prescribed motion constraints, but they need to construct their pseudo-measurements from specific assumptions about the motion. This motivates investigating whether filter-output supervision can refine pseudo-measurements learned directly from IMU data.

We address this question with Differentiable Filtering for Inertial Odometry (DFIO). As shown in Fig. 1, DFIO combines an error-state Kalman filter (ESKF) with IncNet, a temporal network that predicts three-dimensional displacement increments and diagonal measurement covariances in a local gravity-aligned frame. The network is first trained using displacement supervision. Its displacement and covariance heads are then refined together using posterior-position supervision through differentiable filter updates, while the pretrained temporal encoder is held fixed. The propagation model retains the deterministic IMU kinematics; the learnable quantities are the neural measurement predictions and their uncertainties. This allows the training objective to assess those predictions through their effect on the estimated trajectory.

The contributions of this work are:

A learned inertial measurement model that combines temporal residual features and self-attention to predict three-dimensional displacement increments and measurement covariances for an ESKF.

A two-stage training strategy that jointly refines the displacement and covariance heads using filter posterior-position feedback, while retaining the analytical IMU propagation model of the ESKF.

An evaluation on held-out TLIO pedestrian trajectories, with comparisons and ablations examining the effects of displacement and covariance refinement. An additional evaluation on a subset of the OxIOD dataset [21] examines performance with noisy, uncalibrated smartphone IMU measurements.

1. A learned inertial measurement model that combines temporal residual features and self-attention to predict three-dimensional displacement increments and measurement covariances for an ESKF.

2. A two-stage training strategy that jointly refines the displacement and covariance heads using filter posterior-position feedback, while retaining the analytical IMU propagation model of the ESKF.

3. An evaluation on held-out TLIO pedestrian trajectories, with comparisons and ablations examining the effects of displacement and covariance refinement. An additional evaluation on a subset of the OxIOD dataset [21] examines performance with noisy, uncalibrated smartphone IMU measurements.

title: DeRep: Learning Depth Representations for End-to-End Navigation in Cluttered Environments
authors: Hanyu Jin,Kenji Shimada
abstract:
End-to-end navigation in cluttered environments relies
on compact visual representations to support collision avoidance and goal-directed motion. Existing methods typically learn these
representations jointly with the policy or through observation reconstruction, which does not explicitly specify
what information the representation should preserve. Moreover, they are usually
evaluated with a single downstream policy learner, although the
benefit of a representation may depend on how the policy is
learned. It therefore remains unclear how different
representation-learning objectives affect downstream navigation
performance and robustness.
This work proposes DeRep, a navigation-oriented representation-learning method that combines local bird’s-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction. The joint objective encourages the encoder to capture local free-space connectivity while retaining scene information beyond the reachability targets. To compare representation objectives under controlled conditions, we pretrain encoders with a common architecture and freeze them during downstream learning. We evaluate the representations using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with PPO. DeRep achieves the lowest linear policy probe prediction error and outperforms
reconstruction alone across all six tested PPO conditions
by 15.1-21.3 percentage points in mean success rate,
achieving the highest mean success rate in four conditions. In imitation learning, both reachability-based objectives achieve higher mean success rates than reconstruction alone, with similar mean success rates between the reachability-only
and joint objectives. These results demonstrate consistent benefits of incorporating
reachability supervision into depth representation pretraining
across different downstream learning methods and evaluation
conditions. We further deploy the PPO policy with the frozen DeRep encoder in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor without fine-tuning,
demonstrating its capability for zero-shot sim-to-sim and
sim-to-real transfer.
introduction:
Safe navigation is essential for robots performing tasks such as
inspection and exploration in cluttered environments
[1][2].
Modular navigation systems typically separate perception, mapping,
planning, and control [3][4].
End-to-end approaches instead learn a direct mapping from depth
images and robot state to actions or trajectories
[5][6].
For depth-based policies, an encoder typically compresses the depth
image into a latent representation on which the policy bases its
decisions. Transferring a policy from simulation to the real world
therefore depends in part on whether this representation continues
to provide useful navigation information under conditions not
encountered during training.

Existing learning-based navigation methods often train the encoder
jointly with the policy from scratch, allowing the downstream learning objective
to shape the representation [5][7].
This provides task-driven supervision but does not explicitly specify
which information about the environment the representation should
preserve.
Other methods use reconstruction-based objectives to learn depth
representations, either by reconstructing the original observation
[6] or a transformed depth image that accounts for the
robot’s size [8].
While reconstruction-based objectives encourage the preservation
of scene geometry, reconstruction performance alone does not
establish how effectively the resulting features support
downstream navigation.

In this work, we ask what information a depth representation should
preserve to support collision-free, goal-directed navigation.
Specifically, we investigate whether explicitly
supervising local free-space connectivity provides benefits
beyond depth reconstruction alone.
The usefulness of a representation may also depend on how the
downstream policy is learned and on the evaluation conditions
[9].
A controlled comparison is therefore needed to examine how
representation learning objectives affect navigation performance
and robustness under changes in environment geometry and
depth observations.

To investigate these questions, we propose DeRep, a navigation-oriented representation
learning method that combines local reachability supervision with
depth reconstruction.
The reachability objective predicts an ego-centric bird’s-eye-view (BEV)
map of reachable space and the associated shortest-path distance to each reachable cell, encouraging
the representation to capture local free-space connectivity (Sec. IV-A).
Depth reconstruction complements this objective by encouraging
the preservation of pixel-level depth information (Sec. IV-B).

We evaluate the representations using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with PPO. The linear policy probe tests whether expert future displacements can be predicted from the frozen representation and navigation state using a linear readout (Sec. VI-A). The two downstream policy learners then evaluate whether the representations support closed-loop navigation under imitation learning (Sec. VI-B) and reinforcement learning (Sec. VI-C). For reinforcement learning, we further evaluate PPO-trained policies under out-of-distribution (OOD) obstacle geometries unseen during training, and under depth corruption including
Gaussian noise, pixel dropout, and quantization, to examine robustness to changes in environment geometry and depth observations. Finally, we compare the PPO policies qualitatively in Gazebo (Sec. VI-D) and deploy the policy with the DeRep encoder on a physical quadrotor without fine-tuning (Sec. VI-E).

The main contributions of this work are:

A navigation-oriented representation-learning method
that combines BEV reachability supervision with depth
reconstruction to learn features for goal-directed navigation.

A systematic evaluation of representation objectives
using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning,
and PPO.

Zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real deployment
of the PPO policy with the frozen DeRep encoder,
demonstrated through a qualitative comparison in Gazebo simulations
and physical flight experiments.

1. A navigation-oriented representation-learning method
that combines BEV reachability supervision with depth
reconstruction to learn features for goal-directed navigation.

2. A systematic evaluation of representation objectives
using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning,
and PPO.

3. Zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real deployment
of the PPO policy with the frozen DeRep encoder,
demonstrated through a qualitative comparison in Gazebo simulations
and physical flight experiments.

title: Route-Time Conflict Maps for Cooperative End-to-End Autonomous Driving
authors: Haohua Que,Mingkai Liu,Tianle Zhu,Zhipeng Bao,Yiping Li,Handong Yao
abstract:
Existing cooperative end-to-end driving works at Class A (status-sharing) of the SAE J3216 classes of cooperative driving automation (CDA): vehicles exchange what they perceive, not what they intend, so each plans alone when to go, which limits cooperation and leads to deadlock when both vehicles yield or to collisions when both go.
We present When2Go, a cooperative end-to-end driving system that learns when to go by sharing intent under CDA Class B or higher.
Each vehicle broadcasts its LiDAR detections with forecast motion as instance tokens, together with its plan and intended trajectory.
The receiver draws the fused detections, forecasts and partner plans into a route-time conflict map, the occupancy along its route over the planning horizon, on which a planner scores candidate speed profiles.
Where two intended trajectories conflict, an order gate, a precedence network distilled from a right-of-way rule, decides who goes first; both vehicles evaluate it on the same messages and so reach the same order.
When2Go imitates the rule-based expert of V2Xverse, which sees the simulator’s ground truth; stops that When2Go cannot observe within its 22 s planning horizon are relabelled, so that it does not learn to wait without an observable cause.
For our runs only, the benchmarks’ PID controller steers by When2Go’s waypoints instead of the route, and its forced push of long-waiting vehicles is off.
With one model, When2Go sets the state of the art on three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks: 97.897.8 and 90.790.7 driving score on InterDrive without and with traffic (best published 90.190.1 and 78.978.9), 70.070.0 on the public V2Xverse protocol (best of sixteen rerun methods 59.159.1) and 88.288.2 on MDrive (best rerun 85.185.1), with 95.0%95.0\,\% of its vehicles collision-free (87.7%87.7\,\%).
introduction:
Connected vehicles can see for each other: a partner’s LiDAR covers the crosswalk behind a truck, a roadside unit sees the whole junction.
SAE J3216 [62] divides cooperative driving automation (CDA) into four classes: vehicles share their status and perception (Class A, status-sharing) or what they plan to do (Class B, intent-sharing), exchange messages to agree on their actions (Class C, agreement-seeking), or one party directs the others (Class D, prescriptive).
Existing cooperative end-to-end driving [49, 45, 86] works at Class A: it exchanges what the vehicles perceive, not what they intend.
Yet where vehicles meet, at intersections, merges and lane changes, the difficult part is not to see the other vehicle but to decide, for every vehicle, when to go, and each decides alone: if both yield, they wait until the benchmark ends the run as blocked; if both go, they collide.
Language-based negotiation [48, 34], a form of Class C, settles such conflicts with language and vision-language models but degrades in dense traffic and under pose noise [17].

We start from the observation that this decision is one-dimensional along the vehicle’s own route: is the stretch ahead free at the time the vehicle would be there?
When2Go draws everything that can block this stretch, the fused detections with their forecast motion and the plans that partner vehicles broadcast, as occupancy over route position and future time: a route-time conflict map.
A planner scores candidate speed profiles on this map and learns how far to drive in the next two seconds, from standing still to full speed (Fig. 2); the benchmarks’ PID controller tracks its waypoints, and no hand-written rule overrides them.

Two further ingredients make the decisions of several vehicles fit together.
First, the vehicles share intent (Class B): each also broadcasts an intended trajectory, how it would drive along its route if the road were free.
Where two intended trajectories meet, an order gate, a precedence network distilled from a right-of-way rule, decides who goes first.
Both vehicles evaluate it on the same two messages, so with an ideal channel they reach the same order without the message rounds of Class C; each draws the order into its conflict map, and the planner chooses the speed within it.
Second, When2Go imitates the rule-based expert of V2Xverse [49], which sees the simulator’s ground truth and often stops for reasons that When2Go cannot observe within its 22 s planning horizon, e.g. because another vehicle, assumed to keep driving straight, might cross its path.
Copying these stops teaches When2Go to wait without an observable cause, and two such vehicles deadlock; we relabel them with targets based only on what it can observe within this horizon, a temporal form of the learner-expert asymmetry [55].

We evaluate one model in closed loop on three CARLA [22] benchmarks with one to eight controlled vehicles ().
On InterDrive [48], When2Go reaches 97.897.8 and 90.790.7 driving score without and with background traffic (best published 90.190.1 and 78.978.9).
On MDrive [17], it reaches 88.288.2 (best rerun 85.185.1), with 95.0%95.0\,\% of its vehicles collision-free against at most 87.7%87.7\,\%.
On V2Xverse [49], where we rerun sixteen published methods and two variants on the public protocol (all from released checkpoints but one reimplementation), it reaches 70.070.0 against 59.159.1 and collides with another vehicle in 66 of 100100 runs, against 3838 to 6969 for the cooperative reruns. Our contributions are:

A route-time conflict map for cooperative end-to-end planning: fused detections, forecasts and partner plans as occupancy along the ego’s future route, from which a planner learns whether the route ahead will be clear on arrival, supervised by an expert that sees more, whose stops beyond the 22 s horizon are relabelled; to our knowledge, the first CDA Class B-or-higher end-to-end planner.

An order gate for agreement from shared messages: an antisymmetric precedence network on the broadcast intended trajectories yields a cycle-free order, drawn into the conflict map as occupancy.

State-of-the-art closed-loop results on three benchmarks with one end-to-end model, with reruns of sixteen methods and two variants on the public V2Xverse protocol and paired 95%95\,\% confidence intervals for the differences.

1. A route-time conflict map for cooperative end-to-end planning: fused detections, forecasts and partner plans as occupancy along the ego’s future route, from which a planner learns whether the route ahead will be clear on arrival, supervised by an expert that sees more, whose stops beyond the 22 s horizon are relabelled; to our knowledge, the first CDA Class B-or-higher end-to-end planner.

2. An order gate for agreement from shared messages: an antisymmetric precedence network on the broadcast intended trajectories yields a cycle-free order, drawn into the conflict map as occupancy.

3. State-of-the-art closed-loop results on three benchmarks with one end-to-end model, with reruns of sixteen methods and two variants on the public V2Xverse protocol and paired 95%95\,\% confidence intervals for the differences.

title: ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control
authors: Xu Luo,Jiaying Yang,Hao Wu,Junlin Xie,Zijin Hong,Ji Zhang,Lianli Gao,Jingkuan Song
abstract: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.
introduction:
Robot policies trained on demonstration datasets have enabled increasingly complex and generalizable behaviors across a wide range of robotic control tasks [57, 1]. A key technique shared by many of these policies is action chunking [70]. Rather than predicting a single action at each query, action-chunked policies predict a sequence of actions and execute them open-loop, which can help capture non-Markovian structure in demonstrations [32, 39] and reduce compounding errors [32, 68]. A common choice in recent robot policies is to predict long action chunks, often exceeding 20 steps and approaching 50, as in vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} [8] and π0\pi_{0}-FAST [48], and world action models such as DreamZero [65]. By producing many actions per model query, long chunks enable high-frequency control (e.g., 50 Hz) for dexterous tasks such as laundry folding [9], while reducing inference pauses for smoother, faster execution.

These long-chunk robot policies, while performant, are rarely optimal when deployed in the real world due to limited demonstration coverage and imperfect generalization [55]. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a direct way to adapt these policies from online experience. In other domains such as language modeling, online RL has been shown to be quite effective for adapting models pretrained on offline datasets [45, 24, 21]. For robotic control, however, online data collection in the real world is often slow, costly, and sometimes unsafe, making sample efficiency a central requirement.

Yet we observe that long action chunks introduce a major bottleneck for sample-efficient adaptation (Figure , left). RL methods that optimize entire action chunks or their latent variables face an increasingly high-dimensional optimization space as the chunk length grows. This substantially increases the amount of online experience required for adaptation.

This motivates us to seek an adaptation interface whose dimensionality does not grow with the chunk length. We observe that action-chunked policies naturally expose such an interface, namely, how long to execute a predicted chunk before querying the policy again. Although execution length is a simple scalar decision, adapting it to the current state and predicted action chunk can substantially alter policy behavior by controlling the trade-off between longer open-loop execution, which better exploits the benefits of action chunking, and shorter execution, which improves responsiveness to unexpected state changes or dynamics mismatch [39]. This makes execution length a meaningful variable for policy improvement, while being particularly attractive for long chunks: as the chunk size grows, the number of possible execution lengths—and hence the expressivity—increases, whereas the optimization itself remains a low-dimensional discrete problem.

We instantiate this idea as Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a sample-efficient online RL method for adapting long-chunk policies.
It adds a lightweight execution-length policy that selects how many actions from each predicted chunk to execute before replanning, and trains it using standard off-policy RL algorithms. Because this adapter can be learned without modifying the base policy itself, ExRL provides a policy-agnostic interface that can be applied to virtually any class of action-chunked policies. Execution-length control is ultimately bounded by the capabilities of the underlying base policy. To go beyond this limitation, we can further optionally distill successful online trajectories back into the base policy during RL using simple imitation loss, allowing the base policy itself to improve alongside the adapter. Finally, ExRL can also leverage general offline data, such as human demonstrations, by reinterpreting arbitrary trajectory segments as off-policy experience under different execution lengths, further improving online sample efficiency.

We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of ExRL across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, showing state-of-the-art online adaptation performance across a range of long-chunk policies, largely without task-specific hyperparameter tuning. These include standard action-chunked policies, different classes of pretrained VLA models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} [8] and π0\pi_{0}-FAST [48], as well as a world action model, Cosmos Policy [27]. On real-world tasks spanning precise manipulation, long-horizon coordination, and clothing folding, ExRL efficiently adapts frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies, approaching perfect success on cube stacking with about ten minutes of physical interaction.

title: Rhythmic-Semantic Co-Speech Gestures for Emotional Dialogue in Robots
authors: Christian Arzate Cruz,Edwin C. Montiel-Vázquez,Stefanos Gkikas,Miguel Mejia Tobar,Randy Gomez
abstract: Co-speech gestures can increase engagement and improve speech understanding. Yet, most data-driven robot systems generate either rhythmic beat-like motion or semantically meaningful iconic gestures, but not both. We present an emotion-aware rhythmic–semantic co-speech gesture system that generates iconic and beat behaviors in real time from text and the robot’s internal emotional state. We formalize the task of beat–iconic gesture generation using emotion and propose lightweight models that predict iconic timing and intensity, then fill the remaining spans with emotion-conditioned beats at an appropriate intensity level. We train on the BEAT2 dataset and deploy the system on the social robot Haru. In an online user study with 6060 participants, our method shows stronger speech–gesture alignment and is preferred over baseline methods.
introduction:
Humans convey meaning and internal states through body gestures and facial expressions. These cues range from large, deliberate movements that depict what people say to small, rhythmic motions that accompany speech. We call the former iconic gestures and the latter beat gestures [1]. Prior work on robot co-speech gestures rarely models both types in one system, unlike recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) co-speech generation systems for artificial agents [2, 3]. Therefore, we aim to generate a single co-speech gesture system that includes both iconic and beat gestures, while remaining coherent with the utterance and the robot’s emotional state (Figure 1).

Robots must also adapt motion to emotion. Many co-speech approaches do not explicitly model how emotion changes movement [4, 5, 6]. We focus on four emotions from Plutchik’s wheel [7]: joy, anger, sadness, and fear. Given an utterance and a target emotion, our system generates co-speech gestures that communicate both what the robot says and how it feels. In this paper, we use the term iconic to denote content-aligned co-speech animations that convey the intended emotional meaning of what is being said (i.e., emotion-specific variants), while beat gestures refer to non-semantic rhythmic motions that accompany speech.

Another key requirement in robotics is responsiveness. Many data-driven methods assume speech audio is available at inference time for prosody or synchronization [5, 8, 9, 10, 6, 4]. This assumption can add latency for interactive robots that use expressive text-to-speech (TTS) (e.g., about 2 s with GPT-SoVITS [11]). We therefore design a text-only system that takes only the utterance and the intended emotion.

Based on these constraints, we formalize a new robotics task: efficient, text-only generation of joint beat–iconic co-speech gestures that vary with emotion. We train lightweight models on the body-expression-audio-text (BEAT2) dataset [2] and generate iconic and beat motion in one coherent sequence. We deploy the system on the social robot Haru [12, 13, 14, 15] and evaluate it in an online user study (N=60N=60). Participants rate our method higher for speech–gesture correlation across emotions and prefer it in most conversations compared to baselines.

Our contributions are as follows:

1) We define a new task for social robots: generating a single co-speech gesture stream that fuses beat and iconic gestures while accounting for emotion. This allows the use of BEAT2 for non-humanoid robots.

2) We propose lightweight models that predict which words trigger iconic gestures and estimate their intensity only from text and emotion. Likewise, we train the same model architectures to predict beat gesture intensity.

3) We integrate all our models into a gesture generation system that runs in real time without audio at inference and can map to different non-humanoid robot embodiments.

title: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation
authors: Haejoon Lee,Thomas Marshall Vielmetti,Xinyi Wang,Dimitra Panagou
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: Decision making in multi-agent and multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation. Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training. To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases. Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost.
introduction:
Many decision-making problems in multi-robot and broadly multi-agent systems involve inherently discrete choices, such as assigning tasks to robots [18, 35, 11], selecting the modes of hybrid systems [25, 14], and avoiding obstacles [16, 19]. These decisions give rise to combinatorial optimization problems that are often NP-hard, with solution spaces growing exponentially with problem size, making high-quality solutions difficult to obtain within the tight time budgets of online operation.

A representative example, used throughout this paper, is the heterogeneous multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) problem, where robots with different skills, each at a different capability level, must complete spatially distributed tasks as quickly as possible [11, 1, 9] (Figure 1). Specifically, we consider joint coalition formation and scheduling, where each task requires tight coordination [31]: task execution begins only once a coalition with sufficient combined skill capabilities gathers at the task location. Robots must therefore jointly decide which robots serve each task (coalition formation) and when each robot executes its tasks (scheduling) to minimize makespan. This places the problem in the single-task robots, multi-robot tasks, time-extended assignment, cross-schedule dependencies (XD [ST-MR-TA]) category [18], with a combinatorial search space that grows rapidly with the numbers of robots and tasks, and complexity of the skill requirements. Since new tasks, robot dropouts, or travel delays may arise unexpectedly [9], robots must replan within seconds to dynamically adapt to such changing conditions.

There exist numerous approaches to these combinatorial optimization problems. Exact methods formulate problems as optimization programs [11, 8] and employ techniques such as Branch-and-Bound and cutting-plane methods [27], but scale poorly and become computationally expensive for large problems. Metaheuristics, such as simulated annealing (SA) [5], genetic algorithms [4, 26], ant colony optimization [3], and large neighborhood search [30, 39], offer faster solutions but require problem-specific local search operators or heuristics. Learning-based methods [38, 37, 9, 17] enable fast inference but require offline training and may generalize poorly to problem structures unconsidered during the training.

Sampling-based optimization (SBO) offers an alternative. SBO methods iteratively sample candidate solutions from a probability distribution and refine the distribution to concentrate its search on promising regions, without problem-specific local search algorithms or offline training. While closely related methods are known as model-based search algorithms in combinatorial optimization [42], we follow the robotics and control literature [40, 41] and adopt the term SBO in this paper. Classical SBO methods for discrete problems include the cross-entropy method (CEM) [32] and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) [10]. However, these methods struggle to explore large solution spaces with multimodal objective landscapes, i.e., objective functions with many local optima: CEM is prone to premature mode collapse, while SMC suffers from particle degeneracy that reduces sample diversity.

Meanwhile,  MBD (MBD) [29] has emerged as a promising SBO method that adapts the diffusion process of  DDPM (DDPM) [13] to optimization. MBD uses the known objective function to estimate the score function through Monte Carlo sampling, eliminating the need for offline neural network training. By gradually concentrating samples on low-cost regions through the diffusion process, MBD outperforms other SBO methods on nonconvex, non-differentiable problems [29, 20].

Diffusion-based search is also appealing for combinatorial optimization, where solution spaces are often large and highly multimodal [37, 17]. However, MBD denoises in a continuous space and thus cannot directly produce discrete decisions. Its solutions must be rounded, which degrades solution quality [37] and may lead to constraint violations. On the other hand, existing diffusion-based combinatorial optimization solvers [37, 23, 33, 21, 17] denoise directly over discrete variables using discrete diffusion models [15, 2]. However, they rely on a neural network to learn the denoising process offline.

To bridge this gap, we propose  DMBD (DMBD), a training-free SBO method that performs denoising diffusion directly over discrete decision variables, modeling each as a categorical random variable. At each denoising step, DMBD approximates the categorical reverse transition distribution with samples weighted by the known problem formulation, progressively steering the search toward high-quality solutions. The contributions of this paper are as follows:

We propose DMBD, an SBO method for combinatorial optimization that denoises directly over discrete decision variables by approximating the reverse transitions of discrete diffusion with Monte Carlo sampling.

We establish a finite-step probabilistic convergence guarantee for DMBD (Theorem 1) that characterizes its exploration-exploitation trade-off and shows that the probability of finding a global minimizer approaches one as the number of denoising steps increases.

We present a priority-based encoding scheme, inspired by [4], that guarantees every sample decodes into a feasible solution for heterogeneous MRTA, improving sampling efficiency.

We evaluate DMBD on numerous generic unconstrained integer programs and heterogeneous MRTA problems.

1. We propose DMBD, an SBO method for combinatorial optimization that denoises directly over discrete decision variables by approximating the reverse transitions of discrete diffusion with Monte Carlo sampling.

2. We establish a finite-step probabilistic convergence guarantee for DMBD (Theorem 1) that characterizes its exploration-exploitation trade-off and shows that the probability of finding a global minimizer approaches one as the number of denoising steps increases.

3. We present a priority-based encoding scheme, inspired by [4], that guarantees every sample decodes into a feasible solution for heterogeneous MRTA, improving sampling efficiency.

4. We evaluate DMBD on numerous generic unconstrained integer programs and heterogeneous MRTA problems.

title: AHEADance: Anticipatory Humanoid Dance from Streaming Audio
authors: Tianhu Peng,Yukun Wang,Lingfan Bao,Yiyang Jia,Chengxu Zhou
abstract:
A humanoid that dances to streamed music must commit each motion chunk before
it has heard the music that chunk accompanies, and must continue from motion it
has already committed. We present AHEADance, a robot-native streaming dance
generator executed on a humanoid robot by a whole-body tracker.
ListenAhead conditions each chunk on heard music and a frozen music
model’s forecasts of the coming music, aligned to their target times and
weighted by reliability. The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats
almost as well as the actual future; with them, the generator is better
synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at its song’s
beat frequency. Commit Forcing trains continuation from the model’s own
committed chunks, updating both the latent history and the decoded boundary of
the next chunk; it reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%, the level of real
dance. Three music evaluators, each validated on real G1 dance, test
synchronization, song and style. On a physical Unitree G1, it dances while the music plays and comes to rest when it stops, without a fall.
introduction:
A humanoid that dances to streamed music works under constraints that
offline choreography does not face. It hears only the music that has
already played, yet each motion chunk is generated from the music heard up to
the moment its own music begins, so that the delay from music to motion does not
grow with the chunk length. And committed
motion cannot be revised, so every new chunk has to continue from motion
the model itself produced rather than from a clean reference. Unlike
animation, every committed chunk is then executed by a whole-body tracking
controller on the robot, so it must also be trackable, and generation must
keep pace with the controller’s clock. Under these constraints the robot must
keep dancing for as long as the music plays, come to rest when it stops and
dance again when it returns.

Music-to-dance generators, including long-form
ones [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
receive the complete music in advance. Streaming humanoid systems hear the
music causally: DiscoForcing [6] streams with diffusion
forcing and retargets the generated human motion,
RoboPerform [7] maps audio to a control policy, and
InfiniDanceRobot [8] closes the loop between a
planner and its tracker; none of them describes forecasting the coming music.
Autoregressive generators trained on reference histories meet their own outputs
at inference; diffusion forcing [9] and self
forcing [10] address this for the history the generator
conditions on, whereas a chunked robot generator also conditions on the decoded
pose boundary it has committed.
For a robot-native streaming generator, three questions remain:
how much of the coming music a causal generator can use, how to continue
reliably from its own committed chunks when both the latent history and
the decoded pose boundary change, and how to show that the executed
behavior follows the music rather than its own momentum.

We present AHEADance (Figs.  and 2), which generates humanoid
reference motion chunk by chunk from streaming audio and executes it with
a whole-body tracking controller. Our contributions are:

ListenAhead. Each chunk is conditioned on heard music and
on short-horizon forecasts of a frozen music model [11],
aligned to their target times and weighted by their reliability. The
forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future,
and most of what the actual future carries about note onsets; a generator trained with them is
better synchronized
with the music and concentrates more motion energy at the song’s beat
frequency.

Commit Forcing. Continuation is trained from the model’s
own committed outputs: noise-corrupted reference chunks are reconstructed,
decoded and committed in order, and each commit updates both the latent
history and the decoded reference boundary that conditions the next chunk.
Low activity falls from 83.5% under reference-history training to 10.3%,
the level of real dance.

A validated evaluation of music correspondence. Three evaluators
test humanoid dance against its music: synchronization with ChoreoSync, a
detector of our own; song with MMR; and style with a style classifier. Each is
validated on real G1 dance it never saw. On songs unseen in training,
AHEADance reaches the highest ChoreoSync offset accuracy (28.6%) and MMR
(0.187, against at most 0.046) of all compared generators.
