title: PneuGen: Task-Driven Agentic Co-Design of Soft Pneumatic Robots
authors: Shaohong Zhong,Marco Pontin,Perla Maiolino
abstract: Task-driven design of soft robots requires the consideration of factors such as geometry, morphology, material properties, and actuation, resulting in a large and complex design space that is challenging to explore. Computational optimisation methods leverage signals from simulation to iteratively improve designs to achieve task objectives. However, these methods typically demand high computational load for both optimisation and simulation. We present PneuGen, an agentic co-design framework for soft robots that leverages Large Language Model (LLM) agents to search over the soft robot design space efficiently. A designer agent proposes design programs from a parametric component library, and a separate critic agent analyses simulation diagnostics and recommends targeted revisions. Fitted module response models provide reusable physical priors relating geometry and pressure to deformation. Design programs are automatically validated and converted into finite-element simulations, enabling iterative evaluation. Across grasping tasks on primitive shapes and challenging objects, as well as shape-matching tasks that require multi-directional planar and 3D deformation, the proposed framework significantly outperforms prior computational optimisation baselines. Ablation experiments also highlight the utility of the critic agent and the module response model in facilitating efficient design. We additionally demonstrate the agent-generated soft robot designs in real-world shape-matching and grasping tasks.
introduction:
Soft robots offer advantages of mechanical compliance, adaptability, and flexibility to achieve a wide range of behaviours, allowing them to accommodate uncertainty in tasks such as manipulation [1, 2]. However, their behaviour depends strongly on geometry, material properties, and the arrangement of compliant elements. These make the design of soft robots particularly challenging because of the large and complex design space, where morphology and actuation need to be selected jointly [3]. This coupling motivates task-driven design methods that select geometry and actuation together. In this aspect, heuristic methods rely heavily on the designer’s experience, which limits their scalability [4].

Computational methods have shown great potential in soft robot design [3, 5, 6, 4]. Prior approaches have explored both the optimisation of existing actuator families and the generation of new morphologies [5, 6, 4, 7]. Parametric methods optimise geometric and actuation variables using physical models or learned surrogates, enabling task-specific design of pneumatic actuators and tendon-driven soft hands [4]. Shape and topology optimisation extend the search to material distributions and structural features, while graph-based evolutionary methods explore alternative arrangements and connectivity[8]. Differentiable simulation and learned physical models further support the joint optimisation of morphology and actuation or grasp configuration [9, 10]. These advances demonstrate the potential of computational search across increasingly expressive design spaces. However, these methods typically have substantial computational requirements, not only in the design optimisation process, but also through the repeated simulation and evaluation that are required, motivating methods that extract more useful guidance from each evaluation. Furthermore, many of these computational approaches rely on manually crafted loss functions for optimisation, which both limit their generalisability and sometimes do not offer sufficient appropriate signals [9, 10].

Large language models (LLMs) offer a means of incorporating broad prior knowledge into computational design [11, 12, 13]. Through large-scale pretraining, these models are able to interpret task requirements, module behaviour descriptions, and feedback diagnostics. These capabilities help connect a task description to appropriate design choices. Their ability to generate structured descriptions and code also allows these choices to be expressed as design programs and revised in a principled manner within an iterative search. Beyond proposing designs, multimodal LLMs can analyse simulation observations and failure diagnostics to formulate explanations for unsuccessful designs and provide much richer guidance than task scores alone, as well as propose targeted revisions. By employing different instances of LLMs as agents with different roles, we are able to construct a designer-critic paradigm in which appropriate designs can be devised efficiently without extensive computational evaluations and expensive simulation.

In this paper, we present PneuGen, a task-driven agentic co-design framework for soft robots. An overview of the framework is shown in Fig. 1. A designer LLM agent constructs designs from a library of parametric components and jointly selects their spatial arrangement, geometric parameters, and actuation. A separate critic agent interprets simulation diagnostics and proposes revisions for subsequent design iterations. Component-level pressure-to-displacement maps, represented by fitted module response models, provide a physics prior on how geometry and pressure affect deformation. The resulting design programs are automatically converted into CAD models, meshes, and finite-element simulations. The framework also supports selection from different families of soft robot components to satisfy task requirements. Our contributions are:

An agentic co-design loop that combines soft robot geometry and actuation design with simulation-based evaluation and critic-guided refinement.

A library of soft robot components with fitted module response models, geometric and fabrication constraints, and automatic CAD and simulation generation to support task-driven design.

An evaluation on simulated grasping and shape-matching tasks against random search, genetic search, and CMA-ES with real-world demonstrations, and an investigation of the effects of module response models and critic guidance.

title: Large Language Model Explainability for Planning Lunar Rover Trajectories under Uncertainty
authors: Michelle Ho,Maximilian Adang,Zachary Booth,David E. Astle,Margaret Hansen,Edward Balaban,Mykel J. Kochenderfer
abstract: Planning planetary rover trajectories under probabilistic uncertainty is a multi-objective optimization problem that science teams currently iteratively solve and verify by hand. This process becomes impractical when timelines and constraints frequently shift throughout the mission planning phase. Sampling-based planners such as Monte Carlo tree search can speed up this process, but their outputs do not preserve traceability to the science objectives that justify each plan, which the science team needs to verify. We propose an interactive assistant based on a large language model (LLM) that can explain planner trajectories using domain vocabulary and re-run the planner under user-specified conditions to compare alternatives. Previous work has used LLMs inside planner decision-making loops, but we explore using them for post-planning explanation, where they are more likely to be trusted since they do not directly influence planner decisions. Our framework pairs a simulator inspired by the NASA Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) mission with a ReAct queryable interface that calls curated action tools and retrieval functions. We evaluate the assistant on a query bank consisting of plan comparisons, feasibility, and lookup queries. Experiments show that 90.9% of the assistant’s responses are faithful to the planner’s outputs, a nearly 65% improvement over zero-shot prompting of the same LLM without tool access, demonstrating the potential for trustworthy explainability of uncertainty-aware traverses with an LLM-based system.
introduction:
For space missions, planning the science phase typically requires vehicle trajectory optimization for multiple objectives and constraints. These trajectories also depend on many sources of probabilistic uncertainty, which become impractical to reiterate on quickly and frequently by hand. A simulator and an accompanying automated planning algorithm can speed up this iteration process, but their outputs may not be directly useful to the scientists who need to map these outputs to the effects on science data collection. This gap in explainability motivates an automated approach that uses large language models (LLMs) to explain trajectories in a comprehensible form to users who may not be familiar with the inner workings of the planning system.

Advances in robotics have been driven by LLMs applied to motion planning for tasks with high-dimensional observations, multi-modal sequences and behaviors, and complex failure modes [1, 2, 3]. For instance, recent work uses LLMs for planning Martian rover traverses [4], and efforts have begun to integrate LLMs with structured planners as state trackers or plan verifiers within the planning stage [5, 6]. Improvements to LLM in-context reasoning, text generation, and information retrieval [7] suggest that they have the skills to provide comprehensive explainability for these tasks. However, current work does not use LLM reasoning capabilities to explain long-horizon plans made by rigorous techniques for planning under uncertainty.

One application that could benefit from this approach is planning planetary rover traverses. Such missions must account for a fixed time budget, navigation to sites of high scientific value, and uncertain speeds. We are inspired by NASA’s Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER), which must explore a predefined area of high scientific value, called a science station, within a roughly 24-hour period. The rover must collect measurements of volatiles with its three continuously operating spectrometers (neutron, near-infrared, and mass) through prospecting and obtain subsurface regolith samples with its onboard drill [8]. The rover is solar-powered and thus needs to remain in sunlight as much as possible, unless operating within a permanently shadowed region (PSR) science station. The rover’s speed also depends on the sun’s position, as driving in certain directions is difficult or impossible due to the low-rising sun creating imaging issues for the navigation and hazard-avoidance cameras. The rover must also avoid communication shadows and slopes. Verifying by hand whether a handcrafted traverse satisfies all of these objectives and constraints is likely impractical, especially considering probabilistic uncertainties. An interpretable, automated planner is essential when timelines, constraints, and operational windows shift and require frequent replanning and verification.

NASA’s current tool for overseeing health-aware mission planning is the System Health-Enabled Real-time Planning Advisor (SHERPA) [9] is a strategic mission planning AI system in use by NASA. SHERPA uses sampling-based  methods like Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) [10, 11] to compute and evaluate potential traverses for a variety of missions, such as VIPER’s long-range traverses. However, it currently does not have support for the detailed planning inside VIPER’s science stations. Additionally, MCTS plans trajectories by maximizing future rewards and rollouts, while the science team verifies trajectories against mission-specific objectives, such as risk of finishing over the time limit or maximizing prospecting area. The planner’s outputs do not directly trace back to these objectives, so it may require additional analysis to determine whether a given trajectory satisfies them.

To address this gap, we make the following contributions towards producing explainable trajectories:

An MCTS-based optimal trajectory planner coupled with a VIPER-inspired, physics-based simulator. Inputs to the planner include ice stability depth maps and sun-azimuth-dependent probability distributions for rover speeds.

An LLM-based, interactive assistant that dispatches the planner and a set of tools to automate replanning and explanation of trajectories with mission context, evaluated on a bank of science-team-inspired queries.

The proposed framework seen in Figure 1 is designed to allow the science team to efficiently replan under different conditions and constraints, while building trust with the trajectory planning algorithms, by keeping the team engaged in an interactive planning loop and grounding explanations in a familiar vocabulary. The LLM assistant does not override the planner, but rather runs it on behalf of the user with their specified conditions or explains resulting trajectories, without telling the user what they should do.

title: RaMOD: Moving-Object Detection from Raw mmWave Radar Cubes under Ego Motion
authors: Yuan Fang,Long Zhuang,Lingzi Xing,Xijia Wei,Jingqi Jiang,Fangzhan Shi,Simon Julier,Kevin Chetty
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides weather-robust sensing and
direct Doppler measurements, yet automotive perception pipelines often
reduce its output to sparse point clouds or two-dimensional
projections, leaving raw range–azimuth–Doppler (RAD) cubes
underutilized. Ego motion induces Doppler responses from world-static
structures, while Doppler wrapping aliases radial velocities,
complicating moving-object detection and velocity estimation. We
present RaMOD (Radar-based Moving-Object Detection), a real-time
framework for moving-object detection and velocity estimation from
raw RAD cubes acquired by a vehicle-mounted single-chip radar. RaMOD
explicitly estimates frame-wise ego motion and uses the estimated
radar translational velocity to predict the Doppler region of
world-static structures and suppress returns within it. It temporally
encodes the suppressed cubes into multi-scale features to predict
RAD-space boxes with class labels. For each detected object, it
predicts radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and
Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping
probabilities. On our BRIDGE-Liv dataset, RaMOD outperforms all
compared raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, RA, and RD detection
settings, achieving 80.8%80.8\% cube mAP at IoU 0.300.30, 15.715.7 percentage
points above the strongest RAD-cube baseline. Velocity MAE is
1.128​m/s1.128~\mathrm{m/s}, with 99.87%99.87\% Doppler-wrapping accuracy.
introduction:
Moving object detection is a fundamental perception task for assisted and autonomous driving, where independently moving road users must be accurately localized, classified, and assigned reliable motion estimates. In current autonomous driving systems, optical sensors, especially cameras and LiDARs, play a decisive role in perception. In conventional modular pipelines, cameras provide rich semantic information for object detection and segmentation [1], while LiDAR provides accurate range and 3D geometric measurements for object detection [2]. Recent end-to-end driving frameworks further learn driving decisions from sensor observations [3], while emerging vision-language-action (VLA) systems incorporate language guidance into driving [4]. However, object motion in conventional camera- and LiDAR-based pipelines is typically inferred through temporal association, optical flow, scene flow, or frame-to-frame geometric changes, which can be sensitive to occlusion and unreliable correspondences [5, 6]. Moreover, cameras can degrade under poor illumination, glare, contamination, and motion blur, while LiDAR measurements can be affected by rain, fog, and snow [7], as well as smoke [8].

Millimeter-wave radar has therefore become an important complementary sensor in modern vehicles. Compared with optical sensors, mmWave radar uses longer-wavelength electromagnetic signals and is generally more robust under poor illumination and adverse weather conditions. More importantly, radar directly measures radial velocity through Doppler. Advances in semiconductor fabrication and antenna-in-package technologies have also enabled compact, low-power, and low-cost single-chip mmWave radars, making large-scale deployment practical in intelligent vehicles and autonomous systems [9]. Automotive radars have consequently been widely adopted in advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS).

However, automotive radar perception still commonly relies on processed point clouds and the clusters derived from them (Fig. 1(c)). Point clouds are typically generated through peak selection and sparsification, while clustering, data association, and tracking further produce object-level estimates. The resulting detections and tracks provide compact position and velocity information for conventional ADAS functions such as adaptive cruise control, blind-spot detection, collision warning, and automatic emergency braking (AEB) [10]. Nevertheless, peak-based sparsification may discard weak responses and only partially preserve the extended object support and reflection structures present in the full radar measurement tensor (Fig. 1(b)).

For next-generation autonomous driving, mmWave radar has the potential to support high-level perception through its spatial measurements and directly measured Doppler information. Raw range–azimuth–Doppler (RAD) cubes preserve these measurement distributions before point-cloud sparsification, providing richer evidence for learning-based object detection, classification, and velocity estimation. Among these capabilities, identifying independently moving road users through spatial and Doppler evidence is particularly important for interaction, motion prediction, and collision-risk assessment.

However, identifying independently moving road users becomes more
challenging when the radar itself is moving. World-static structures,
such as buildings and parked vehicles, also produce Doppler shifts
under ego motion, so non-zero Doppler alone does not indicate
independent object motion. Their responses may overlap with those of
moving objects. Doppler wrapping introduces further ambiguity: when
the relative radial velocity falls outside the unambiguous velocity
interval, the return is mapped to an aliased Doppler bin, potentially
increasing static–dynamic overlap. The extent of this overlap depends
on radar Doppler coverage and the relative motions in the scene.
The world-static Doppler field and the resulting ambiguity after
wrapping are analyzed in
Secs. III-C and
III-D.

Motivated by these observations, we propose RaMOD, a real-time
framework for moving-object detection from raw RAD cubes acquired
by a single-chip radar on a moving vehicle. It supports both
single-frame and short-sequence inputs. Since
world-static Doppler depends on radar motion and viewing direction,
RaMOD estimates frame-wise ego motion as an explicit output and uses
the estimated radar translational velocity to predict the
static-consistent Doppler region. Suppressing returns within this
region reduces ego-motion-induced background responses before
detection. The suppressed radar representation is encoded into
multi-scale features for RAD-space object localization and
classification. RaMOD also predicts radial and
object-level forward velocities under raw-Doppler and
Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping
probabilities. Experiments on BRIDGE-Liv, which contains moving-ego
urban and highway sequences, show that RaMOD outperforms all compared
raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, range–azimuth (RA), and range–Doppler (RD)
detection settings.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose RaMOD, a real-time moving-object detection and motion-estimation framework that directly processes raw RAD cubes from a single-chip radar under ego motion. It retains Doppler as an explicit detection dimension and combines multi-scale cube encoding, cross-scale feature refinement, and cross-view RA/RD auxiliary supervision for RAD-space object localization and classification.

We develop an ego-motion-guided Doppler suppression mechanism. Frame-wise ego motion is estimated directly from unmasked RAD cubes as an explicit output. Its translational component is combined with the world-static Doppler model to construct an internal cube-level mask that suppresses returns within the predicted static-consistent Doppler region before detection.

We design object-level velocity heads that predict radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. These probabilities guide selection between the two velocity pairs, associating each detected object with a velocity estimate that accounts for Doppler ambiguity.

title: Force-Closure Condition for Cooperative Multi-robot Pushing of Rectangular Objects
authors: Duy Anh Nguyen,Trung Dung Ngo
abstract: In cooperative object manipulation, the placement of pushing contacts determines whether force closure can be achieved and agents can generate arbitrary forces and torques on the object correspondingly. This study derives a necessary and sufficient closed-form condition for the planar force closure of a rectangular object, a common object shape in everyday settings, under four frictionless pushing contacts. For a rectangle of length bb and width aa, force closure holds if and only if (l1+l3−b)​(l2+l4−a)<0(l_{1}+l_{3}-b)(l_{2}+l_{4}-a)<0, where l1,l2,l3,l4l_{1},l_{2},l_{3},l_{4} are the four edge contact locations. This condition is independent of the object’s center of mass and is used to verify contact configurations before contact force allocation. When the condition is not satisfied, the signs of the two factors indicate which opposing contact pair should be adjusted. The condition and adjustment rule are then integrated into a full-pose trajectory-tracking framework as a geometric feasibility layer to demonstrate their use in control. Static wrench feasibility tests validate the proposed condition, while narrow-passage floating-body simulations show that maintaining a force-closure configuration reduces the RMS tracking errors in xx, yy, and unwrapped yaw from 12.0512.05 m, 18.1118.11 m, and 535.96∘535.96^{\circ} to 2.242.24 m, 2.662.66 m, and 2.69∘2.69^{\circ}, respectively.
introduction:
Cooperative object manipulation by multiple robots becomes necessary when a task exceeds the force, moment, or workspace capacity of any single agent [1, 2]. In marine settings, tugboats are deployed in groups to dock large vessels, reposition heavy floating barges, and move floating structures through narrow waterways, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Multiple agents, such as robots or vessels, can manipulate a shared floating object in several ways, including attaching, caging, towing, and pushing [2]. Among these, pushing requires the least mechanical setup: it needs no cables, attachments, or grasping mechanisms, and tugboats carry it out by pressing their bow or stern fenders against the hull of the target object.

Cooperative pushing is nontrivial because object motion depends on both the control law and the contact locations. Under unilateral frictionless pushing, the contact normals and nonnegative contact force magnitudes define a wrench cone; if the commanded object wrench lies outside this cone, no nonnegative contact force can realize it [3]. Force closure provides the classical framework for this feasibility check. A contact configuration achieves force closure when contact forces can balance any external wrench on the object, or equivalently generate arbitrary planar wrenches [3]. Nguyen’s work established a constructive approach for synthesizing planar force closure grasps from the geometry of the object [4]. The method identifies independent contact regions and provides algorithms for constructing grasps from object shape information. These works provide a basis for contact-feasibility analysis, but rely on general geometric or algorithmic frameworks rather than a compact closed-form condition for the cooperative pushing geometry considered here.

This contact feasibility issue is especially relevant in cooperative object manipulation, where multiple agents must jointly generate the forces and moments required for transport. Esposito [5] studied swarm-based cooperative pushing of floating objects in autonomous tugboat scenarios, highlighting how robot placement affects the manipulation capability of the team. Cooperative floating object transport has also been studied through layered control frameworks involving trajectory tracking, wrench allocation, and vessel formation control [6]. More generally, constrained control allocation has been widely studied for marine vehicles [7, 8]. Autonomous tugboat systems have addressed towing, waypoint following, heading regulation, and collision avoidance [9, 10]. Related pushing-based work with soft tactile sensing handled distributed force regulation and motion direction control for a rectangular object [11], where feasibility is assessed through moment arm signs relative to the object center of mass for a specific target direction. Recent work has also addressed collaborative planar pushing of polytopic objects using hybrid mode optimization and nonlinear MPC [12]. These approaches either assume that the selected contact geometry can produce the required object wrench or evaluate feasibility through numerical optimization. For one unilateral edge normal contact on each edge of a rectangular body, a closed-form condition that is independent of the object’s center of mass remains underexplored.

This study tackles these gaps by deriving a necessary and sufficient closed-form condition for force closure with four frictionless, unilateral contacts on a rectangular floating object, stated purely in terms of the four edge contact positions. The condition is a single checkable algebraic inequality that requires no wrench-space computation and can be evaluated at the contact placement stage before applying a control technique. To demonstrate its use in control, we embed this result into a simple 3-DOF floating-body trajectory-tracking framework: the condition is checked once upfront to confirm that the contact geometry supports full-pose tracking, and if not, a pair-and-direction adjustment rule corrects the configuration before contact force allocation. In this framework, the pushing agents are modeled as ideal unilateral normal-force actuators at the contact points, allowing the study to isolate the effect of contact geometry on wrench generation. Simulation results demonstrate that contact configurations satisfying the proposed force-closure condition can produce the commanded planar forces and yaw moments required for full-pose tracking, while configurations that violate the condition lead to wrench errors and poorer tracking performance.

The paper is organized as follows: Section II covers the problem formulation, Section III derives the force-closure condition, Section IV presents the tracking framework, Section V reports simulation results, and Section VI concludes.

title: Curie's Jarvis: Autonomous Robotic Chemistry Experiments from Printed Protocols
authors: Rumi Loghmani,Bozhang Song,Victor Alvarado,Aliyah Redding,Amir Barati Farimani
comment: . Rumi Loghmani and Bozhang Song contributed equally
abstract:
A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction
sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them,
and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually
works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and
containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present
Curie’s Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry
experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo
of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed
positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading
their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every
step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from
what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie’s Jarvis completed 5 of 5
runs of one protocol from a children’s chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of
another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and
handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings
robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.
introduction:
A student running a bench protocol works from a printed instruction sheet.
The reagents sit in containers that have been labelled by hand and set down
wherever there was room, and identical cups are told apart only by their
labels. The bench is shared, so a cup may not be where it was a minute ago;
the student looks again before each step and finds it. The student also
adjusts each step to what is being handled, carrying an empty cup quickly and
a full one slowly. None of this is arranged for a robot: the instructions,
the labels and the layout are all meant for people.

Existing robots for automated experiments mostly adapt the experiment’s
procedure, objects and layout to the system. The instructions have to be
written as a script or in a chemical programming
language [1, 2, 3];
every container and instrument needs a fixed or known
position [4, 5]; and some systems
identify containers by fiducial markers such as AprilTags rather than by
the labels placed with them [6]. This makes
automated experiments fast and accurate, but at the cost of flexibility: a
new experiment requires substantial manual reprogramming instead of simply
handing the system a printed instruction sheet, and if an object is moved
during the experiment, the run may not be able to continue.

This work aims to close this gap by letting a robotic system adapt to a lab
arranged for people. We make this goal concrete as five properties. Our system, Curie’s Jarvis, (P1) starts from the printed instruction sheet, with no manual
rewriting into a script; (P2) works on an ordinary bench, where containers
need no fixed or preset positions and no visual markers; (P3) tells
identical-looking containers apart by their hand-written or printed labels;
(P4) looks at the bench again before every step, so it finds objects that
have been moved; and (P5) adapts how each step is executed (how fast to move, how far to tip, how deep to dig) to what is handled and what the step asks for. Section II
compares related work along these properties (Table I), and
Section VII evaluates each of them.

We implement Curie’s Jarvis with all five properties on a Franka Panda arm
(Fig. 1). (P1) A vision-language model (VLM) extracts the
steps from a photo of the sheet, and a planner turns them into parameterized
calls to a fixed set of skills. (P2) SAM 3 [7] segments
objects in four camera views, and positions come from multi-view geometry:
the depth point cloud for opaque objects and silhouettes for transparent
ones. The system only needs a list of the objects on the bench (with the
size of each transparent container), not their positions. (P3) The VLM
reads each container’s label in every view, and the cameras vote.
(P4) Before each skill call, the target is located again if it has been
handled or its image has changed. (P5) The VLM chooses each call’s pour
angle from the wording of the step and its speed from what is held; a fixed
rule sets the angles when the same container is poured from, or into, more
than once, and the scoop depth comes from the measured powder surface.

The contributions of Curie’s Jarvis are as follows:

A system that carries out a chemistry experiment on a Franka Panda
arm from a photo of the printed instruction sheet, on an ordinary bench
with no fixed positions or markers for the containers. It completed 5 of
5 Magic Beaker runs and 4 of 5 jellyfish runs with no human
intervention.

A way to tell identical-looking containers apart by their
hand-written or printed labels, which they stand on, read in each of four
camera views and combined by a cross-camera vote. Because the position of
each container comes from multi-view geometry, the label only needs to say
what the container is and can be placed loosely. In 160 locates on
printed labels and the handwriting of three people, every container was
identified correctly.

Re-locating and re-identifying the containers before every step,
so the robot can find a container a person has moved between steps,
even among identical-looking ones.

title: Incorporating World Models in Decision Making for Next Best View Selection in Active Sensing
authors: Nikita Sarawgi,Omey M. Manyar,Satyandra K. Gupta
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026 Workshop "Do Robots Need World Models?"
abstract: Efficient robotic 3D reconstruction requires selecting views that contribute new surface measurements with few physical captures. Pretrained world models can guide this choice, but a predicted surface may not produce valid depth measurements under the operating conditions of the deployed sensor. We present a deployment adaptation methodology for next-best-view selection that learns a sensor-return adapter from limited local calibration data while keeping the pretrained predictor fixed. The adapter estimates measurement dropout over each predicted surface, allowing the selection method to favor views likely to fill gaps in the measured reconstruction. In a real-robot experiment with a structured-light sensor, the adapted method achieves higher measured surface coverage with 60% fewer captures than nominal selection. The adapted method recovers a surface region that the nominal method repeatedly targets but fails to measure. These results suggest that robots can reuse pretrained predictive models while adapting their decisions to local operating conditions in data-scarce environments.
introduction:
Object reconstruction from sensor measurements supports several crucial applications such as robotic inspection, manipulation, and surface processing [13, 12]. In industrial processing which requires millimeter-level accuracy and high surface resolution, reconstruction quality is critical. Access to a CAD model or predefined geometric primitives cannot be assumed in high-mix production [7]; even when available, nominal geometry alone does not capture the surface deviations or placement of the manufactured part [12]. Processing at this tolerance therefore requires measurements of the part as presented to the robot. Despite advances in structured-light and laser-line sensors, measurement quality remains sensitive to deployment conditions. In high-mix manufacturing, parts vary in geometry, texture, and finish [7], where sensor settings, illumination, and surface reflectivity dictate whether geometrically visible regions yield valid depth measurements, and missing regions can change with viewpoint [17, 16]. Because successful strategies on one setup can fail on another, sensing must adapt to local deployment conditions.

Pretrained action-conditioned world models guide the selection of sensing actions by predicting state transitions before execution [10, 1]. However, selection using nominal predictions assumes visible surfaces equal valid depth measurements. When predictions do not account for local sensor-return behavior, selection risks overvaluing views that give invalid measurements, resulting in wasted captures. Fine-tuning on cell-specific data consumes costly production time, whereas discarding predictions ignores generalizable task dynamics. These constraints motivate preserving a fixed predictor for general task dynamics while learning sensor behavior from limited local experience.

Our main contribution is a methodology that adapts how predictions guide action selection under local conditions using limited calibration data while keeping the pretrained model fixed.
We demonstrate this framework in next-best-view (NBV) selection, where a manipulator selects views to reconstruct a static object. Traditional NBV methods prioritize geometric visibility and surface coverage [6, 3, 11, 4, 2]. Our framework accounts for whether the deployed sensor obtains valid depth from visible surfaces. A fixed action-conditioned world model provides candidate views and expected surface geometry [14] while a separate adapter predicts measurement dropout under deployment conditions.
The view-selection method filters predicted geometry using these estimates before selection. Decoupling task-level prediction from local sensor behavior ensures calibration data is spent on learning deployment-specific sensor returns, enabling model reuse across setups.

We evaluate this framework on a real robot, training the adapter on 50 captures across four helmets and testing on a held-out reflective helmet under fixed lighting and sensor settings. While nominal selection repeatedly selects views that produce invalid depth, realizing 11.7% of its predicted coverage gain, deployment-aware selection filters candidates by estimated sensor return. It reaches the 98% coverage target in four captures, whereas nominal method fails after ten. These results show that a lightweight adapter prevents repeated acquisition failures using fixed pretrained predictions.

title: Latent Barrier Steering: Hierarchical Safety for Generative Planning
authors: Renhao Zhang,Mingzhe Li,Bruno Castro da Silva
abstract: We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator’s behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.
introduction:
Robotic path planning must combine expressive behavior generation with strong safety guarantees.
Generative policies, including diffusion and flow-matching planners, are attractive because they model multimodal trajectory distributions and synthesize diverse high-dimensional behaviors from demonstrations [16, 10, 34, 23, 17, 5, 3, 2].
Yet deployment safety is not inherited from offline training: new obstacles, workspace limits, or feasibility constraints can shift the test-time problem away from the demonstrations used to train the generator.
This has motivated safe generative planners that combine learned samplers with control barrier functions (CBFs), which encode safety through a barrier-defined set, and impose constraints through quadratic programs or related filtering steps [1, 13, 27, 39, 40, 8, 41].
Existing CBF-based generative planners instantiate this idea primarily as path-level repair: they inject barrier constraints into the denoising or flow-generation process, or apply a CBF correction phase after a trajectory has been generated [40, 8, 41].
In both cases, the intervention acts on sample or waypoint coordinates, pushing unsafe portions of the trajectory back toward the safe set while staying close to the generator’s original output.
This is effective when the generated trajectory is already nearly safe, so that only a short segment must be moved away from an obstacle.
Under larger constraint shifts, however, the new constraint may block a substantial portion of the selected behavior mode.
The corrector is then no longer making a local geometric repair: it must reshape a long connected segment of the rollout, which can increase intervention energy and leave the final trajectory safe but far from the goal.

When path-level repair has to reshape a long segment of a rollout, the desired solution may be another behavior that the generator already knows how to produce.
A multimodal demonstration dataset can contain several valid ways to solve the same start-goal task, such as passing above, below, or between obstacles, and generative policies can represent these alternatives as diverse rollouts.
In standard generative planners, however, this diversity is usually accessed through stochastic sampling: the initial noise or sampling seed determines which behavior appears, with no direct handle for a safety filter to choose a rollout that is easier to certify.
Geometry-aligned behavior latents, as in parameterized diffusion policies (PDP), provide such a handle by learning a low-dimensional coordinate in which nearby latent values decode to similar trajectories and larger latent moves induce more substantial behavior changes [43].
This suggests a different division of labor for safe generative planning as shown in Figure 1: use the behavior latent to select or interpolate a safer rollout before asking a path-level CBF corrector to enforce the final constraints.

In this paper, we propose Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a two-stage framework for safe parameterized flow matching that separates behavior selection from path certification.
LBS first applies a CBF quadratic program (CBF-QP) in the behavior latent space to steer the decoded rollout toward a larger robust safety margin.
It then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF-QP only to the remaining waypoint-level violations.
This semantic-to-path structure lets the planner change the selected behavior before invoking local path repair.
Theoretically, we show that latent steering improves the safety margin handed to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time latent recovery when a safe latent is reachable and tighter path-level correction-time and intervention-energy certificates.
Empirically, LBS improves safety, goal reaching, and correction efficiency across constrained planning tasks.
Our contributions are:

Introduce semantic-to-path safety with parameterized flow matching.
We build on a parameterized flow-matching planner whose geometry-aligned latent indexes different rollout behaviors.
LBS uses this latent as the first point of safety intervention, steering the selected behavior before applying path-space CBF certification.

Analyze when latent steering reduces path-space correction.
We show that increasing the latent safety margin gives the path-space corrector a less-violating warm start.
This yields finite-time latent recovery when a safe latent is reachable, and tighter correction-time and intervention-energy certificates for the downstream CBF-QP.

Demonstrate safer and more goal-directed constrained planning.
Across constrained planning tasks, LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction energy compared with path-level safety filters.

title: Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control for Underactuated Upright Physical Assistance
authors: Darren Biskup,Jeonghan Yu,Zibo Yu,Sunil K. Agrawal
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), October 2026.
abstract: Many rehabilitation robots execute prescribed motions using reactive tracking controllers that do not explicitly incorporate the user’s instantaneous human–ground interaction. This paper presents Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC), a framework for upright physical assistance. By integrating live GRF and center of pressure (CoP) measurements directly into a human centroidal dynamics model, GRF-MPC formulates a real-time quadratic program (QP) that optimizes assistive forces and moments over a receding horizon. We deployed GRF-MPC on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST) in an underactuated 4-cable configuration and evaluated it against a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline in nearly 300 trials across six healthy participants. Across tasks spanning impulsive perturbations, lunge trajectories, and voluntary limits of stability, GRF-MPC reduced peak planar center-of-mass (CoM) error by 19.6% during perturbations, lowered trajectory tracking error by 24.1%, required 28.7% less net mechanical work, and permitted a 45.9% greater normalized voluntary excursion area. The underlying QP solves in under 1 ms, comfortably enabling 100 Hz replanning and demonstrating that incorporating live human–ground interaction into predictive control yields stronger, more transparent physical assistance with half the actuators.
introduction:
Individuals with mobility impairments resulting from spinal cord injury (SCI), cerebral palsy, and stroke are often wheelchair-bound or need significant assistance to stand. These conditions affect millions worldwide, with approximately 17,000 new SCI cases annually in the United States alone [1]. Prolonged sitting leads to further muscle deterioration, creating a vicious cycle where weakened muscles make it increasingly difficult to stand leading to further degeneration. To break this cycle, robot-assisted rehabilitation offers customized targeted interventions that enable precise motion control, quantitative assessment capabilities, and reduced physical burden on therapists [2].

However, many robots for human assistance or rehabilitation, including frame-mounted mechanisms or exosuits, primarily employ control strategies focused on kinematic outcomes or provide joint-level torque assistance. During healthy overground locomotion, humans generate stability and propulsion through ground-contact forces at the foot-ground interface. When an assistive controller injects forces based on trajectory deviations without accounting for these existing ground reaction forces (GRFs), the resulting net force can produce center of mass (CoM) accelerations that are misaligned with the intended movement direction. Such mismatch can lead to corrective assistance that opposes natural motion or requires compensatory action from the user or therapist.

To address the lack of GRF consideration in real-time rehabilitative control, this paper adapts predictive techniques from legged locomotion to physical human-robot interaction. We propose a novel GRF-aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC) framework that proactively optimizes assistance at every time step using real-time centroidal dynamics. Measured net GRF and center of pressure (CoP) are incorporated directly into the human centroidal dynamics, providing the external human-ground interaction needed to predict CoM evolution without estimating internal joint torques or forecasting a detailed multibody motion. Embedding this measurement-driven model in a constrained quadratic program (QP) inherently handles underactuation while explicitly enforcing cable tension limits. We experimentally validate this formulation on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST), a custom frame-mounted, cable-driven system (Fig. 1) that applies configurable forces to the user’s body with minimal added inertia [3, 4, 5]. Compared to an impedance control baseline, GRF-MPC demonstrates improved dynamic tracking and greater efficiency, despite allowing a larger permissible volitional workspace. The principal contributions are:

The formulation of GRF-MPC, a centroidal dynamics controller for human physical assistance in which live GRF measurements serve as the enabling observation that completes the predictive model.

The formulation of GRF-MPC, a centroidal dynamics controller for human physical assistance in which live GRF measurements serve as the enabling observation that completes the predictive model.

A convex QP formulation with sub-millisecond solve times and 100 Hz replanning that natively accommodates underactuation and tension constraints.

Human-subject validation on the RobUST platform across disturbance rejection, prescribed CoM tracking, net mechanical work, and voluntary workspace, comparing the underactuated 4-cable GRF-MPC against an 8-cable impedance-control baseline.

title: How Much of Your VLA Is kNN
authors: Denis Grachev,Damien LaRocque,Omar Moured
comment: accepted to the CoRL 2026 G2A/TAG workshop
abstract:
VLA (VLA) models now exceed 95 %95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations.
In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 %91.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} on LIBERO without policy training.
Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies.
Across nine publicly available VLA, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLA remain close to the demonstrations.
In addition, we introduce  LAC (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions.
We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key.
Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
introduction:
Modern VLA models typically combine a large pretrained vision-language backbone with an action-generation head (e.g., regression, diffusion, or flow matching).
These models are further pretrained on large, heterogeneous collections of robot trajectories and subsequently fine-tuned for downstream manipulation tasks [3].
Their performance is commonly evaluated on standardized benchmarks, which measure closed-loop task success across predefined tasks and initial conditions.

Among these, the  LIBERO (LIBERO) [18] is one of the most widely used simulation benchmarks, consisting of 130130 language-conditioned Franka manipulation tasks across five suites: LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, with 1010 tasks each, and LIBERO-90 and LIBERO-Long, with 9090 and 1010 tasks, respectively.
Each task comes with 5050 demonstrations.
VLA are commonly fine-tuned on these demonstrations and evaluated in closed loop from a fixed set of benchmark initial states.

Recent progress has pushed LIBERO close to saturation, with several modern VLA reporting success rates around or above 97 %97\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} [15, 3, 30], making further gains increasingly difficult to interpret as improved generalization.
Yet, recent studies show that policy performance can degrade substantially under changes in viewpoint, robot initialization, language, appearance, or object layout [9].
These findings raise the question of how much benchmark success reflects generalization beyond the demonstrations, and how much can be achieved through demonstration retrieval alone.

To quantify how much benchmark performance can be explained by retrieval, we propose a training-free  kNN (kNN) approach that retrieves demonstration states similar to the current observation and combines the action chunks that follow them, as shown in Fig. 1. Our contributions are as follows:

Quantify the extent to which benchmark performance can be explained by retrieval alone.

Quantify the extent to which benchmark performance can be explained by retrieval alone.

Use retrieval to evaluate the backbones of nine public VLA before and after fine-tuning, and compare them with the full policies.

Introduce LAC, an offline metric of embedding quality for retrieval, and use it to guide the training of a retrieval key.

title: DOBB: Dynamic Oriented Bounding Boxes for Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance under State Uncertainty and Heterogeneous Dynamics
authors: Pedro Antonio Alarcon Granadeno,Jane Cleland-Huang
abstract: Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance must remain reliable under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics. Existing methods typically address these factors through training-domain variation or by exposing uncertainty and capability estimates to the policy at runtime. However, both leave the policy to infer how these quantities should alter the physical separation required for safe interaction, which can couple collision-avoidance behavior to relationships learned from the training distribution. We introduce the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. We derive geometric features that jointly characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents’ DOBBs, along with a reward function that preserves the physical interpretation of those interactions. Across four evaluation environments, DOBB achieves the lowest mean total failure rate of 2.6%. This performance persists under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty, with collision-based failure remaining at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this robustness to the geometric abstraction of the safety margin, which is less coupled to the specific uncertainty and actuation regimes encountered during training. Code open-sourced at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DOBB-Collision-Avoidance-8D16/README.md
introduction:
Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance (DCA) enables multi-agent navigation from locally available observations without centralized coordination. In physical fleets, the safety of an interaction depends not only on the estimated relative configuration, but also on uncertainty in that estimate and differences in agent physical footprint and actuation response. State-estimation uncertainty and agent heterogeneity have therefore become recurring concerns in learning-based DCA.

Two recurring themes characterize much of the learning-based DCA literature. First, and most commonly, experience-based approaches accommodate uncertainty and heterogeneity through the observations, interactions, and temporal context available to the policy during training. Examples include noise-augmented observations, variation in agent(s) properties (i.e. radius, swarm size) or behavior (cooperative vs. non-cooperative), and temporal context from stacked observations fed to recurrent encoders [1, 2, 3, 4]. These mechanisms improve robustness by emulating real-life conditions and interactions during learning and/or leverage recurrent architectures for latent-state inference. Second, more recently with a smaller body of work, explicit-runtime approaches quantify uncertainty or related predictive confidence during execution and incorporate it directly into the decision process. Depending on the formulation, the resulting estimate may enter the policy observation or reward, modify an optimization objective or action distribution, or trigger a fallback controller [5, 6, 7, 8].

These two approaches impose different inference burdens on the collision-avoidance policy. Consider an experience-based policy trained with noise-augmented position measurements to emulate localization uncertainty. At execution, the policy observes the corrupted measurements but is not given the underlying noise magnitude; it must infer the severity of uncertainty from the observed fluctuations and subsequently learn how that uncertainty should alter its avoidance behavior. An explicit-runtime formulation can partially alleviate this burden by quantifying an estimate of this uncertainty (e.g. position covariance) at each time step. Explicit access to uncertainty therefore removes the need to infer its severity, but it does not specify how uncertainty and agent heterogeneity should alter the separation required for safe interaction.

This limitation can be viewed as a representation problem. In collision avoidance, state uncertainty and agent response characteristics affect the spatial margin that should be maintained during an interaction. Consequently, the same estimated relative configuration can imply different separation requirements across uncertainty levels and agent capabilities, where these effects may be directionally dependent. For example, identical estimated positions and velocities can correspond to materially different interactions when one agent is poorly localized and has tighter acceleration limits (e.g., due to a lower thrust-to-weight ratio), whereas another is accurately localized and more maneuverable. When these quantities are provided only as policy inputs, their spatial implications must still be learned from experience. This learned mapping can become coupled to the uncertainty and actuation regimes represented during training, making the resulting collision-avoidance behavior susceptible to degradation when deployment conditions depart from that distribution.

We address this representation problem with the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric abstraction that maps the current state estimate, its uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. Rather than exposing these quantities independently to the policy, DOBB represents their joint effect on the spatial relationship between interacting agents and recomputes this representation as operating conditions change. We further derive geometric interaction features that characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents’ DOBBs, along with a reward that preserves the physical interpretation of these interactions. The evaluation in Sec. VI shows that DOBB reduces collision failures relative to both experience-based and explicit-runtime representations, with the improvement persisting under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty.

title: ASPIRE: An Agentic System-Identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration
authors: Erik Derner,Jiří Kubalík,Robert Babuška
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method. ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds. We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18. The most frequent discrepancy, found in nine models, concerned inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection.
introduction:
In industrial applications, white-box models based on closed-form mathematical expressions are usually preferred to black-box models. Closed-form models relate inputs, states, and outputs through a small set of named parameters and, as such, are useful wherever a model must be interpreted, checked against physical knowledge, extrapolated beyond the range of the data, or embedded in model-based control. Obtaining such models from measured data requires several decisions by an expert: the identification method, the model class, how prior physical knowledge enters the estimation, the estimation criterion, and the validation procedure that matches the model’s intended use. Techniques such as symbolic regression (SR) and sparse regression automate the search for model structure [3, 7], and some SR tools allow for incorporating physical requirements and prior knowledge [20, 5, 6, 23, 44].

Agents based on large language models (LLMs) that write and execute code can choose the identification method: they can inspect the data, propose model structures informed by physical knowledge, implement a fitting procedure, or call an existing SR package and iterate. Recent systems couple LLM-proposed equation structures with numerical parameter fitting [36, 11], give an LLM a fixed set of code-execution tools for equation discovery [43], or let an agent apply physics-based analysis tools to infer properties of the system and then configure existing SR and sparse-regression packages accordingly [48]. In system identification, ASIA [32] delegates the choice of the model class, the training algorithm, and the hyperparameters to an autonomous coding agent.

Existing agentic equation-discovery methods have several limitations: they do not support the specification and verification of physics-based requirements, evaluation on test data inaccessible to the agent, and documentation of the identification procedure. Furthermore, each delivered model should include a record of its structure and parameter estimation, distinguishing estimated parameters, fixed constants, and parameters derived from other parameters. The record should contain sufficient information to check the reported identification procedure against the executed code and execution logs.
To the best of our knowledge, no published framework combines these features with agent-selected identification methods and a protocol for reporting variability across repeated runs.

We propose ASPIRE11

          ASPIRE stands for Agentic System-identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration. It is unrelated to the robot-skill system of the same name [27]., a framework for system identification using LLM agents. ASPIRE constructs closed-form static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the model’s intended use, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. The agent selects and executes the identification method, which may involve physically motivated model structures, symbolic or sparse regression, or custom estimation code. Each candidate model is accompanied by its parameter values, estimation procedure, interpretation, limitations, and test error. The agent also recommends one of the candidates. ASPIRE supports autonomous and interactive operation; in the latter, the agent can request information from the user, who can also request analyses and further identification rounds. The framework consists of one or more LLM agents responsible for identification and a software harness that executes their commands, enforces computational budgets, checks and evaluates candidate models, and records the identification runs.

In summary, the main contributions of this paper are:

We introduce ASPIRE, an agentic framework for system identification in which LLM agents autonomously select, implement, and execute identification methods to obtain nonlinear closed-form models from measured data. Unlike systems based on predefined modeling pipelines or restricted toolboxes, ASPIRE allows the agent to develop and compare alternative model structures and estimation procedures, including methods not specified in advance.

Unlike systems based on predefined modeling pipelines or restricted toolboxes, ASPIRE allows the agent to develop and compare alternative model structures and estimation procedures, including methods not specified in advance.

We integrate physical knowledge and user interaction into agentic system identification. The results show that the agent can construct models with competitive predictive accuracy while satisfying physical requirements that are not enforced by conventional symbolic regression and sparse identification methods. The experiments also quantify run-to-run variability and computational cost.

title: Robo-MLT: Dual-System Robotic Manipulation for Long-Horizon Medical Laboratory Tasks
authors: Zequan Zeng,Kai Wang,Delvin Ce Zhang,Huaping Liu,Zhipeng Yuan,Junqin Yang,YunLong Zhang
abstract: This work is motivated by the many short, strictly ordered sample-handling procedures that clinical laboratories still perform by hand. Each procedure is simple on its own, but it must be carried out in a fixed order, and a step performed out of order can invalidate a result. Dedicated automation handles high and stable sample volumes well, yet every new protocol, consumable, or bench layout has to be engineered into it. This paper describes a robot that instead keeps the protocol as an explicit, ordered list of named operations. A planner reads the protocol and the initial view of the bench and writes the list; a monitor watches the camera streams and decides when the current operation has finished, or when something in the workspace has made it impossible to finish; a learned controller performs each operation. Because the planner is not retrained, a laboratory can reorder or repeat operations that the robot already knows—for example, run the same assay for however many tubes happen to be on the rack—without collecting data or retraining anything. Teaching a genuinely new operation is more expensive: it requires teleoperated demonstrations and retraining of the monitor. The system requires a dual-arm manipulator, three RGB cameras, and a single workstation-class GPU. Its main demonstrated practical benefit is workflow continuity: when an operator removes a sample from the robot’s gripper during execution, the system can revise the remaining plan and continue processing other samples rather than becoming stalled. Current validation is limited to two laboratory protocols, a single workspace, and one type of external intervention, without deployment in a production laboratory. Future work will focus on expanding the atomic-skill library and evaluating the system across a wider range of disturbances and laboratory configurations.
introduction:
Medical laboratory automation aims to reduce repetitive manual work, increase testing throughput, and limit personnel exposure to clinical samples. These benefits require robots to complete entire workflows reliably, not merely to demonstrate isolated manipulation skills. In blood gas analysis, for example, a robot must handle a sample, prepare it for testing, interact precisely with the analyzer, and then withdraw and discard it in the prescribed order. These operations depend on one another: a successful grasp does not ensure a successful test, and a physically feasible action may still be wrong for the current workflow stage. Reliable automation therefore requires both accurate manipulation and consistent execution of the operating protocol [1, 2, 3].

Meeting these requirements is difficult in a laboratory workspace shared with people. Sample positions vary, instrument interfaces demand precise alignment, and operators may intervene while a task is running. Different workflow stages can also produce nearly identical observations: a sample at an analyzer inlet must be inserted before testing but withdrawn afterward, yet the local images look alike (Fig. 1). Choosing the correct action therefore requires knowing what has already been completed. Disturbances add a further difficulty. A displaced target may only require the ongoing motion to be adjusted, whereas removing the sample from the gripper makes the current step impossible to complete and forces the remaining workflow to be revised.

Existing approaches relevant to these requirements fall into three categories. The first is fixed-program and task-specific laboratory automation, which implements procedures through predefined control logic, calibrated motions, dedicated fixtures, and purpose-built mechanisms [4, 5]. In clinical laboratories, total laboratory automation lines handle tube transport and sample preparation while human operators oversee the workflow and make non-routine decisions [6]. The same principle underlies task-specific devices such as microtube cappers [7], the KANKA tube sorter [8], and swab-sampling robots [9], while research architectures encode the workflow as state machines [10], behavior trees [11], or modular integration frameworks [12]. Within their intended operating conditions, these designs provide procedural consistency and predictable cycle times by construction; because every transition is enumerated in advance, however, a new workspace configuration or an unanticipated contingency requires the sensing, control logic, and recovery branches to be authored by hand for each task. Demonstration-trained manipulation skills offer a complementary route: they generate actions from visual observations and can be reused across supported variations in object pose without reprogramming individual trajectories [13].

The second category comprises end-to-end imitation-learning and vision–language–action (VLA) policies. Methods such as ACT [14], Diffusion Policy [15], π0\pi_{0} [16], and SmolVLA [17] learn actions from demonstrations, and VLA models add language conditioning and pretrained visual–semantic representations. Because they act on the current observation, they suit the manipulation studied here: tube poses differ between runs, and seating a tube in an analyzer inlet with roughly 5 mm of clearance requires alignment from the live view rather than a calibrated waypoint. Their language conditioning also offers a natural interface to a higher-level component. A policy that does not explicitly maintain workflow progress, however, must infer the current stage from its observations and conditioning inputs. When stages look alike, insufficient temporal context can lead to repeated or stage-inconsistent actions. Moreover, adapting a trajectory to a displaced target does not determine how the workflow should proceed once the current operation is no longer feasible.

The third category separates high-level planning or semantic reasoning from low-level execution. In laboratory robotics, ORGANA [18] combines language-guided planning with visual feedback, and RoboChemist [1] couples vision–language model (VLM) planning and monitoring with VLA control, advancing once a subtask is verified and repeating it otherwise. General hierarchical systems such as RoboDual [19], Fast-in-Slow [20], and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [21] connect semantic decisions to continuous manipulation. Recent VLA frameworks also bring progress and recovery inside the policy: PALM [22] predicts within-subtask progress jointly with actions, and TCoT [23] couples success assessment with trajectory-level recovery. Progress representations and recovery mechanisms therefore already exist; systems differ in the level at which they act. For a prescribed laboratory protocol, the governing decisions are discrete and ordered: which step is active, whether it is finished, and which of the remaining steps should follow when an intervention makes the active step impossible.

Taken together, these lines of work leave three connected requirements for reliable medical laboratory manipulation. The first is workflow-stage identification: the robot must distinguish visually similar stages using execution history and protocol progress, so that finishing one step leads to the next step rather than to a repetition. The second is recovery within the protocol: when a disruption makes the active skill impossible to complete, the robot must recognize this promptly and revise the remaining steps in the order the protocol prescribes. The third is coordination of monitoring and manipulation: workflow decisions rest on temporal observations and semantic assessment, whereas physical execution needs an uninterrupted action stream, so the two must run at different rates without the slower one stalling the arm.

To this end, we propose Robo-MLT (Robotic Medical Laboratory Tasks), a hierarchical dual-system framework inspired by dual-process theory [24] and summarized in Fig. 1 (bottom).
A frozen vision–language planner first composes an ordered plan over an atomic-skill library from the task, the operating protocol, and the initial workspace observation. System 2 tracks the active plan step with a lightweight multiframe monitor. Its completion head confirms that the active skill has finished, while its recovery head is trained to detect states in which that skill can no longer be completed; a stall timeout serves as a backup trigger. Recovery then replans the remaining steps from the protocol, the completed steps, and the current observation. System 1 generates continuous action chunks conditioned on the active skill and the current observations, and an asynchronous runtime streams them at the robot control rate.

The main contributions are as follows:

We propose Robo-MLT, a hierarchical framework that separates explicit, low-frequency workflow monitoring from high-frequency generative control for long-horizon medical laboratory manipulation.

We develop a lightweight multiframe execution monitor whose two decision heads determine when the active skill has completed and when it can no longer be completed, in which case the remaining workflow is replanned from the protocol and the current scene.

We evaluate Robo-MLT on two real-world tasks, blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, through comparative and ablation experiments, an offline switch-timing analysis of the monitor, and sample-removal disturbance tests, reporting end-to-end task success and recovery success after intervention.

1. We propose Robo-MLT, a hierarchical framework that separates explicit, low-frequency workflow monitoring from high-frequency generative control for long-horizon medical laboratory manipulation.

2. We develop a lightweight multiframe execution monitor whose two decision heads determine when the active skill has completed and when it can no longer be completed, in which case the remaining workflow is replanned from the protocol and the current scene.

3. We evaluate Robo-MLT on two real-world tasks, blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, through comparative and ablation experiments, an offline switch-timing analysis of the monitor, and sample-removal disturbance tests, reporting end-to-end task success and recovery success after intervention.
