title: RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement
authors: Delin Zhao,Zhengrong Yue,Junlin He,Yali Wang
abstract:
Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery
strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the
search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent’s
current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be
revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework
that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen
foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability
evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness
responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one
side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed
snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set
of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms
the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family
panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial
deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA
controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided
practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.
introduction:
Robot agents increasingly improve their own software through interaction:
RoboRSI refines reusable skills, Zetta develops critics and recovery skills,
and DynaHarness revises interfaces between semantic decisions and physical
execution
[33, 5, 3].
Together with RAX, which turns exploration feedback into reusable programs,
these systems make execution procedures revisable [11].
An equally important choice is what the agent practices next, because a
fixed source leaves unprobed weaknesses outside the feedback driving
revision. Improving execution alone leaves this choice unchanged.

Useful practice changes as an agent’s capabilities develop. A drawer skill
that succeeds alone can still fail when composed with object placement,
so practice must probe the composition as well as its individual steps.
Selecting such practice requires interpreting prior outcomes, identifying
prerequisites, and retaining conditions that reveal regressions. Automatic
curricula already connect practice selection with skill accumulation
[28], but the selection procedure itself must also
adapt as failures are resolved and new interactions emerge. Earlier rules
for finding informative challenges can then become inadequate. This motivates a
robot self-improvement loop that revises how it chooses practice alongside
how it executes tasks.

We introduce RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), in which a
curriculum harness and an execution harness evolve through an adversarial
interaction (Figure 1). A harness contains the
prompts, skills, tools, interfaces, and agent-readable memory that organize
behavior around frozen foundation models. The curriculum side uses prior
capability evidence to expose weaknesses in the current execution
harness. The execution side responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities, and
its changing capabilities redirect the curriculum’s search. Independent
agents make runtime decisions on each side, while external optimizers
use the resulting evidence to install revisions for future runs.

Adversarial challenge generation requires a stable reference for judging
progress, so RoboACE alternates the two updates. With execution
fixed, the curriculum side revises its procedures and proposes practice;
admission checks validity and consistency before fixing a comparison
snapshot. The execution side then evaluates candidate revisions on that
snapshot, and consolidated outcomes inform the next curriculum update.
This order separates challenge selection from the response it elicits,
while an infrequently invoked Strategic Advisor reviews longer histories
to reconsider repetitive or stalled revision directions.

RoboACE brings together software self-improvement and evolving
curricula through persistent revisions to both harnesses. RPG constructs
practice from offline data and refines execution on the resulting fixed
task set [32]; our curriculum side also revises the procedures
that select and construct subsequent practice. POET evolves environments
together with their solutions [30, 31];
our implementation instead adapts the software that organizes challenge
production and robot execution around frozen models. The changing task
library is an output of curriculum-harness evolution, alongside the
execution revisions it prompts.

We instantiate this loop in simulated manipulation, beginning with a compact
set of LIBERO practice conditions and evaluating frozen deployments on
LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO, and LIBERO-X. The final deployment outperforms
the evaluated systems on all four panels (Table 2).
On LIBERO-PRO, it improves over the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage
points and over direct execution by the same VLA controller by 13.5 points.
Case studies show how evidence-reading guidance changes independent
practice selection and how execution revisions clarify skill grounding
and controller handoffs. Together, the framework and empirical study
establish a concrete implementation of robot self-improvement in which
both the practice-selection procedure and the execution software remain
open to revision.

title: CAFE: Closed-Loop Autonomous Task Formulation and Execution without Instance-Specific Instructions
authors: Mingjia Chen,Xuewen Zhao,Philip Dames,Qi Mao,Fei Xie,Jun Chen
abstract: Scene-driven robot autonomy requires selecting tasks from observations as well as executing them. We study scene-driven task formulation and execution under predefined cleaning, safety, and storage/organization categories, without instance-specific goals or action sequences. CAFE maintains online memory of objects, functional zones, and execution states. A rule-guided Trigger-LLM admits formulation from accumulated evidence; Draft, Complete, and Audit propose goals, resolve execution details, and check dependencies. Outcomes update memory for correction and subsequent discovery. Evaluation in 12 AI2-THOR scenes compares three backbones and task-complexity tiers using coverage, constraint, and execution metrics. Tri-LLM records higher GCR scores than the evaluated baselines across three backbones and task-complexity tiers. Controls examine completion, auditing, zones, feedback, triggering, and prompt examples. LimoCobot traces illustrate storage, cleanup, and recovery from a failed grasp. The study examines how shared scene state connects task discovery to execution and outcome-driven revision. Project page: https://github.com/submissionforpaper/CAFE-Closed-Loop-Autonomous-Task-Formulation-and-Execution-without-Instance-Specific-Instructions.
introduction:
Language and vision-language models have extended robotic planning to goal-directed navigation, open-vocabulary manipulation, and long-horizon execution [1, 2, 3, 4]. PaLM-E and SayCan connect supplied goals to observations and executable skills [5, 6]. Exploration can recover missing information for an instruction [7], while task-discovery methods identify opportunities from environmental and human cues [8]. A robot operating without scene-specific instructions must additionally decide which observed conditions call for action and when enough evidence is available to formulate a task.

This setting requires a recurrent connection between exploration, formulation, and execution. An observation of a dirty bowl may suggest washing, but an executable plan also needs a sink, tools, preparation steps, and dependencies. Those bindings must remain available as the robot moves, and observed action outcomes must update the state used to select subsequent tasks. Persistent scene representations provide spatial and semantic context [9, 10]; observation filtering helps select useful evidence [11]. CAFE connects that evidence to concrete proposals, resolves their physical parameters and dependencies, and revises behavior after execution.

Our objective is to connect scene-supported task discovery, executable-plan formation, and outcome-driven revision in a recurrent loop. CAFE addresses this objective under predefined cleaning, safety, and storage/organization categories. The robot receives no instance-specific goal, target-object list, or action sequence. Online semantic memory stores objects, functional zones, and execution states. Trigger-LLM admits formulation from accumulated evidence, and a staged Tri-LLM pipeline separates Draft, Complete, and Audit. Execution outcomes update the same memory for recovery and subsequent task discovery.

The contributions are:

A memory-centered autonomy loop linking scene-driven task discovery to execution-state updates without instance-specific human task instructions.

A mechanism for recurrent task formulation from scene state, implemented through selective admission, task-status context, and Draft–Complete–Audit reasoning.

Evaluation across three backbones and complexity tiers, with controls for formulation, feedback, triggering, and prompt examples, plus physical storage, cleanup, and grasp-recovery demonstrations.

2. A mechanism for recurrent task formulation from scene state, implemented through selective admission, task-status context, and Draft–Complete–Audit reasoning.

3. Evaluation across three backbones and complexity tiers, with controls for formulation, feedback, triggering, and prompt examples, plus physical storage, cleanup, and grasp-recovery demonstrations.

5. 最终标签总结：

   - VLA: 否
   - Humanoid Loco-manipulation: 是

title: Maze Runner: Autonomous Maze Navigation with Line-Based Localization and Control Barrier Functions
authors: Alvaro J. Gaona,Lucas Gómez-Velayos,Peter Pasuy-Quevedo
abstract: Maze navigation requires localization from sparse, repetitive geometry, planning through narrow corridors, and control that stays safe when the estimate or the map is wrong. We present Maze Runner, an open autonomy stack in C++ and ROS 2 that addresses these needs end to end on a simulated Husarion ROSbot XL with a 2D LiDAR in Gazebo. Perception extracts wall lines from each scan with RANSAC and total least squares, with per-line uncertainty. The same line front end feeds two estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that localizes against a line map built from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM variant that builds the line map online. Planning runs online on an inflated occupancy grid with A* plus line-of-sight shortcutting, or with a forward-only Hybrid A*. A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) tracks the plan while discrete-time Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) on world-frame LiDAR points keep the robot clear of walls and unmapped obstacles. The algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested core library, and the whole stack builds and runs from a single reproducible environment. In simulation, the robot drives a 135 m route through the maze with 1.0 cm localization RMSE against the known map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, the planner returns a path in 6 ms, and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never exceeding its 80 ms budget.
introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots have attracted sustained interest over the past three decades as they tackle tasks previously beyond practical reach. Representative applications include inspection of electrical grids, thermal anomaly detection on photovoltaic components, package delivery, and exploration of unstructured environments. These and many related use cases continue to drive research and industrial development in this subfield of robotics. 
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), commonly known as drones, have become a central focus of robotics research, enabling numerous applications thanks to their agile dynamics and maneuverability. In particular, nano-drones operating as swarms have shown promise for exploration in unstructured environments [1]. The energy industry is also increasingly automating key sectors, including solar power generation, where photovoltaic (PV) modules require regular maintenance and robotic platforms can survey large arrays of modules at lower cost [2]. Drones have likewise emerged as a promising solution for power line inspection, reducing worker exposure to hazardous conditions while improving operational efficiency [3]. 
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) operating in constrained environments such as mazes, corridors, and indoor spaces must address three interconnected challenges: perceiving sparse and often ambiguous geometry, planning feasible motions through narrow passages, and executing control robustly despite process and measurement uncertainty. Localization must run in real time without exception; continuous pose estimation is what lets the robot follow a plan safely. Planning, in turn, must be fast enough to replan whenever the goal changes. 
In this article, we present a maze navigation stack built on ROS 2 [4] and Gazebo [5] that runs in real time and needs no infrastructure in the environment. The stack integrates: (i) geometric perception via RANSAC line extraction with total least squares refinement; (ii) line-based EKF localization against a map derived from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM mode that builds that map online; (iii) online grid planning with A* and line-of-sight shortcutting, or Hybrid A*; and (iv) path tracking with NMPC constrained by discrete-time CBFs [6] on LiDAR points. An earlier version of this work was prototyped in MATLAB; this paper describes the redesigned C++ implementation and evaluates it in Gazebo.

Concisely, our contributions are outlined as follows:

An open ROS 2 implementation whose algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested C++ library, built and run from a single reproducible environment.

An open ROS 2 implementation whose algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested C++ library, built and run from a single reproducible environment.

A shared line front end (RANSAC with total least squares and per-line uncertainty) that serves both EKF localization against a mesh-derived line map and EKF SLAM with line landmarks.

An NMPC with discrete-time CBF constraints on world-frame LiDAR points, with a sector-based obstacle selection that bounds the problem size, solved in real time.

A comparison of online grid planners (A*, A* with shortcutting, and Hybrid A*) on the maze.

The remainder of the paper reviews related work, describes the planning, mapping, localization, SLAM, and control layers, details the simulated platform, and reports experiments in Gazebo.

title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
authors: Amani Kiruga,Zhiyi Li,Ruojin Cai,Hansen Lillemark,Xiaoshan Wu,Ayush Tewari,Yilun Du
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis.
We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose.
By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model.
This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry.
We demonstrate UGG’s effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at ugg-model.github.io.
introduction:
For embodied agents to perceive and act intelligently in the physical world, they must understand its 3D structure and predict how it will evolve over time (11, 62, 4). However, visual observations provide only partial 2D projections of the world, each capturing a limited set of viewpoints, visible surfaces, and changes over time. Robust 4D scene understanding therefore requires inferring what is not directly observed, namely the 3D geometry, camera viewpoint, scene appearance from unseen views, and scene evolution.

Current methods have made strong progress on different parts of this problem, but they are often separated into geometric prediction and visual generation.
Feedforward models can directly estimate scene geometry, including depth, camera pose, and 3D structure, from images or videos.
These methods are efficient and often accurate under the training distribution, but they typically produce a single deterministic estimate and can struggle when the observations are sparse or out of distribution.
Generative models, in contrast, learn strong visual priors for completing missing observations, synthesizing novel views, and predicting plausible dynamic futures.
However, they often lack explicit geometric grounding, which can lead to outputs that are visually plausible but inconsistent in 3D.
Recent work has begun to narrow this gap by repurposing generative video models for geometric prediction (21, 34, 77), or by injecting geometric representations into generative models to improve 3D consistency (38, 58, 20). Nevertheless, generation and prediction are still commonly treated as separate capabilities, rather than as two forms of inference in the same underlying scene model.

In this work, we introduce UGG, a unified generative geometry model that treats visual generation and geometric prediction as different conditional queries of the same underlying 4D scene representation. The appearance (RGB video), 3D structure (depth), and viewpoint (camera geometry) all provide complementary observations of a dynamic scene. Depending on what is observed, a joint model can infer missing scene components from the observed ones.

We instantiate this formulation by representing RGB, depth, and camera geometry as spatially aligned modalities, with camera pose encoded as dense ray maps. A multimodal transformer jointly processes these representation through shared self-attention and modality-specific layers. Modality flexibility is achieved through an extension of Diffusion Forcing (10): different tasks are specified through noise patterns over both modality and time, where observed components serve as conditioning context and missing components are denoised. This conditional completion mechanism enables the same model to condition on a text prompt, a single RGB frame, an RGB sequence, camera poses, depth maps, or any combination of these, and complete the remaining modalities. Moreover, the model can learn from heterogeneous datasets by applying the loss only on available modalities, instead of requiring every example to contain complete annotations of pose and depth.

Our generative formulation also enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene completions. Instead of committing to a single geometric prediction, we sample multiple candidates and select the one with the strongest cross-modal consistency, measured through photometric reprojection. This inference-time search capability is also consistent with the cognitive theory of perception as inference: human scene understanding requires inferring latent scene causes from incomplete observations, and may rely on internal simulation to evaluate possible scene explanations (24, 66, 3, 35).

Overall, our contributions are threefold:
i) We formulate 4D scene understanding as joint generative modeling over appearance and geometry, treating visual generation and geometric prediction as missing-modality denoising within a single conditional model.
ii) We introduce a unified generative-predictive model that represents RGB, depth, and camera pose as spatially aligned modalities, enabling arbitrary conditioning and learning from heterogeneous datasets with incomplete supervision.
iii) Finally, we leverage the generative formulation for inference-time search over multiple 4D scene hypotheses, using geometric consistency to improve geometric prediction.

title: From Video Frames to Robot Meta-Frames: A Unified Latent Interface for World Action Models
authors: Guoqiang Liang,Yiqi Lin,Yanzhe Chen,Kevin Yuchen Ma,Mike Zheng Shou
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations.
Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g., proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders.
We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem:
how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising.
Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less.
Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change.
A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables.
On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks.
Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models have become a powerful paradigm for generalist robot
control, yet they learn reactive observation-to-action mappings without modeling how the world
evolves under their actions [1].
World Action Models (WAMs) close this gap by adapting pretrained video diffusion models
(VDMs), which carry strong spatiotemporal priors over scene dynamics, to predict actions and
future observations jointly.
Existing WAMs differ mainly in how they couple world prediction and control. Cascaded
WAMs use the video model as a learned simulator and recover actions through a separate
inverse-dynamics model or policy [2, 3, 4], while Joint WAMs let one
generative backbone emit actions, future observations, and values within a single denoising
process [5, 6]. Across these designs, a key interface is often
treated as a formatting detail: how low-dimensional robot variables, such as proprioception,
actions, task type, and values, should enter a latent space shaped by natural-video statistics.
This raises the question: how should structured robot signals be represented so that a
pretrained VDM treats them as in-distribution during denoising?

A straightforward solution injects each robot signal as its own video-like latent frame,
either by spatially tiling the raw signal across the frame [5] or by
rendering it into an image and re-encoding it through the pretrained VAE [7];
both preserve backbone compatibility but inflate the sequence length and the quadratic attention
cost it incurs. Other designs attach dedicated action encoders or decoders [6],
improving action modeling at the cost of modifying the pretrained backbone. We view signal
injection as a distribution-alignment problem: a useful representation must remain
compatible with the VDM prior seen by the pretrained denoiser. As previewed in
Fig. 1(b), frequency-domain encoding produces latents that the frozen denoiser
corrects far less than spatial encodings.

To examine this design space, we run diagnostic experiments that trace candidate injections through
VDM denoising, covering both single-signal injection and multi-signal packing, and measure how
strongly a frozen denoiser corrects the injected latent across noise levels. These experiments show
that the arrangement of robot signals in latent space measurably affects the denoiser:
frequency-domain packing yields latents it corrects far less than spatial tiling or discontinuous
canvas layouts. Compactness alone is therefore insufficient; an effective interface must be
distribution-aware.

Motivated by these findings, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all heterogeneous robot signals into
a single unified meta-frame (Fig. 1(a)). Rather than allocating a latent frame
to each signal, MetaWAM assigns every signal, including current and future proprioception, action
chunks, task type, and value, to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band within one frame, and
lifts the packed coefficients to the spatial latent via an analytical inverse DCT. This produces
smooth latent patterns well aligned with the pretrained denoiser, while a single meta-frame becomes
a multiplexed carrier for many low-dimensional signals. The design requires no additional action
encoder, learned decoder, or modification to the denoising architecture, and recovers each signal
analytically at readout.

We instantiate MetaWAM on a Cosmos-Predict2 backbone and evaluate it on RoboCasa, LIBERO,
LIBERO-Plus, and three real-world Franka tabletop tasks. MetaWAM exceeds the RoboCasa frame-injection baseline while collapsing
multiple robot-signal frames into one. Our contributions are:
(1) we recast robot-signal injection as a distribution-aware latent-interface problem for Joint WAMs;
(2) we provide diagnostic evidence that frequency-domain packing aligns better with a pretrained
VDM prior than spatial signal encodings; and
(3) we introduce a unified frequency-domain meta-frame that carries all robot signals in a single
decoder-free latent frame without architectural changes.

title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
authors: Mehmet Onur Keskin,Berk Buzcu,Nikhil Churamani,Reyhan Aydogan,Hatice Gunes,Catholijn Jonker
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing
abstract:
Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap.
We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent’s target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.
introduction:
Negotiating resources, tasks, and conflicting interests is a fundamental capability for socially intelligent agents collaborating with humans [1, 2]. Traditionally, Automated Negotiation has been modeled with Game Theory and AI, viewing agents as rational utility maximizers that exchange offers based on fixed mathematical functions, heuristics, or reinforcement learning policies [3, 4].
Recent agents demonstrate sophisticated strategic reasoning in human-agent negotiation: from the tool-integrated ASTRA agent that performs dynamic offer optimization [5] to competitive bargaining models like ChargingBoul [6] and systems that analyze strategic trade-offs in multi-agent environments [7]. These approaches advance strategic decision-making, while situated human interaction also requires attention to individual preferences and affective cues [8, 9]. Balancing utility with human social acceptance is still a challenge [10, 11]. As embodied agents transition from industrial environments to unstructured social roles (e.g., mediators, tutors, and caretakers), affective intelligence becomes a functional necessity, and expressions serve as social signs of the interaction partner’s affective state.
For example, a tense or serious expression may signal resistance before a rejection is verbalized. At the same time, a slight or mild smile may indicate mutual agreement [12, 13]. Recent work has begun to utilize this, with agents using affect for dispute resolution [14] and persuasion [15].

Affect perception is not only perspective-dependent but also highly personal. Models built on static datasets commonly fail to detect the dynamics of a social task in which the observer is an active participant. This failure creates what is known as a generalization gap [16]. Gunes et al. point out that high accuracy on static benchmarks does not guarantee functional adaptation in the wild.
Generic models such as FaceChannel [17] provide a common affect representation, but contextual interpretation remains difficult [16]; for instance, a concentrated expression need not indicate anger. In a negotiation context, this is critical: if the agent misinterprets concentration as anger, it may alter its concession target in response to an ambiguous signal.
This need for adaptation raises the plasticity-stability dilemma: the agent needs plasticity to learn the current participant’s idiosyncratic expressions, while excessive adaptation can lead to catastrophic forgetting of previously learned affective knowledge.

We address this challenge by adapting affect perception to observations from the ongoing negotiation, with generative replay to support retention of general affective representations.
Our agent integrates continual learning (CL) to personalize affective perception. A CL-enabled system retains general knowledge while incrementally updating its parameters using the current participant’s facial observations [18, 19]. We pursue three objectives: (i) to enhance negotiation efficiency through personalized perception, (ii) to improve human-agent negotiation outcomes, and (iii) to validate continual learning as allowing real-time adaptation for affect understanding. To realize these objectives, we extend the Solver Agent [20, 21] from categorical affective feedback to differential feedback from continuous valence-arousal estimates. FaceChannel uses a fixed pretrained affect model, while CLIFER combines participant-specific demo training with continued adaptation during negotiation; both share the differential-feedback policy.

We compare these two perception conditions in human-agent negotiation under the following Research Questions (RQs):

RQ1 (Affective Feedback): Does continual learning produce a behaviorally useful affective signal versus generic models? We analyze how personalized adaptation changes arousal/valence estimates and whether these representations produce affect signals influencing negotiation behavior.

RQ1 (Affective Feedback): Does continual learning produce a behaviorally useful affective signal versus generic models? We analyze how personalized adaptation changes arousal/valence estimates and whether these representations produce affect signals influencing negotiation behavior.

RQ2 (Behavioral Influence): How does the agent’s personalized behavior influence human negotiation behavior? We examine whether an agent that adapts its affective feedback during the interaction induces a behavioral shift. We explore whether changes in human concession rates statistically mediate differences in agent utility.

RQ3 (Negotiation Efficiency): Does personalized affective perception enable the agent to gain higher individual utility without degrading joint optimality (Nash distance) in fewer negotiation rounds? We test whether adapting perception improves the agent’s return and negotiation speed, and examine the accompanying participant utility and Nash distance. We hypothesize that personalized affective feedback helps the agent adapt its strategy early and reach agreements efficiently.

RQ4 (Questionnaire Analysis): Do participants perceive the CL-enabled agent as more sophisticated? We examine participants’ ratings of preference modeling, affective awareness, and persuasiveness to assess how personalized affective perception shapes their experience of its negotiation behavior.

Our methodological contribution is a differential affective feedback rule that turns angular and radial changes in continually personalized valence-arousal estimates into negotiation target-utility adjustments. We couple this rule to asynchronous CLIFER updates within the Solver Agent and Negotiator framework [18, 20, 21, 22], keeping perceptual adaptation active during the exchange. In a 66-participant human-robot study using a shared negotiation policy, the CL-enabled system achieved higher agent utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the fixed-perception baseline.

We examine whether an agent that adapts its affective feedback during the interaction induces a behavioral shift. title: HiPFuse: Real-Time LiDAR Semantic Segmentation for Robotic Perception on Edge Devices
authors: Haiyang Wu,George Vosselman,Ville Lehtola
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Real-time robotic perception requires accurate LiDAR semantics under limited resources. Bird’s-eye-view (BEV) aggregation is efficient but can mix differently labeled surfaces in columns. We present HiPFuse, a point–BEV fusion framework that exchanges point and height-partitioned BEV features across horizontal scales, combining point-wise detail with 2D spatial context from one LiDAR scan. Fixed height assignments preserve separate vertical aggregation groups, with auxiliary supervision of initial BEV features using targets from the same 3D cells. A dual-scale BEV context module adds broader context from a coarser grid. On SemanticKITTI and MCD, HiPFuse achieves 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, respectively, exceeding the 10 Hz scan rate. Separate training and evaluation show indoor applicability. Replacing only the baseline semantic front end with HiPFuse in fixed robotic systems reduces odometry absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences and increases accepted-loop recall by 8.7 percentage points on SemanticKITTI. Qualitative semantic maps show more continuous road labeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/haiyang2022/HiPFuse.
introduction:
Beyond scene understanding, semantic information from LiDAR scans can support state estimation tasks such as LiDAR–inertial odometry by informing how observations are selected, associated, and modeled [1, 2]. Semantic cues also support loop retrieval [3] and semantic mapping [4], allowing point-wise semantic predictions to serve several components of a robotic perception pipeline. The benefit of these predictions depends on both their quality and the cost of producing them, since semantic segmentation must share computational resources with the downstream algorithms, especially on edge devices.

In an online perception pipeline, this calls for a semantic front end that keeps pace with incoming scans within a limited computational budget. Projecting point cloud features onto 2D grids enables efficient convolutional processing, as exemplified by the range-image networks RangeNet++ [5] and SalsaNext [6]. However, range-image projection introduces distance-dependent variations in object scale [7]. A bird’s-eye-view (BEV) grid instead uses fixed-size horizontal cells, providing a consistent scale for spatial processing without requiring a regular arrangement of scan lines.

This leads to a follow-up problem: surfaces at different heights within a BEV column may belong to different semantic classes, yet methods such as PolarNet [8] combine all observations in the column into one descriptor before 2D spatial processing.

The vertical axis need not be collapsed, however: height partitioning keeps separate descriptors for different height intervals within each column. Related ideas of retaining height information in BEV channels have been used in point cloud registration and LiDAR perception [9, 10]. For segmentation, the challenge is to learn features that distinguish surfaces with different labels within the same BEV column.

A point branch offers a complementary way to preserve local detail, as demonstrated by HARP-NeXt [11] and sparse point–voxel convolution [12]. Keeping individual point descriptors alongside grid context does not itself separate height partitions during BEV aggregation. We bring these ideas together in HiPFuse, a point–BEV fusion framework for semantic segmentation from a single LiDAR scan. Within this framework, point features and height-partitioned BEV context are learned jointly across scales, preserving separate height groups during aggregation and individual point features during fusion.

Even with height partitioning and point-wise detail, similar local surfaces can belong to different semantic classes. Their interpretation can therefore benefit from surrounding structures and spatial relationships. To gather this context at limited additional cost, we further introduce a dual-scale BEV context (DSC) module that processes a coarser spatial grid and fuses the resulting context with features at the current resolution.

To assess HiPFuse as a semantic front end for resource-constrained robotic perception, we evaluate its accuracy and throughput on the outdoor benchmarks SemanticKITTI [13] and MCD [14]. Our method achieves a favorable accuracy–throughput trade-off relative to the evaluated baselines, with scan-rate segmentation on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin (Fig. 1). Separate training and evaluation on Semantic-ITC [15] examine indoor applicability, with segmentation throughput also exceeding the scan rate.

To determine whether this segmentation performance translates into benefits for downstream robotic perception, we replace the semantic inputs to Hybrid-VoxelMap [2] odometry, SGLC [3] loop retrieval, and SG-SLAM [4] semantic mapping while keeping the downstream algorithms and settings fixed. Compared with semantic inputs from SalsaNext [6] and HARP-NeXt [11], HiPFuse predictions reduce outdoor odometry errors and increase loop retrieval recall. Qualitative map comparisons also show more continuous road labeling.

The main contributions are as follows:

We introduce HiPFuse, a point–BEV fusion framework for real-time LiDAR semantic segmentation whose integrated design combines height partitioning along the LiDAR zz-axis, point-wise detail, and 2D spatial context learning.

We expand the context available for semantic interpretation with a dual-scale BEV module, limiting the added spatial computation by extracting broader context on a coarser grid.

We demonstrate a favorable accuracy–efficiency balance with scan-rate segmentation throughput on an edge device, and show that HiPFuse, requiring only the current scan, can be plugged in as the semantic front end of existing systems and benefits multiple robotic perception tasks while keeping their algorithms and settings fixed.

1. We introduce HiPFuse, a point–BEV fusion framework for real-time LiDAR semantic segmentation whose integrated design combines height partitioning along the LiDAR zz-axis, point-wise detail, and 2D spatial context learning.

2. We expand the context available for semantic interpretation with a dual-scale BEV module, limiting the added spatial computation by extracting broader context on a coarser grid.

3. We demonstrate a favorable accuracy–efficiency balance with scan-rate segmentation throughput on an edge device, and show that HiPFuse, requiring only the current scan, can be plugged in as the semantic front end of existing systems and benefits multiple robotic perception tasks while keeping their algorithms and settings fixed.

title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery
authors: Niran Nataraj,Maina Sogabe,Masamichi Yamashita,Norihiko Ito,Kenji Kawashima
subjects: Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.
introduction:
During ophthalmic microsurgery, the surgeon views the operative field through a high-magnification live video feed [1]. At this scale, the view must remain continuous and geometrically stable: displacements of tens of micrometres matter, and temporary concealment of a microscopic feature can leave pathology unaddressed. Surgical instruments must nevertheless enter the field and thereby occlude the tissue under treatment. Occlusion is particularly consequential during fine dissection and instrument exchange, when no alternative view of the covered tissue is available and the surgeon’s cognitive load and task difficulty increase [2, 3]. The surgeon may consequently pause or reposition the instrument, responses that prolong operating time, and any inference about the covered tissue may itself be inaccurate [4].

The same occlusion also constrains automated systems that process the operative view. Intraoperative scene perception in robot-assisted ophthalmic surgery is built on the microscope video stream, and an instrument crossing the field removes part of the scene from any component that performs registration, tissue tracking, workflow monitoring or visual servoing on that stream. Recovering the hidden context without inventing it is therefore a perception and reconstruction problem before it is a display problem. We investigate whether that context can be recovered in real time from previously observed pixels, with the absence of synthesis established by construction and reconstruction fidelity established by measurement.

Cataract surgery is the setting examined here. Instruments such as a phacoemulsification tip and a hook are introduced into the anterior chamber through corneal incisions in order to sculpt, divide and rotate the lens nucleus [5]. Each incision acts as a fulcrum that constrains the motion of the instrument passing through it, and the whole working field spans only a few millimetres. In a field of that size an instrument covering the tissue under treatment is difficult to avoid, and the surgeon commonly continues the manoeuvre rather than pausing, estimating the covered region from the frames seen a moment earlier and from the motion of the surrounding tissue.

Moving the instrument aside is not a free alternative. Its range of motion is limited by the position of the incision and by the geometry of the eye, and withdrawing and reinserting an instrument in order to look interrupts the manoeuvre and disturbs the anterior chamber and the incision itself. Presenting the tissue behind the instrument without interrupting the manipulation would therefore supply visual information that is otherwise unavailable. Neither the time lost to these repeated brief occlusions nor the additional demand they place on the surgeon is routinely recorded, which motivates the controlled pre-clinical investigation reported here, whose procedure scope is described in Section 3.3.

The most direct existing approaches address only part of this problem. Augmented-reality systems in other surgical fields can prevent virtual overlays from covering the tools [6, 7], but these systems do not recover the tissue concealed by the instrument. Existing general-purpose video inpainters are unsuitable for a different reason: they are generative, so the content reconstructed within the occluded region is synthesised rather than observed and cannot be treated as direct visual evidence during surgery.

Our objective is to restore occluded tissue in real time without synthesising anatomy and to mark pixels that lack support from an observed reference. TransGHOST addresses this objective through safe-mode reconstruction (Figure 1), which leaves each output value unchanged or obtains it by geometrically resampling a recent recorded frame. It also provides per-pixel provenance and abstains when the reference cannot support a reconstruction. All headline fidelity, latency and provenance results refer to this output, which remains within the sub-100 ms window for live surgical guidance at both the median and the 95th percentile on the new veterinary clinical corpus.

This study makes five contributions to reference-guided reconstruction for surgical video. (i) We show that instrument occlusion in this setting can be resolved without synthesising tissue: each restored value is resampled from a recorded frame under transforms fitted only to visible regions, and it carries the reference frame and source coordinate it came from, so a downstream component can separate observed pixels from unsupported ones. (ii) We define a region-aware reference-selection policy that chooses, from a bounded causal buffer, the newest frame whose instrument mask leaves the restoration region visible, and we measure what target-region visibility is worth against recency. (iii) We construct a benchmark in which candidate references may themselves be occluded, which is the condition under which a selection rule can be measured at all. (iv) We establish an evaluation protocol comprising scoring within the masked region, separation of each scoring target from its reference, reference-free controls, a cutout-disjoint held-out cohort and an analysis of fidelity against reference age. (v) We introduce a pixel-annotated ophthalmic corpus labelled for both instruments and anatomy, which supports the semi-synthetic construction that human patient-derived ophthalmic corpora do not readily permit (Section 3.1).

The occluded-reference benchmark (iii) is necessary to evaluate the selection policy (ii) because conventional composited benchmarks supply only instrument-free candidate frames. When every candidate leaves the target region visible, an overlap-aware policy becomes indistinguishable from recency. Occluded candidates are therefore required to measure the effect of regional visibility on selection.

Scored over the occluded region alone, the system reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at a 95th-percentile latency of 85.5 ms. On the held-out cohort using training-excluded instrument cutouts, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR at 86.1 ms for the same latency percentile.

title: Persistent Metric-Semantic Maritime Scene Memory from Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graphs
authors: Kim Alexander Christensen,Dina Zimmermann,Martin Steinert,Eleni Kelasidi
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide robots with persistent metric-semantic representations for spatial reasoning, but the existing methods have primarily been developed for indoor and terrestrial environments. In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed. Our experiments show that zero-shot representative outdoor 3DSG descriptions agree with our labeled ground truth for a majority of geometry-supported objects on our data, but the resulting map exhibits considerable physical-entity fragmentation, and its terrestrial higher-level assumptions don’t capture maritime spatial organization needs. We therefore keep the underlying mapping method and post-process its accumulated evidence. We show a metric-semantic consolidation method followed by geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning that reconciles remaining fragments into physical entities and groups entities through observations into local places. In parallel, we construct maritime macro regions using map priors and onboard water and structure observations, and associate them with the local places. The resulting representation reduces physical-entity fragmentation beyond both the baseline and our geometry-semantic consolidation component alone, supports correspondence of fixed local places across repeated maritime traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on our reviewed queries over tested baselines. These results show how an outdoor open-vocabulary map can be adapted into persistent maritime scene memory with our methods for object/place identity and spatial abstractions.
introduction:
Autonomous surface vessels (ASVs) are being developed for transportation, inspection, monitoring, and other repeated operations in harbors, inland waterways, and coastal areas [1, 2, 3]. Such operations require more than just obstacle tracking and detection in the moment. A vessel revisiting the same area should retain a memory of persistent objects, distinguish them from temporary occupants, and reason about semantic observations in their spatial context. This motivates a metric-semantic scene memory of the maritime environment.

Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide such representations by connecting metric geometry with semantic entities, relations, and higher-level spatial abstractions [4, 5, 6, 7]. Recent open-vocabulary systems extend this capability beyond the previously fixed semantic taxonomies [8, 9, 10]. However, 3DSG hierarchies are strongly domain dependent. Indoor systems are concerned with rooms and floors, while outdoor systems use abstractions such as roads, lanes, terrain, or task-dependent regions [11, 12, 13, 14]. An ASV instead operates through large scale open areas like canals, harbors and open water. Existing outdoor open-vocabulary 3DSGs do not establish which parts of their representation transfer to maritime environments, and which parts require domain-specific adaptations.

We study this transfer using OpenGraph [10], a representative hierarchical open-vocabulary RGB–LiDAR 3DSG designed for large-scale outdoor mapping, as a baseline. We find that for discrete maritime objects with good geometric map support, accumulated OpenGraph descriptions agree with the ground-truth class in 99.1% of cases, while extended and partially hidden waterfront structures are less reliable. Despite this transfer, the resulting mapped object representation shows considerable fragmentation, while its terrestrial higher-level organization assumptions does not provide the spatial structure required for maritime scene understanding. We therefore use the released perception and incremental mapping substrate while contributing a maritime-adapted method for fragment consolidation followed by grounded multi-view vision-language reasoning at the physical-entity and local-place levels. Higher level maritime macro regions are constructed separately from geographic topology and onboard water/structure evidence. Our proposed method is summarized in Fig. 1.

The complete adaptation reduces physical-entity fragmentation while preserving vessel recovery, reducing nodes per recovered vessel from 1.9571.957 to 1.2981.298 and fragmented vessels from 2525 to 1111 in our evaluation. We show that independently constructed local places correspond across traversals despite differences in reconstruction and different object occupants, with 12 reciprocal correspondences across ten evaluated geographic contexts. The resulting contextual representation also improves paired-survey retrieval F1 from 0.3780.378 to 0.8100.810 compared to a local metric baseline.

Our contributions are as follows:

A layer-wise maritime transfer evaluation of an outdoor open-vocabulary 3DSG. We show that semantic descriptions transfer well for geometry-supported discrete objects, while mapped physical-entity consistency and higher-level spatial organization require adaptation.

A layer-wise maritime transfer evaluation of an outdoor open-vocabulary 3DSG. We show that semantic descriptions transfer well for geometry-supported discrete objects, while mapped physical-entity consistency and higher-level spatial organization require adaptation.

A grounded maritime scene-memory construction. We keep the underlying open-vocabulary perception and incremental mapping pipeline, but adapt its accumulated representation through maritime-specific consolidation and grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning to form physical entities and local places. Higher-level maritime context is constructed separately by combining geographic topology with onboard water and structure observations.

An evaluation of persistence and contextual use across repeated maritime surveys. We evaluate physical-entity consistency, cross-traversal local-place correspondence, macro-region repeatability, and contextual retrieval compared to simpler spatial baselines.

title: A computational framework for understanding embodied plans
authors: Aalap D. Shah,Basil Saeed,Joshua B. Tenenbaum,Tobias Gerstenberg,Hyowon Gweon,Ilker Yildirim
abstract: Reasoning about people’s plans and goals based on their actions is fundamental to human social interaction and essential for cooperative, embodied artificial intelligence. Formalizing this capacity in naturalistic, embodied settings has been a longstanding challenge. Here, we present GenEA, a novel agent representation capable of reasoning over multi-step, long-horizon embodied plans. At the heart of GenEA lies a multilevel state-space that couples the coarse biomechanics of an articulated body and its interactions with nearby objects by extending the task-and-motion planning framework from robotics with simulation-based intuitive physics. By embedding this state-space in a generative model, GenEA yields a joint probability distribution over goals and embodied plans. Across several experiments spanning the qualitatively distinct domains of object manipulation and navigation, featuring diverse tasks and multiple behavioral measures, we show that GenEA, through simple transformations of this joint distribution, recapitulates how humans reason about embodied plans. Crucially, GenEA consistently outperforms strong alternative models, including plausible heuristics, standard task-and-motion planning, and a state-of-the-art vision-language model. GenEA thereby offers a new perspective on the architecture of human reasoning and social cognition, suggesting that embodied artificial intelligence systems seeking to seamlessly interact with humans should adopt GenEA-like generative models of action planning.

title: MouldIt: Data Efficiency of Multi-Task Temporal Representation Learning in Injection Moulding
authors: Abdullah Ayad
abstract: Sorting injection moulded parts automatically requires a system that recognizes common defects and also flags defects it has never seen. Defect data are expensive to collect, so engineers need to know how much data such a system requires and whether additional sensors are worth installing. Better sorting raises quality by shipping fewer faulty parts and reduces waste by rejecting fewer good ones, and one model that handles both recognition and flagging avoids maintaining two. We studied these questions on synthetic cycles generated from one recorded cycle of a real part. With only a cavity pressure sensor, random forests with a separate check for unknown defects sort parts best when data are scarce, and our neural network overtakes them only from about 4000 cycles. With a temperature sensor and two ultrasound sensors added, the network sorts best at every dataset size we tested, although the random forests match it at 16000 cycles. These results can guide a first choice of sensors and methods, but do not replace testing on a real line: all cycles derive from one part and one material, the synthetic defect sizes are modeling choices, and about 5% false alarms is high for production. Before deployment, the system should be validated on real defects, and its alarm threshold set by weighing the cost of shipping a faulty part against that of rejecting a good one. The learned representations of the process could also be used for control, not only for sorting.
introduction:
Industrial production has traditionally relied on custom pre-programmed solutions that operate in known and optimized environments with reliability, productivity, and cost reduction as their objectives. Meanwhile, in other domains like language, general-purpose solutions have offered us a different problem-solving perspective. Instead of targeting a single objective, language models aim to understand their data in a way that allows them to address multiple downstream tasks. Inspired by this progress, we expect similar benefits from learning representations of industrial processes.

Learning such representations has to account for the nature of industrial process data, which are generally temporal and usually tabular. Temporal neural network architectures with suitable inductive biases can offer more than the prediction strengths of classical methods like random forests or the encoding strengths of methods like PCA.

Injection moulding is a suitable candidate for evaluating such models, as it is a critical process for most industries, and it typically employs multi-modal data. The process is characterized by static machine setting parameters (MSPs) and dynamic process parameters (PPs), typically recorded on the producing machines. These process parameters are commonly used for tasks such as monitoring for anomaly detection, process optimization, and process control. For fine-grained dynamic information, in-mould sensors are usually installed, such as pressure, temperature, and ultrasound sensors. Ultrasound, for example, can track gap development between the part and the cavity wall, which pressure cannot monitor [1]. The process outputs usually have a number of quality metrics, like weight, size, or specific part deformation labels.

A natural application in this process is automated part sorting, where a decision can go wrong in either direction: good parts are rejected, or faulty parts are shipped. Sorting builds on two tasks, classifying known faults and detecting unknown ones, since a classifier trained on known faults alone can ship a new fault as a good part. A single model that performs both tasks would also avoid maintaining separate models. Automated sorting thus addresses three concerns of production: quality, by keeping faulty parts from shipping; efficiency, by not rejecting good ones; and reliability, by flagging unseen faults.

Naturally, the wide adoption of such models in industry faces barriers. These models are unpredictable and not well understood; therefore, works on explainability, on necessary conditions for those models to excel, and on production metrics may facilitate their adoption.

Data efficiency is among these necessary conditions, since representation learning typically requires large amounts of data to learn the underlying process. This raises four questions: how much data is needed for model performance to saturate; whether incorporating additional modalities can reduce this requirement; whether, at such a saturation point, representation-learning models improve over classical alternatives on production-relevant metrics; and whether their learned representations generalize to unknown failure modes.

Answering these questions requires data that cover many failure modes. However, since representation learning is not yet widely used in this industry, foundational injection moulding datasets are not yet available. Additionally, access to industry-grade simulation software is often proprietary. Synthetic data is thus a practical way to explain and benchmark such models.

We therefore address them on synthetic injection moulding data (Fig. 1), with the following contributions:

an injection moulding data synthesis method requiring a single real sample, inspired by the success of [2] with synthetic training.

a novel multi-objective temporal representation learning model for injection moulding in-mould data (pressure, temperature, and ultrasound).

an analysis of the effect of dataset size and input modalities on model performance across known-class classification and unknown-class detection.

a latent analysis of how MouldIt detects unknown faults.

an evaluation of part sorting losses across the same dataset sizes and input modalities.

title: One Trajectory, Two Requirements: Accuracy and Local Stability in Euler Sampling for Flow Matching Policies
authors: Mahindra Rautela
abstract: Flow matching robot policies commonly use a fixed Euler step count selected from offline accuracy sweeps. At inference time, however, each policy input (visual observation, robot state, and language instruction) together with a source-noise draw defines a different ODE trajectory and sequence of local Jacobians. We ask whether a step count that accurately follows the nominal noise-to-action trajectory can still be too coarse for strongly contracting directions around it. An exact two-coordinate system and a controlled augmentation of six trained flow models show that trajectory accuracy and local Euler stability can impose different step requirements even when the original learned transport is unchanged. We then study a frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5}-LIBERO checkpoint without modifying its weights or action dynamics. Across 30 policy inputs from 10 LIBERO-10 tasks, the Jacobian exhibits strong contracting directions near the action endpoint, yet no sampled mode violates the Euler non-expansion condition. On five of those inputs, accuracy sweeps require 4–9 Euler steps at 5% terminal error and 87–112 at 1%. These five paired cases are therefore consistent with accuracy-limited rather than stability-limited sampling under this local criterion, while the controlled experiments show why endpoint accuracy alone cannot rule out a separate stability requirement.
introduction:
Flow matching policies for robot control.
Flow matching is increasingly used for continuous action generation in robot policies. Recent SOTA vision–language–action (VLA) models such as π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5} use a flow matching action expert to generate action chunks conditioned on visual observations, robot state, and language instructions [1, 12]. Related flow-based policies have also explored reducing the number of sampling steps for faster action generation [20, 4]. Because these policies generate actions by numerically integrating a learned flow, the choice of integration step count becomes part of the inference procedure.

Fixed Euler step budgets.
For flow matching policies, actions are generated by integrating a learned ordinary differential equation (ODE) from source noise to an action. The π0\pi_{0} family, for example, uses a flow matching action expert that maps noise to an action chunk [1, 12]. Each Euler step requires another evaluation of the action expert, so fewer steps directly reduce inference cost. In practice, the step count is often selected by sweeping several values on a fixed evaluation set and choosing one that gives acceptable endpoint accuracy.

At inference time, each policy input (visual observation, robot state, and language instruction) together with the source-noise draw defines a different noise-to-action trajectory. Along this trajectory, the state Jacobian Jv=∂vθ/∂xJ_{v}=\partial v_{\theta}/\partial x describes how nearby states locally contract or expand. Because these local dynamics vary across trajectories, a step count chosen only from offline endpoint-accuracy sweeps may not be sufficient for every inference trajectory.

Accuracy and stability answer different questions.
Trajectory accuracy asks whether the nominal Euler path ends close to a refined numerical solution of the learned ODE. Local stability asks what Euler does to nearby perturbations. At a point on the path, the state Jacobian can contain a direction that the continuous flow contracts rapidly. If the Euler step is too large, that same direction can be amplified instead. A trajectory can therefore be accurate at its endpoint while the local Euler update misrepresents how nearby states should behave. Conversely, a large Jacobian does not automatically force a larger step count: the contraction rate must be compared with the actual timestep used by the sampler.

We ask: for a frozen flow matching policy and a stated numerical tolerance, is the Euler step budget set by trajectory accuracy alone, or can local stability impose an additional requirement?
We study this question in three stages. First, an exact two-coordinate system shows that accuracy and stability can require different Euler budgets. Second, a controlled contraction added to trained flow matching models changes the stability requirement without changing the original learned transport. Third, we derive a grid-aware Euler stability condition and evaluate it on a frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5}-LIBERO checkpoint. Across 30 policy inputs from 10 LIBERO tasks, we find strong local contraction but no sampled stability violation. On five inputs with paired accuracy sweeps, the step budget is instead set by trajectory accuracy under our criterion.

title: PhysMoE: Fast Spatial Grounding with Single-Token Coordinate Representation in Modality-Decoupled VLMs
authors: Ruimeng Liu,Denan Liang,Ruofei Bai,Fuming Zhang,Kuan Xu,Shenghai Yuan,Lihua Xie
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation.
However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets.
To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions:
(1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference;
(2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder’s learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and
(3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders.
Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31×8.31\times throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.
introduction:
Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have emerged as powerful backbones for robotic planning and control [7, 65, 15, 6]. An effective embodied agent must not only understand language instructions and reason over visual scenes, but also ground decisions into fine-grained 2D coordinates—such as identifying grasp contact points, object placement regions, and dynamic manipulation trajectories [59, 30].

Despite rapid advances, existing autoregressive VLMs struggle to balance continuous spatial manipulation with high-level multimodal reasoning due to two fundamental bottlenecks:

1. Fragmented Spatial Tokenization and Modality Interference in Dense Decoders.
Mainstream architectures represent coordinates either as character-level text strings [9, 6] or discrete spatial bin tokens [38]. Under standard VLM sub-word tokenizers, a single coordinate pair such as "[342, 518]" is partitioned into a sequence of isolated character and delimiter tokens (e.g., [, 3, 4, 2, ,, 5, 1, 8, ]). This representation breaks the holistic spatial integrity of pixel positions and imposes an unnecessary representational burden on semantic understanding. Moreover, generating coordinates autoregressively requires 8 to 10 sequential decoding passes per point, severely inflating inference latency and introducing quantization errors. When these disparate tasks are processed through standard dense decoders where all tokens share identical Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs), high-magnitude spatial regression gradients interfere with pre-trained linguistic weights, creating modality conflicts between categorical text generation and geometric modeling.

2. Multi-Peak Affordance Ambiguity.
Physical affordances rarely correspond to an isolated, unique point. For tasks such as grasping a utensil handle or placing a bowl onto a table, multiple contact locations across the object part are equally functional, forming a distinct multi-peak distribution. Conventional point grounding enforces single-point regression (e.g., ℓ1\ell_{1} or ℓ2\ell_{2} distance to an arbitrary center). This formulation is fundamentally mismatched with multi-peak targets: it penalizes the model for predicting any valid contact mode away from the center and often forces the network to regress to a blurred average of multiple modes that lands in invalid physical space. Conversely, full mask prediction models like Qwen3-VL-Seg [57] introduce substantial compute and memory overhead.

To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, an embodied vision-language model featuring three synergistic innovations:
Firstly, we represent a 2D coordinate as a unified token ⟨|x,y|⟩\langle|x,y|\rangle and derive their representations by reusing the pre-trained learned positional embeddings of the visual encoder. This preserves holistic 2D spatial integrity and simplify model training. Secondly, we keep the lower decoder layers fully shared, and in the top KK decoder layers we preserve shared attention across all tokens for unified scene context while routing tokens between a linguistic expert (FFNlang\text{FFN}_{\text{lang}}) and a specialized spatial expert (FFNpix\text{FFN}_{\text{pix}}) paired with decoupled output heads (a continuous coordinate regression head and a discrete LM head for language), resolving modality interference. Thirdly, we formulate a differentiable Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) loss to accommodate multi-peak affordances without auxiliary mask decoders. By sampling continuous coordinates directly from target ESDF maps built from binary masks, our asymmetric loss rewards points falling anywhere inside valid affordance regions while providing steep restorative gradients for exterior predictions.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We encode each 2D coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder’s learned positional embeddings, aligning coordinates with visual features to ease training.

We propose a PhysMoE architecture that shares lower layers while routing the top KK layers to modality-specific linguistic and spatial experts, eliminating gradient interference.

We introduce differentiable ESDF supervision on pointing, accommodating multi-contact affordances and irregular targets without mask decoders.

Across 20 benchmarks, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31×8.31\times speedup on 9 coordinate-based grounding tasks while preserving reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.
